#3138. Trump Asked Grok AI About Invading Venezuela. Democrats Want His Chat History

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

An AI chatbot was consulted about military action, raising questions about security risks, sycophancy and hallucination.

House Democrats are trying to force the White House to turn over President Donald Trump’s conversations with AI chatbots, including when he consulted Elon Musk’s Grok about deposing Venezuela’s former president Nicolás Maduro at the start of the year.

In a joint letter to Trump last week, Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, and Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat, argued that the president’s AI prompts — and the responses he received — should be considered public records under the 1978 Presidential Records Act. Lawmakers also raised ethical and security concerns about the president’s reliance on “unsecured, privately operated AI systems” to carry out foreign policy decisions, alleging that Trump consulted Grok, but not Congress, on military deployment to Venezuela.

According to public reporting cited in the letter, in December 2025, just weeks before ordering the military operation and Maduro’s arrest, Trump spent multiple hours prompting Grok about how Venezuelans would respond to the leader’s capture. Trump reportedly “came away thinking Grok was ingenious.”

Garcia and Raskin argue that Trump’s use of AI “exposes the country to malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties.” A January executive summary of a General Services Administration report, reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, concluded that xAI’s Grok “does not meet the safety and alignment expectations required” for general federal use and may pose a security risk in classified settings.

Using Grok as an informal policy adviser also raises questions over Musk’s political influence over a system he owns and has repeatedly altered to reduce content filters. “If the American President is relying on the policy advice of a Musk-designed, Hitler-friendly chatbot with a predilection for child pornography in order to carry out his official duties, Americans have a right to know,” reads the joint letter (PDF), referring to Grok’s infamous antisemitic episode in 2025 when the chatbot referred to itself as “MechaHitler.”

The letter also refers to the White House’s ongoing use of AI chatbots in military adventures abroad, including in the war with Iran: “If the United States military killed dozens of innocent schoolchildren based on the faulty advice of an AI chatbot, we have a right to know that too.” In June, months after the US military strike on an Iranian elementary school killed at least 123 children, the Pentagon’s artificial intelligence chief said the Grok chatbot’s continued operation was “a matter of paramount national security.”

Reached for comment, the White House referred CNET to the Pentagon, which didn’t immediately respond. Rep. Garcia’s office didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The case for using an AI chatbot for tactical decision-making is usually framed in terms of efficiency. But large language models, or LLMs, are merely probabilistic text generators that can often sound authoritative while producing biased or fabricated information. In a military context, those failure points can end in missile strikes, arrests and civilian deaths.

AI models are also known to amplify existing biases, feeding users with responses that agree with their strongly held beliefs. This sycophancy often leads to answers that mirror those found in an online echo chamber. One journalist found that previous Grok models had “tripled” sycophancy rates compared with popular ChatGPT and Claude models, representing a shift in “behavior that MIT researchers identify as actively harmful.”

In other words, if the president believes he has a brilliant invasion plan, it’s Grok’s modus operandi to serve as a “yes man” and validate that course of action.

Another problem with using an AI chatbot for military decisions is the material on which a model is built. An LLM is a compilation of code that produces contextual responses based on its massive training data — a wealth of information scraped from the internet, including (but not limited to) blog posts, scientific papers, legal documents and code. Grok models, in particular, are also trained on the public interactions from X, a platform infested with bot farms and right-wing engagement bait.

When Trump was prompting Grok in December 2025, officials alleged that the chatbot told the president “that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall.” In the wake of the Venezuelan invasion, X users continued to prompt Grok about the operation, asking if the South American country “deserved” to be bombed.

The other problem is what’s commonly referred to as “hallucination.” LLMs are known to invent outputs if they don’t have the information necessary to respond to a particular prompt. From fabricated cases in legal briefs, phantom citations in government reports and other serious documents bungled by AI, there’s no way to completely prevent false intelligence from trickling through.

Earlier this year, according to reporting cited in the letter, US military officials received an intelligence report alleging that a Chinese vessel in the Middle East was carrying components for a nuclear weapons program. Only as the military prepared to intercept the ship — an action that many say could have escalated into a confrontation with China — did officials discover that the report’s author had relied on an AI chatbot and misidentified the cargo. The error didn’t cause a war, but it revealed how dangerously a fabricated AI output can slip into a military decision chain.

Moreover, if the president or his advisers use a consumer AI product rather than a hardened government system, those chats could be processed by a private company’s infrastructure. Garcia and Raskin have asked the White House to explain whether it restricts classified information from AI chatbots and whether vendors, subcontractors or other external parties can access prompts, outputs, logs or metadata.

Trump’s use of AI in the Venezuela operation would be concerning even if it were isolated. But Garcia and Raskin argue that it fits a broader pattern of AI entering high-stakes government decisions without adequate safeguards.

The Pentagon said in a sworn statement (PDF) that xAI’s latest models enabled US forces to deploy over 2,000 munitions to target 2,000 different locations within 96 hours during Operation Epic Fury, the US campaign against Iran. Grok isn’t the whole story. Palantir’s Maven Smart System, which integrates intelligence from satellites, drones and other sources to identify military targets, reportedly played a central role in the US campaign against Iran. The Defense Department has also awarded contracts worth up to $200 million each to Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI to accelerate military adoption of advanced AI.

Globally, AI systems are being used to make decisions about who lives and who dies. Researchers have regularly pointed to Israel’s indiscriminate bombing of Gaza as a clear example of AI-first warfighting. According to analysis cited by Georgetown Security Studies Review, Israel’s Lavender system marked roughly 37,000 Palestinians as suspected Hamas or Islamic Jihad operatives early in the war, with an estimated error rate of 10%.

The Lavender system “dramatically expanded” Israel’s kill list by relying on signals such as communication patterns and group-chat membership, producing misidentifications that included Palestinian police, aid workers, relatives of militants and people with similar names or nicknames. A related Israeli system, “Where’s Daddy?” tracked marked Palestinians and alerted the military when they entered their homes, striking multiple private family residences.

While the political shock of an AI chatbot influencing military strategy dominates the headlines, the real battleground is legal. Demanding that President Trump’s AI chatbot prompts and outputs be marked as official government property under the Presidential Records Act would turn AI conversations into public records, opening the door for Congress to subpoena the executive branch. Raskin and Garcia are requesting a full description of the president’s personal use of the technology and a closed-door briefing by Nov. 11 to review the administration’s AI protocols and cybersecurity safeguards.

Regardless of how the legal side shakes out, the question is no longer whether AI will be used in war, but whether the public will be allowed to see where AI begins and human responsibility ends.

#3137. Here's how to adjust Apple AirPods for small ears

Adjusting AirPods for smaller ears improves the user experience, but may require external accessories.

Your ears are as unique as your fingerprint, with very little chance that two people share the same ear shape. In fact, sometimes even your own two ears aren't the same shape, and might require a different ear tip size in each ear. AirPods users in particular should seek the best available fit, because a tight fit will help you get the most out of them. A good fit optimizes music playback, bass and noise cancellation performance, while a poor fit means you'll experience more external noise and a higher chance of your AirPods falling out during workouts.

Apple currently sells two different AirPods models: AirPods 5, which are solid earbuds without ear tips, and AirPods Pro 3, which offer active noise cancellation (not the same as passive noise cancellation) and come with ear tips in multiple sizes. Of course, when trying to decide on the best wireless earbuds to buy, it's better to choose a set that fits your ears best, even if they're not made by Apple. However, if you have your heart set on AirPods, there are ways to adjust the fit and improve performance.

With AirPods that have no ear tips, getting the best fit is limited to pushing them into your ears and rotating the stem toward your face until they lock in place. People with small ear canals may find it difficult to get the tight fit they need, and if that's the case, these might not be the best AirPods option for you. However, there are third-party AirPods hooks which loop around your ear to hold the earbuds in place from manufacturers such as KeyBudz and AhaStyle. These cost between $10 and $15. Ultimately, some users may achieve a better fit by upgrading to AirPods Pro.

AirPods Pro offer ear tips in three to five sizes, depending on the model: the first generation has S, M and L; the second generation has XS, S, M and L; and the third generation has XXS, XS, S, M and L. Out of the box, you'll find the medium-sized ear tips installed by default, but you should try other sizes to find the tight fit you need.

Remove the current tip by pulling it firmly away from the connector until it snaps off. Align your new tip to the oval base and push until it clicks in place. Try using different sizes in each ear — it's not unusual to need a small tip in one ear and a medium tip in the other, for example. You can check the seal to make sure you have the appropriate tips by playing bass-heavy music or using Apple's ear tip test.

Apple has built an Acoustic Seal Test (an earlier test called Ear Tip Fit Test is available on AirPods Pro 1 or 2) to help you find the best-fitting ear tip. To use it, put your AirPods Pro in your ears, open Settings > [Your AirPods] > Test Acoustic Seal or Ear Tip Fit Test, tap Continue, then Play. You'll hear a little music, and the test results will tell you if you have a Good Seal or if you need to Adjust or Try a Different Size.

Most AirPods Pro ship with ear tips made of silicone, which, if treated correctly, should last as long as the earbuds. The snag is that some people find they aren't as comfortable or snug-fitting as foam ear tips. Apple has introduced foam-infused tips with AirPods Pro 3, but pure foam tips may still work better for some.

Typically, soft, pliable foam ear tips are compressed before you put them in your ear. Once in place, they expand with your body heat to mold tightly — and comfortably — in your ear canal. The tight seal can help get a good fit even with smaller ears. The drawback is that foam ear tips must be replaced more frequently.

Third-party manufacturers, including Comply and Foam Masters, sell foam ear tips for AirPods Pro for between $25 and $30 per set. When purchasing them, please note that Apple redesigned the ear tip connector used in third-generation AirPods Pro, so make sure you choose tips that are compatible with your model.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Some of the biggest names in travel are turning to “practical AI” to simplify trip booking and planning.

Between Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s, it’s the time of year when your luggage stays packed. With millions of Americans planning to travel sometime between now and the end of the year, it’s time to start thinking about how to make the most of your trip.

Right on time, Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo just rolled out more than 30 new travel features. Expedia Group, which owns all three brands, said the goal is to make trip planning and execution easier with practical AI.

“Travel is a series of decisions, and travelers want the joy of discovery and planning to last through every stage of the journey,” Shilpa Ranganathan, chief product officer at Expedia Group, said. “That’s why we’re building AI-powered experiences across our brands that help travelers make informed decisions, give them flexibility and value, and personalize every step of their trip. And when travelers need a person, our human agents step in with the full context to make things right.”

Here’s what’s new from each travel brand.

Expedia says it’s introducing a more personal homepage, flexible travel packages, more straightforward bookings for families, interactive maps of your travel destination for easier planning and expanded airport perks like Clear Plus discounts and free lounge access for flight delays.

Two new AI-powered products are also rolling out to make trip planning smoother once a trip is already booked. Expedia’s new Activity Planner is an AI-powered conversational shopping assistant that can find and book activities, restaurants and events based on your itinerary. You can also receive tailored recommendations based on your preferences.

Another is a Property Expert, which lets you ask questions about a business and get AI-generated insights on the property, reviews, reservations and other details.

The platform is improving its AI Compare experience to help you compare multiple hotels in one place. The comparisons are personalized to your interests and preferences for location, amenities, price and policy details.

The Hotels.com homepage will also adapt to the type of trip you booked, such as a vacation or work trip, and include suggested links tailored to your booking, like options to extend your stay and access to receipts for easier work-trip expenses.

The Airbnb rival is launching several new features and services, including a tool to make group bookings easier to manage, an option to reserve now, pay later, and enhanced customer support.

With Vrbo’s natural language search, you can describe in plain language what kind of rental property you’re looking for. Rather than spending hours researching options one by one, you can simply say you’re looking for a beachfront home in South Florida with a kitchen and outdoor gathering space that’s dog-friendly. The enhanced search feature allows you to narrow down your options without relying on traditional filters.

Vrbo’s Arrival Experience is getting an upgrade to make your rental details more accessible. Key property information, such as check-in and checkout times, door codes, directions and house rules, will now be aggregated in one place, so you can stay on top of your booking without searching through multiple emails or messages.

For more holiday travel tips, explore the 12 travel essentials you always need to pack and the worst airlines for flight delays and cancellations. You can also reference this travel checklist for smarter travel.

September was also an all-time monthly record, so we are very happy with that. So, September was very strong, and we started off Q4 on plan. So, October was extremely solid. An important point is, sequentially, we also grew from Q2. So, very pleased with the orders, very pleased with the order momentum.

Both EIG and EMG happen to be up 17% organically, so it is rock solid.

Nicole DeBlase: That's great to hear. Thanks, Dave. I will pass it on.

Dalip Puri: Matt, you mentioned year one synergies.

Dalip Puri: As indicated when we announced the Indicor acquisition, I guess it was about six weeks ago, seven weeks ago. We talked about 10%-12% being our synergy target. That is over three years, and we are going to track probably from your perspective, think about that cadence as being ratable.

The results speak to the highly differentiated nature of the AMETEK product portfolio, and we got leadership positions in these niche markets around the globe. Andy Kaplowitz: Yeah, that's helpful. Your power-focused business continues to be in that mid-single digit growth area. I know, Dave, you said it could grow faster. Does it start to grow faster in 2027, or maybe why isn't it growing a bit faster now?

Dave Zapico: I think our M&A team is doing an excellent job, Chris. I think we have some of the best people in the industry. We have a dedicated team. We have a dedicated investment of 12 M&A professionals. They work closely with our businesses and our operators to identify strategic acquisitions. They own our process. The acquisitions at AMETEK are a combination of a set of well-defined processes. They are not a single event. Dave Zapico: Yeah, I think we had an excellent quarter in terms of margins. In EMG, the core margins were up 210 basis points, and it was driven by excellent productivity and very solid positive price inflation, price cost. So, that drove it. We had a similar performance in EIG. We had good productivity, and we had good price cost. One of the things that I look at are always the incrementals.

#3133. NVIDIA's controversial DLSS 5 is coming to RTX Remix to 'enhance' older games

The NVIDIA modding platform lets you remaster classic games with modern graphics.

In case you've been hibernating under a boulder for the past six months, you probably know that the internet utterly hates DLSS 5 with a flaming passion. NVIDIA's DLSS 5 launched with NBA 2K27, and people really aren't feeling Team Green's latest tech breakthrough. Not that public opinion is overly swaying the company that loves to champion AI/occasional GPU manufacturer's passion for Neural Rendering techniques.

With DLSS 5 now hitting its RTX Remix software, NVIDIA clearly wants modders to start injecting the tech into older games. Is this a good thing? The internet would tell you that it alters the original artistic intent of a game to a wholly objectionable degree. As a reluctant defender of DLSS 5, I can see both sides. Let's get into the latest DLSS 5 announcements, before breaking down how you can install it into almost any game through third-party apps, and the performance price you can expect to pay once it's enabled.

NVIDIA's RTX Remix tool has been available for free since early 2024. This modding platform allows users/programmers to add ray tracing and AI-upscaled textures to older titles, and DLSS 5 is being added to this software on October 23. Before that on October 16, the technology is coming to RTX Spark, Team Green's new SoC (system-on-a-chip). We've found RTX Spark is good for Windows, even if you don't need local AI.

The tech, which radically alters in-game character lighting, will also be officially added to Hogwarts Legacy on November 5. From the screens that NVIDIA have shown off so far, DLSS 5 seems to have been toned down slightly, with the students within those wizarding walls no longer looking quite as yassified as they were in the initial reveal footage.

Whether DLSS coming to RTX Remix and RTX Spark is actually a good thing is an entirely different matter. Unlike every previous generation of DLSS, it negatively impacts frame rates, it doesn't boost them. If you're curious about the tech, but don't want to wait for NVIDIA to officially inject the tech into some of your favorite games, there's an easy way you can get DLSS 5 working in pretty much any game.

Thanks to an early build of NBA 2K27 being leaked, modders quickly gained access to DLSS 5's Neural Rendering, and now community built apps let you inject the tech into almost any PC game (providing you own an NVIDIA RTX GPU). Software like DLSS 5 Manager and DLSS 5 Swapper allow you to insert advanced lighting techniques into all manner of Vulkan and DirectX titles (with the latter spanning DX9, DX10, DX11 and DX12 generations). I've been using DLSS 5 Swapper for a little while now, and although the neural rendered results are obviously going to be subjective, at least this app is a doddle to use.

Installation is a breeze. Once you download and install the software from the link above, it will automatically scan your drives and game libraries for titles it can inject DLSS 5 into. After you select a game you want to insert Neural Rendering into, simply click "Install DLSS 5" and the necessary DLL files and Reshade will be installed within a few seconds. DLSS 5 Swapper instantly detects the correct rendering API, so there's really no work for you to do. And if you don't like the results, a simple click of "Restore originals" will remove the NR files and restore the game to its original state.

One word of caution: DLSS 5 mods generally don't play nicely with games that use anti-cheat software. As much as I wanted to see DLSS 5 injected into GTA V: Enhanced Edition, the mandatory BattlEye software required to run the Los Santos classic prevented the game from launching. Once NVIDIA starts officially supporting DLSS 5 in more games, I'd imagine this current anti-cheat roadblock will become a non-issue.

DLSS 5 has been met with all the enthusiasm of a vegan turning up to an all-you–can-eat panda buffet. But why is the internet so upset about NVIDIA's DLSS 5? Many gamers feel that rather than adding greater visual fidelity, the technology is fundamentally betraying the artistic integrity of titles. Now that the mods mentioned above allow you to get DLSS 5 working in pretty much any game, the lighting in thousands of titles can be drastically altered at the touch of a button.

I totally get the vitriol aimed at DLSS 5. I really do. Slashing performance by 50 percent or more in certain games, it's incredibly expensive to run. All the talk about its 3D-Guided Neural Rendering being nothing more than an AI slop-inspired beauty filter has dominated online debates since NVIDIA first revealed the tech. While I understand this criticism, I've actually had a pretty good time messing around with DLSS 5.

I've mainly used Team Green's new tech in Cyberpunk 2077, Control, and the Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3 remakes. In all four of these games I honestly prefer the overall look when DLSS 5 is enabled. Put away your pitchforks, please! In Remedy's 2019 action-adventure, the tech has a transformative effect on Jesse Faden's face, as it does with the mugs of Leon and Claire in Resi 2 and Jill Valentine in Resi 3.

While DLSS 5 can have a huge impact on characters, changes to overly lightning are relatively minimal based on my testing. Shadows perhaps looking a little deeper, but the changes to the look of environments is pretty subtle. For that reason, considering the hefty hit DLSS 5 normally causes, I suggest you only enable it in games where you're regularly seeing your character's face.

When the first third-party DLSS 5 apps launched, the performance hit was pretty brutal. 30-60 percent FPS drops were the order of the day once Neural Rendering was enabled through Reshade. Thankfully, a recent update has boosted performance in NBA 2K27 (as reported by PC Gamer), with frame rates "merely" dropping 25 percent at 1440p.

After installing the update via an NVIDIA app beta driver, I've definitely seen performance boosts in several games I've be using DLSS 5 in. In Control at 4K and with max settings enabled, I went from around 80 FPS with DLSS 5 enabled to close to 100 FPS. For context, I am privileged enough to be playing games on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 (my bank balance hates me). With the recent remaster of Metal Gear Solid 4, I'd drop to sub 55 FPS levels before the update at 4K, but now I can squeak out an average performance of 70 FPS. Without DLSS 5 in either of those games? I'd comfortably be well north of 120 FPS.

DLSS 5 is clearly still punishing to run. Unless you own (at least) an RTX 5070 or AMD Radeon RX 9070, there's no way you should enable this burgeoning tech. Considering the lighting effects are so divisive and GPU-intensive, NVIDIA's Neural Rendering is likely going to remain a feature only the most hardcore PC gamers with cutting edge rigs can comfortably run. I like DLSS 5 more than most, but the yassification factor isn't worth buying a new graphics card for.

#3132. California fights "preposterous" Trump admin demand to scrap state broadband laws

State tries to obtain broadband funds despite rejecting Trump admin condition.

California is accepting $1.86 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration’s demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations.

California’s stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds.

The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction.

State officials argue that California should be able to obtain the money and keep enforcing its laws because the Trump administration’s demand would violate the state’s constitutional rights. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) made its view clear in a carefully worded letter yesterday to Assistant Secretary of Commerce and NTIA Administrator Arielle Roth.

“The CPUC cannot be bound by any terms or conditions that are unconstitutional or not authorized by law and it expressly does not waive or concede any arguments or challenges concerning the legality, interpretation, or applicability of any term or condition,” CPUC President John Reynolds told Roth.

Reynolds’ letter also said the CPUC cannot prevent other California agencies from enforcing state laws, suggesting that the attorney general would maintain the right to punish misbehaving Internet providers.

Reynolds’ letter acknowledged that the NTIA may not agree with the CPUC’s stance and said the state thus will not distribute any funding to ISPs until after the state and federal agency sort out any differences. If the NTIA refuses to change its position, California could sue the Trump administration on the grounds that the condition is unconstitutional.

The NTIA does not appear likely to bend. “As noted in the Department’s response to CPUC, the terms and conditions of the award constitute the entire agreement between NTIA and CPUC. No part of the letter outlining CPUC’s concerns is incorporated into or made part of the award,” an NTIA spokesperson told Ars today.

Consumer advocacy group Public Knowledge supported CPUC’s position. The Trump administration’s demand to preempt state laws is “brazen and meritless,” the group said.

The CPUC voted to ratify the funding plan in September. But Reynolds said in yesterday’s letter to the Trump administration that his agency’s acceptance of the funds is “based on the CPUC’s best understanding of the effect of Section 50” of the BEAD terms and conditions. Section 50 of the BEAD rules says each state:

shall commit that it will not enforce any law, regulation, order, contracting requirement, or other enforceable obligation that directly or indirectly regulates the rates, terms, and conditions of broadband Internet service… or imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules on broadband Internet service, against a Subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service within the State (i.e., both BEAD and non-BEAD locations), while that Subgrantee has any subgrant that is still within its period of performance, extended period of performance, or federal interest period.

The BEAD rules specify that a net neutrality rule is one prohibiting ISPs from “blocking content, throttling speeds, imposing data caps, or engaging in paid prioritization.” ISPs obtaining BEAD funding could be exempt from such laws for up to 14 years.

Reynolds’ letter said the NTIA-imposed condition is “vague and ambiguous as to its scope and its relationship to Section 47 U.S.C. § 1702(g)(2)(A)(i) of the BEAD statute,” the US law that created the BEAD program. He wrote:

The CPUC does not interpret Section 50 to require the CPUC to waive, release, or otherwise forfeit any rights, claims, arguments, or defenses concerning potential implications of Section 50 that may violate applicable laws. Further, the CPUC’s acceptance of funds under this award should not be understood as agreement either to refrain from compliance with mandatory legal duties or obligations, or to constrain other State of California entities in the exercise of their authorities to enforce state law, which is outside the scope of the CPUC’s authority. Moreover, California’s net neutrality law expressly provides that “any waiver of the provisions of this title is contrary to public policy and shall be unenforceable and void.” Likewise, many of the CPUC’s own programs that touch on broadband Internet access service are mandated by the California Public Utilities Code, and are neither discretionary nor waivable.

The NTIA today updated its BEAD progress dashboard to reflect that California has signed its final agreement with the federal agency. California was the last state or territory to turn in its final agreement.

“All 56 states and territories have signed and returned their award agreement, finalizing the process,” the NTIA’s updated dashboard page said.

California could face legal problems if and when it distributes the money, which is to be given to Internet service providers in exchange for deploying broadband in unserved and underserved areas. ISPs could insist that they don’t have to follow state law and sue California, or simply decide to violate consumer protection laws and defend against any lawsuits the state attorney general might file against them.

Reynolds apparently hopes to avoid that outcome by holding discussions with the NTIA to resolve any disagreement over the enforceability of California state law.

“To the extent that NTIA and the CPUC disagree about the CPUC’s obligations under Section 50 and other terms and conditions, the CPUC will execute any subgrant agreements if and when the CPUC and NTIA are able to resolve such disagreements and any other applicable conditions are met,” Reynolds wrote. “To that end, we will direct our staff to work diligently and cooperatively with NTIA staff to find such a solution.”

Whether California’s strategy works “depends on what happens next,” Stanford Law professor Barbara van Schewick, a longtime proponent of net neutrality and other telecom regulations, told Ars today.

“The letter doesn’t change the terms of California’s award: Condition 50 is still in it, and only a court or NTIA agreeing in writing can take it out,” she said. “The letter puts California’s position on the record before any contracts with providers are signed and preserves California’s legal arguments against Condition 50.”

Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office declined to comment when contacted by Ars today. A spokesperson for California Gov. Gavin Newsom said California is not giving up its right to enforce state laws against Internet providers.

“California is accepting federal broadband funding to bring high-speed Internet to hundreds of thousands of homes and businesses, many of them in rural and underserved communities,” a governor’s spokesperson said in a statement provided to Ars. “We’re ready to get these projects built with our local and federal partners. Connecting these communities is the goal, and so is protecting them. California’s laws, including our net neutrality protections, still stand.”

California’s net neutrality law prohibits ISPs from blocking or throttling lawful traffic and says ISPs may not require fees from websites or online services to deliver or prioritize their traffic to Internet users. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws, and California defeated ISPs that challenged the state law in court.

California also has a law that prohibits mobile providers from throttling first responders during emergencies. That law was passed in 2019, a year after Verizon throttled an “unlimited” data plan used by Santa Clara County firefighters during a wildfire. Local wildfire-preparedness groups warned that the BEAD condition could prevent California from enforcing the throttling law and requirements for battery backups on cell towers.

According to van Schewick, “California has strong arguments that Condition 50 is illegal. Congress designed BEAD to get broadband built while making sure the providers who take the money follow the law: the statute directs states to ensure funded providers can carry out their work ‘in compliance with all applicable Federal, State, and local laws.’”

But van Schewick said the letter is just an initial step. “The real test comes the first time a BEAD provider blocks a competitor’s app, throttles firefighters, or walks away from a price commitment,” she said. “If the state enforces its laws when that happens, the letter will have protected Californians. If the state looks the other way, Condition 50 will have worked exactly as the providers intended, without a single court ever ruling on it.”

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#3131. Arvinas (ARVN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management maps 2027 readouts across BCL6, polyQ-AR and HPK1 programs.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Arvinas, Inc. (ARVN -5.72%) reported its third quarter 2026 financial results, highlighting a strategic shift toward prioritizing capital for clinical programs with the highest potential for value creation. Management reported a disciplined expense profile, with total non-GAAP spending decreasing 25% year over year, while maintaining a cash runway extending into the second half of 2028. The company is advancing a diverse pipeline of PROTAC protein degraders across oncology and neurology, with four distinct programs moving through Phase I clinical trials. The company stated that it is entering a period of significant clinical milestones, including multiple data readouts scheduled for 2027 across its BCL6, polyQ-AR, and HPK1 programs.

Joining us on the call today, we have Randy Teel, our President and CEO, Angela Cacace, our Chief Scientific Officer, and Andrew Saik, our Chief Financial Officer. These risks and uncertainties are outlined in today's press release and in the company's recent filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which I urge you to read.

Our actual results may differ materially from what is discussed on today's call. A replay of this call, as well as today's press release and an updated corporate deck, will be available on the investor and media section of our website. Now I will turn the call over to Randy Teel. Randy?

Randy Teel: Thanks, Jeff, and good morning, everyone. I will start by reiterating our commitment to prioritizing investments in programs where emerging evidence supports the greatest potential for value creation, letting the data drive our capital allocation decisions. If we execute on that commitment, we believe Arvinas can create important medicines for patients and significant long-term value for shareholders. We are entering an important period of clinical milestones that we believe will further define both our individual programs and the broader potential of our platform. During the call, I will provide an overview of our portfolio and plans. Angela will share additional information on our clinical programs, and Andrew will give an overview of our finances and approach to capital allocation.

I will begin with ARV-393, our oral BCL6 de grader, and a great example of a program with strong scientific rationale for differentiation. BCL6 is a key driver of lymphoma biology, and we believe our ability to degrade this classically undruggable transcription factor could offer a differentiated approach to treating B and T-cell lymphomas. We see the potential for our BCL6 de grader to become a backbone of future treatment strategies as both a monotherapy and in combination with standards of care. This could include reducing, delaying, or sparing chemotherapy for patients.

During the quarter, as we continued enrolling the monotherapy and combination cohorts of our phase I trial, we submitted our initial monotherapy dose escalation data for presentation at the ASH Conference in December. This will be the first of two data readouts for the program, with the second readout expected in mid-2027. The first disclosure will focus on patients with T-cell lymphomas, where there are limited treatment options available. These data support our belief that ARV-393 is an active de grader of BCL6, with the potential to be very competitive as we continue development.

The data we share in 2027 will include a greater proportion of patients dosed at levels expected to reach efficacious exposures in B-cell lymphomas, more robust data on durability, and initial data from the combination with glofitamab, the first of our planned combination cohorts. I'll move next to ARV-027, our first-in-class oral androgen receptor de grader targeting the root cause of spinal bulbar muscular atrophy, or SBMA, also known as Kennedy's disease. This de grader targets the polyglutamine repeat androgen receptor, or polyQ AR, which is found in patients with this genetically defined disease. SBMA is an X-linked disease where the polyQ AR aggregates and gains a toxic function, driving progressive muscle weakness and functional decline.

By eliminating the toxic accumulation of polyQ AR in muscle, we have the potential to create the first-ever disease-modifying therapy for patients with this rare neuromuscular disease. The SBMA program is advancing through multiple dose cohorts in its phase I trial, and we intend to share initial data from the healthy volunteer cohorts in the first half of 2027. We also intend to begin dosing patients with SBMA in the first half of 2027. If successful, we believe the phase I data for this program will significantly de-risk the program, and we will begin discussions with health authorities about initiating a registration-enabling trial. I'll turn next to our first immuno-oncology de grader, ARV-6723.

By impacting the immune system beyond the ability of current IO therapies, we believe this first-in-class oral HPK1 de grader could become an important treatment for patients in 3 distinct ways. First, following a checkpoint inhibitor. Second, in combination with a checkpoint inhibitor. And third, in indications where checkpoint inhibitors have not shown benefit. Based on promising monotherapy and combination preclinical data, we initiated a phase I trial in the third quarter. Monotherapy dose escalation is ongoing, and we plan to initiate dosing in combination with pembrolizumab in the first half of 2027.

HPK1 is a protein that dampens multiple parts of the cancer immunity cascade, and we believe that by removing it, our de grader has the potential to harness the body's natural tumor immunity to fight cancer. We look forward to providing initial data from this program in the second half of 2027. Rounding out our clinical progress, I'll next provide a brief update on current plans for our LRRK2 de grader, ARV-102. Following scientific advice from CHMP, we're now prioritizing the initiation of a phase I-B trial in the E.U. and the U.K. Next month, we plan to submit clinical trial applications for a phase I-B trial in patients with progressive supranuclear palsy, or PSP.

Trial initiation is targeted for 2027. In parallel, we are in consultation with Japanese health authorities to inform potential development in Japan as part of a long-term global clinical strategy. In the U.S., we continue discussions with the FDA about the ongoing clinical hold of our IND. Our current objective is now to include U.S. sites in future trials after completing the phase I-B trial in the E.U. and the U.K. Last month, we reported additional and novel biomarker findings from our phase I trial, including improvements in an objective and quantifiable measure of impaired eye movement associated with Parkinson's disease.

The totality of evidence from our phase I trial strengthens our belief in the potential of LRRK2 degradation to create novel clinical breakthroughs for patients with devastating neurodegenerative diseases. What is common across all of our programs is the scientific premise that by degrading the proteins that cause disease, we can create transformational treatments to address unmet patient need. We are pursuing targets where removing the protein has the potential to change the treatment landscape and improve outcomes for patients. The progress we are making today is laying the foundation for the next wave of innovation at Arvinas and advancing our mission of delivering transformative medicines to patients. With that, I will turn the call over to Angela. Angela?

Angela Cacace: Thank you, Randy. As we approach key pipeline milestones, I will highlight how our preclinical data support our differentiated science, inform clinical development, and position our portfolio to deliver value. Starting with ARV-393, our strategy is to establish its potential both as a single agent and in combinations that could expand treatment options for patients with lymphoma. We have shown strong single-agent activity in preclinical DLBCL models with enhanced activity, including complete tumor regressions when combined with chemotherapy, biologics, and investigational oral agents. The results with R-CHOP and bispecific antibodies support the combination strategy we are advancing in the clinic.

The first phase I disclosure will provide an early look at safety and tolerability, drug exposure, target engagement, and anti-tumor activity. These initial cohorts were treated at doses below those predicted to be efficacious in preclinical DLBCL models. Even at these early dose levels, we have observed responses across NHL subtypes, including B and T-cell lymphomas. The disclosure will focus on safety, PK, and PD from all patients, and preliminary efficacy from early cohorts in patients with T-cell lymphoma, where treatment options remain limited. These data will help guide dose selection and expansion plans.

Our next update, expected in mid-2027, will include more patients with B-cell lymphoma treated at doses in the predicted efficacious range with longer follow-up, along with initial combination data with glofitamab. Turning to our polyQ AR de grader, ARV-027, our phase I study is designed to establish safety and tolerability and determine whether the drug degrades the androgen receptor in skeletal muscle. Importantly, we are seeing profound preclinical activity in muscle strength and endurance, two of the most fundamental manifestations of SBMA disease progression. In an aggressive mouse model of SBMA, ARV-027 induced polyQ-AR degradation in muscle, and we are excited by the data showing rescue of muscle strength, endurance, and survival.

Our therapeutic goal builds on the internal data and literature evidence showing that approximately 50% reduction in polyQ-AR in muscle improved mouse model strength and restored treadmill endurance. We believe that the forthcoming multiple ascending dose data in healthy volunteers and patients with SBMA will help determine whether ARV-027 produces the biologic effects needed to support the advancement of ARV-027 into a registrational trial. These results, together with chronic toxicology data and regulatory interactions, will guide dose selection and our SBMA clinical trial design. We look forward to sharing initial data from our phase I trial in the first half of 2027.

Now, let's turn to our first-in-class immuno-oncology asset, ARV-6723, our oral HPK1 de grader, now in a first-in-human phase I trial. By removing HPK1, we aim to eliminate both its kinase and scaffolding functions to release the brakes on innate and adaptive immunity more fully than kinase inhibition alone. Specifically, our preclinical data demonstrates three compelling findings. First, robust single-agent anti-tumor activity across seven checkpoint-resistant models, where a clinical HPK1 inhibitor and checkpoint therapies showed no activity. Second, complete tumor regressions with anti-PD-1 combination treatment. Third, intratumoral immune effects extending beyond T-cell activation, including enhanced interferon signaling and remodeling the myeloid compartment.

This broader remodeling of the tumor microenvironment may help explain oral ARV-6723's differentiated activity and its potential to address tumors that respond poorly to current immunotherapies. Later this week at the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer annual meeting, we will present additional preclinical data reinforcing this differentiation and supporting our monotherapy and combination development strategy. Our phase I monotherapy trial will assess safety, drug exposure, HPK1 degradation, and biologic effects in tumors. Measures of immune activation, including NK and T-cell activation, will enable us to translate the promising preclinical biology to patients and further guide clinical development.

Moving to ARV-102, one of the central goals of the program has been to establish a comprehensive understanding of how LRRK2 degradation affects biologically relevant pathways associated with neurodegenerative disease. The phase I data presented at MDS Congress last month expanded our biomarker evaluation and further informed our understanding of the molecule's pharmacology. The data showed ARV-102 achieved brain penetration and retained its potent and deep reduction of LRRK2 in the cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, of patients with Parkinson's disease. ARV-102 also reduces endolysosomal and neuroinflammatory markers in the CSF that have been shown to be elevated in neurodegenerative diseases. Importantly, we presented novel data showing improvements in an objective measure of impaired eye movement associated with Parkinson's disease.

The data showed that reductions in LRRK2 and CSF after treatment with ARV-102 is correlated with changes in ocular motor function and in synaptic biomarkers associated with enhanced plasticity and cognitive resilience. These findings strengthen our confidence in ARV-102's potential to advance treatment for neurologic diseases such as Parkinson's disease and progressive supranuclear palsy. As we continue development, we are building on these results with biomarkers and functional measures to connect target degradation with downstream biologic effects and potential patient benefits. In closing, we are excited about the potential of each of these programs, with key data insights providing evidence to guide their advancement. We look forward to sharing our progress over the next several quarters.

Tolerability will be really important, especially for a program like this that over time, the development plan will include both monotherapy and combinations. We have also disclosed that we began dosing at quite low doses, well below exposures that we would expect to be efficacious. We want to see good degradation of BCL6. This is a transcription factor that is rapidly resynthesized, so need to see solid degradation of BCL6. On the efficacy front, we are going to focus the first disclosure on T-cell patients. If you are a second-line plus patient with nTFHL right now, you are getting something like a 35% to 45% response rate with drugs that are on the market now. Despite there being no specifically approved therapies for second-line T-cell patients like this, which is actually a good reminder of the unmet need in this space.

With therapies on the market getting something like 35% to 45% in a first-dose escalation study with low doses like we are in now, we and the investigators would be pretty excited with anything over really a 30% response rate. Certainly would look for that to go higher as we dose higher, but in an early setting like this with most patients dosed at doses below where we were expecting efficacy, that would be a reasonable bar to set. Hope that helps, Yigal.

Yigal Nochomovitz: Yeah. No, thank you. That is very helpful. Thanks.

Operator: Your next question will be coming from the line of Jonathan Miller of Evercore ISI. Your line is open.

Jonathan Miller: Hi, guys. Thanks so much for taking the question, and congrats on the progress. I will follow up on Yigal's question on ASH. So, that is where we believe that if we take the patients that we have now, and you cut down the end by the number of patients that are dosed at a level that you would expect efficacy with various indications, with response-evaluable capabilities or factors, that number gets to be pretty small. So, I think that there could be some transferability, but it will be more informative to wait till we show the data in B-cell patients, where you can really get a good sense with more patients, higher doses, more durability.

Jonathan Miller: Great. Thank you so much for that. If I can sneak in one more on LRRK2, I was wondering if we could talk more medium to long-term about how this phase I-B in E.U. and U.K. is going to translate to potential registrational paradigms. What is your updated thought on timeline to getting into registration?

Randy Teel: Yeah. Good question. Thanks. The thinking now, John, you will remember that we had maybe a year ago talked about the potential for two trials, a phase I-B in the U.S. and a more global registrational trial. What that is folding into now is a phase I-B trial first that, as we said, will be in Europe, and then look to move to registration after that. It is a little early to give too much in terms of specifics for that trial, but we will want to be dosing patients with PSP now for a longer time period. A reminder that we had dosed in the healthy volunteer and PD patients only for 28 days.

This would be longer and enough time to get a good sense of safety, PK/PD as always, and also perhaps some efficacy-oriented endpoints as well, where the goal of that phase I-B trial is to get the confidence to move into a registrational trial that is larger and later on. That is how it plays out now. Going back to the remarks we made on the call, there could be an opportunity at that point to make it a more global development program, potentially including Japan and the U.S. and other geographies.

But we will need to get through the phase I-B trial first, and as we said on the call, we will look to start that trial in 2027 after getting through the CTA process in the E.U. and the U.K.

Operator: Our next question will be coming from the line of Nick Lorusso of TD Cowen. Your line is open, Nick.

Nick Lorusso: Hey, guys. Thanks very much for taking our question. Moving back to 393 again. You provided the bars for the early data at ASH, which was very helpful. Moving into BCL6 after the early success with AR and ER was an opportunity to show what a de grader can do in a space where no programs for BCL6 had moved into the clinic. So, the question of what does good look like for BCL6 is starting to get answered by our competitors in the space already, which is great news because it shows that the target we picked a while ago had some efficacy. With respect to what does good actually look like, that bar is going to get set, right? Angela Cacace: And then just to add to what Randy said, the strong B-cell combination rationale also is due to the enhanced CD20 expression that we see, where we would expect to see enhanced combinability with rituximab, so R-CHOP, and then also the bispecifics like glofitamab. #3128. How CISOs Can Set Guardrails On AI Agents Without Killing Adoption

Nidhi Jain is CEO & Founder of CloudEagle.ai, an AI governance platform that secures AI agents, machine identities, and SaaS access.

In July 2026, the U.K.’s AI Security Institute disclosed that AI agents under evaluation had taken sustained, unsanctioned action against real people and organizations. In the most serious case, an agent researched the maintainers of a public open-source project on GitHub, created multiple fake identities and attempted to socially engineer a maintainer into approving a malicious pull request. The maintainer rejected the code. AISI detected unusual network traffic on July 28 and contained the incident within an hour of the alert.

Many enterprises deploying Salesforce Agentforce, Microsoft Copilot Studio, ServiceNow Now Assist, Google Vertex AI Agents and AWS Bedrock lack these safeguards.

Gartner predicts that 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025. The Cloud Security Alliance found that 65% of enterprises have already experienced an AI agent-related security incident, and 82% have unknown AI agents running in their environment.

Blocking is not the answer. The question is what guardrails let adoption and security coexist.​

In almost every conversation I have with a CISO rolling out agents, the same assumption shows up: Governance is a Phase 2 problem. Deploy first; govern later. The CSA data shows what Phase 2 actually looks like.

AI agents break traditional access models in three ways:

• They inherit the deploying user’s permissions instead of their own scoped identity. A Salesforce Agentforce agent built by a sales ops lead inherits the sales ops lead’s full access. The agent runs with permissions it never needed.

• They act across systems through delegated OAuth. A ServiceNow Now Assist agent connected to Jira, Confluence and Slack holds OAuth tokens to all three. One compromise reaches four systems.

• They persist beyond the use case. CSA reported that only 21% of enterprises have formal decommissioning processes for AI agents. Most keep running long after the use case ends, with credentials still valid.​

Most CISOs I speak with are being asked to approve agents already in late-stage pilots. The checklist below is designed around one principle: Friction scales with risk.

Low-risk actions get no friction. High-risk actions get human review. The business keeps its speed; security keeps control over actions that matter:

1. Require a scoped-access review for every agent before deployment. The agent gets its own identity, scoped to the specific task. Microsoft Copilot Studio and Salesforce Agentforce both support agent-level identities, but most teams default to user inheritance.

2. Define human-in-the-loop checkpoints for high-risk actions. Reading data: no checkpoint. Writing to a record of truth, moving money, sending an external communication or modifying production configurations: human approval before execution. This is a policy decision, not a technical one.

3. Mandate audit logging at the action level, not the prompt level. Prompt logs show what the user asked. Action logs show what the agent did across every system it touched. For AWS Bedrock Agents, Google Vertex AI and Anthropic Claude agents, action-level logging has to be configured at deployment, not retrofitted.

4. Set an expiration date for every agent. If the agent is still useful in six months, renew it with a fresh access review. If not, decommission. This single control closes the retirement debt CSA flagged.​

If agents are already live, discovery comes first:

1. Pull an inventory from every agent platform in use. Microsoft Copilot Studio, Salesforce Agentforce, ServiceNow Now Assist, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and any custom LangChain or CrewAI deployments. Admin consoles expose this; most security teams have not pulled the reports.

2. Cross-reference OAuth grants with agent identities. Grants to unfamiliar app IDs, especially those tied to AI model providers, are candidates for review.

3. Classify agents by action risk. An agent that reads Jira tickets is a different control problem than an agent that posts to customers or writes to the general ledger.

4. Revoke access for orphaned agents. When the builder leaves, the agent does not. If no human owner can be named, the agent is orphaned, and orphaned agents are retired.​

​There are three common objections when starting this work. The first is that guardrails will slow business adoption. They do not have to if they are designed around the risk of each action: Read-only agents can operate at full speed, while agents that write back to systems require approval. This preserves productivity across most use cases.

The second objection is that organizations cannot audit activity they cannot see. Yet the admin consoles for Microsoft, Salesforce, ServiceNow, AWS and Google already expose agent activity. In many cases, organizations simply have not enabled the relevant logs.

The third is that no one owns agent governance. Responsibility often falls between security, IT, legal and the business function that deployed the agent. Organizations making the most progress assign a cross-functional AI governance lead who reports to the CISO.​

The agent platforms have shipped faster than their security defaults can keep up.

Vendors should ship agents with least-privilege defaults, not broad inheritance. Action-level audit logging should be on by default. Decommissioning workflows should exist natively in every agent platform. Although frameworks such as the OWASP Agentic AI Top 10 and NIST AI RMF offer useful guidance, they stop short of making agent governance a core security requirement rather than an operational consideration.​​

The next AI agent incident will not look like a misconfiguration. It will look like an agent executing exactly what it was permitted to do, using credentials it inherited, with no human in the loop to catch the error.

Guardrails and adoption are not in opposition. The companies that figure out the balance now will be the ones setting the pace on AI agents in two years. The ones treating it as a trade-off will spend those two years explaining incidents instead of shipping agents.​

#3127. BioNTech (BNTX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Oncology pivot and a CEO transition shape a quarter with a revised revenue outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

BioNTech SE (BNTX -0.70%) reported a strategic shift toward a tumor-centric clinical development approach, prioritizing its lung cancer franchise and bispecific antibody candidates. Management reported a revised full-year revenue midpoint and a stable financial position with EUR 16.2 billion in cash assets. The company stated that it is transitioning several oncology programs into pivotal stages while optimizing its operational efficiency through divestitures and restructured partnerships. Management confirmed that it remains on track to become a diversified multi-product company by 2030, with multiple registrations planned for its late-stage pipeline candidates.

On the next slide, you will see our forward-looking statements disclaimer. Additional information about these statements and other risks are described in our filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, or SEC.

Forward-looking statements on this call are subject to significant risks and uncertainties and speak only as of the date of this conference call.
