This is a setting where chemotherapy has remained the standard of care for more than a decade, and with gotistobart, we aim to provide a chemotherapy-free monotherapy for patients who progressed after first-line therapy. We are encouraged by the data, and the pivotal stage of the trial is ongoing. Second, our combination therapy strategy continues to gain momentum. We recently entered into a clinical trial collaboration and supply agreement with Gilead to evaluate pumitamig in combination with their TROP2-directed antibody drug conjugate as first-line treatment for patients with metastatic PD-L1 low or negative triple-negative breast cancer.

If approved by regulators, this would be the first phase III trial of pumitamig in combination with an antibody drug conjugate and an important milestone in advancing our combination therapy strategy towards registration. Third, we continue our shift from a platform-centric to a tumor-centric clinical development approach in cancers with the greatest unmet medical need. At World Conference on Lung Cancer, we presented the first global combination data for any anti-PD-L1 VEGF bispecific immunomodulator and an ADC in lung cancer. This combination of pumitamig and LSD demonstrated encouraging early efficacy and manageable safety profile in small cell lung cancer across lines of treatment, including activity in first-line patients.

These data are the signal-seeking evidence we set out to generate this year. The observed clinical responses are encouraging and speak to the potential of novel combinations in lifting survival curves. These data we have seen support our phase III registration and planning for pumitamig in combination with LSD. Looking ahead, BioNTech is well-positioned for the next phase of growth. With a growing pipeline of potentially registrational trials, strong partnerships, and financial strength, we are on track to become a diversified multi-product company by 2030. Our late-stage development program includes multiple pivotal trials with readouts to 2030 and beyond, spanning multiple tumor types and different lines of treatment.

As we announced last quarter, Guido Oelkers will take office as CEO by 1st February at latest. I am confident that he will bring in his valuable experience to continue advancing BioNTech's unique and strong pipeline. Management and supervisory board members have been actively engaged in supporting a seamless transition. We have built BioNTech from a startup into a global biopharmaceutical company with a strong foundation across next-generation immunomodulators, ADCs, and mRNA. We have also established a distinguished combination therapy strategy in oncology. At the heart of our work is a shared purpose: advancing medical innovation to improve patient lives. Our employees have been instrumental in bringing this purpose to life with their expertise, dedication, and commitment.

It is their collective contribution that helps turn scientific discovery into meaningful progress for humanity and better outcomes for patients. We see significant potential in BioNTech. As this will be my last earnings call, I would like to thank the many exceptional and dedicated BioNTech team members and leaders, the management and the supervisory board, our founding partners, shareholders, and collaborators. I would also like to thank the patients, investigators, and other healthcare professionals who have been contributing to our trials and our colleagues in the science community. Without all these contributors, none of this would have been possible.

The impact we have created together to break through innovation for science, medicine, and patients is something I will look back on with deep gratitude. While we hand over the operational responsibility to our successors, Özlem and I will continue to follow BioNTech as founding shareholders. With this, I will hand over to Özlem.

Özlem Türeci: Thank you, Uğur. I am glad to be speaking with everyone today. Our ambition at BioNTech is to address the full continuum of cancer care by exploring the synergies of immune modulators, ADCs, and mRNA cancer immunotherapies. We have defined a tumor-type-focused strategy to address unmet medical need in disease areas where our novel combinations can extend survival for patients. In the past two months, we presented data at key conferences for three of our leading product candidates: pumitamig, gotistobart, and Alpha-D. The data validate their potential clinical benefit across key tumor types, most notably in lung cancer. I will review the data and discuss how it is supportive of the lung cancer franchise BioNTech is building.

Lung cancer is an area of high medical need, and we have a broad and diverse development approach to maximize our pipeline potential. At the core of our approach is pumitamig, a bispecific immunomodulator targeting PD-L1 and VEGF-A, being developed with our partner BMS across multiple tumor types. I will focus on non-small cell lung cancer first. We are running four registrational programs for pumitamig in combination with standard of care or monotherapy. In parallel to these registrational trials, we are generating novel combination data with our ADCs and our mRNA immunotherapies to inform the first wave of chemotherapy-free combination trials with registrational intent. Gotistobart is another key candidate of our non-small cell lung cancer strategy.

As a reminder, gotistobart is a selective Treg-depleting antibody targeting CTLA-4, developed with OncoC4. We are advancing gotistobart through the pivotal stage of a global phase III trial in patients with metastatic squamous non-small cell lung cancer who progressed following platinum-based chemotherapy and checkpoint inhibitor treatment. This is a setting with very few effective options and poor prognosis, where median survival with current standard of care is less than one year. At the World Conference on Lung Cancer, we presented updated overall survival data from the non-pivotal initial part of this trial, with a median follow-up of 25.4 months. Median overall survival was 18.5 months with gotistobart versus 10 months with docetaxel, with a hazard ratio of 0.56.

Gotistobart reduced the risk of death by 44% compared with chemotherapy. The observed safety profile of gotistobart was consistent with previous findings. These results reinforce the potential of gotistobart to provide a significant overall survival benefit as a chemotherapy-free monotherapy in this large, underserved patient population. In the pivotal part of the trial designed with identical protocol inclusion and exclusion criteria to stage I, we anticipate an interim analysis before year-end. This serves as an early data point ahead of the next pre-planned interim analysis next year. Turning to small cell lung cancer, where we are evaluating pumitamig in combination with chemotherapy, in combination with a DLL3 T-cell engager, and in combination with Alpha-D in front and later lines.

Alpha-D is our B7-H3-targeted ADC developed with DualityBio. Alpha-D's clinical profile positions it as a potentially versatile oncology asset across a wide range of solid tumors. More than 1,000 patients have now been treated with Alpha-D across over 10 tumor types, including more than 500 patients treated with Alpha-D in combination with pumitamig. This was a global dataset from our phase I/II trial of pumitamig plus Alpha-D in patients with advanced small cell and non-small cell lung cancer. This combination brings together three independent mechanisms of action: checkpoint inhibition, VEGF-A neutralization, and the tumor cell-targeted cytotoxic payload of Alpha-D.

In 71 patients with small cell lung cancer across 4 dose levels, the combination showed a remarkable 92% overall response rate in first line, 76% objective response rate in second line, and 52% objective response rate in third line and later. Importantly, we saw activity in patients previously treated with immunotherapy, with a 60% objective response rate, and in the small group of patients previously treated with a DLL3-targeted T-cell engager, with an encouraging 88% response rate. The safety profile was manageable and consistent with data from each agent individually, with limited overlap between pumitamig and Alpha-D-associated toxicities. No dose-limiting toxicities were observed, and the ILD rate for the combination was 2.9%.

These combination data support our broader strategy of evaluating pumitamig as a potential backbone for combination regimens of complementary mechanisms. They will help to inform the clinical development strategy to address today's unmet need and tomorrow's evolving small cell lung cancer standard of care. These data we have seen in this trial will help guide our novel combination strategy in lung cancer into potential registration, with first trials expected to begin in 2027. In triple-negative breast cancer, our pumitamig plus ADC combination strategy is now entering the pivotal stage.

At ESMO Breast in May, pumitamig in combination with a TROP2-targeted ADC showed a confirmed objective response rate of 76.7% and a disease control rate of 96.7% as first-line treatment in 30 patients with metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. These data confirm that pumitamig combined with a TROP2 ADC has a manageable safety profile and warrant further investigation as first-line treatment. When we initiated ROSETTA Breast-01, chemotherapy was the only option for patients with PD-L1-negative advanced TNBC. However, in 2026, the standard of care for first-line TNBC changed following updated NCCN and ESMO guidelines, as well as the FDA approval of TROP2 ADCs. TROP2-targeted ADCs, such as sacituzumab govitecan, are quickly becoming the new standard of care.

As a result of the evolving treatment landscape, we are adapting ROSETTA Breast-01 to replace chemotherapy with sacituzumab govitecan. We have entered into a clinical collaboration with Gilead. Pending the green light from regulators, this would be the first global phase III trial of our PD-L1/VEGF bispecific, pumitamig, in combination with an antibody-drug conjugate. Adapting ROSETTA Breast-01 to reflect the evolving standard of care gives the trial the best chance to inform clinical practice and ultimately treatment decisions for patients. Moving to mRNA cancer immunotherapies. As announced in August, the decision was made in alignment with Genentech to discontinue the phase II trial of autogene cevumeran as adjuvant monotherapy in ctDNA-positive stage II high-risk or stage III colorectal cancer.

This decision followed a review from the independent data safety monitoring board in which they identified a numerical imbalance in overall survival between the treatment arms in this specific patient population and determined that continuing the trial was unlikely to change the efficacy outcome. No new safety signals were identified. The phase II IMcode003 trial in adjuvant pancreatic cancer, where autogene cevumeran is being evaluated in combination with atezolizumab and modified FOLFIRINOX, has completed enrollment and continues as planned. BNT113, our off-the-shelf mRNA immunotherapy, is being evaluated in a pivotal phase II/III trial in combination with pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab alone as first-line treatment for patients with metastatic HPV16-positive PD-L1-expressing head and neck cancer.

In October, we announced top-line results from the first pre-specified interim analysis of AHEAD-MERIT. While the trial did not meet its first dual primary endpoint of progression-free survival, it is continuing as planned to assess the second dual primary endpoint of overall survival. The independent data monitoring committee recommended that the trial continue in accordance with the trial protocol. As immune-mediated anti-tumor effects build and deepen over time, the analysis of the overall survival endpoint will be critical to fully assess the potential of this approach to deliver durable benefit for patients with HPV-driven head and neck cancer.

Under the trial's statistical design, which pre-specifies dual primary endpoints of PFS and OS, a statistically significant improvement in OS would establish a positive trial outcome, irrespective of the PFS result. BioNTech is leveraging novel combinations with next-generation IO, targeted therapies, and mRNA cancer immunotherapy to maximize pipeline potential and elevate outcomes for patients with solid tumors. The potential of mRNA cancer immunotherapies in combination regimens lies in their ability to induce immune responses that may translate into durable clinical benefit and ultimately prolong survival of patients. Let me now move to our other late-stage milestones.

Recently, we announced that our global phase III trial evaluating T-Pam, an investigational HER2 ADC developed in collaboration with DualityBio in patients with HR-positive HER2-low metastatic breast cancer after endocrine therapy who are chemotherapy-naive, met its primary endpoint, demonstrating a statistically significant yet modest improvement in progression-free survival. At this interim analysis for the secondary endpoint of overall survival, data were not mature. A higher rate of interstitial lung disease was reported in this trial compared to prior trials, with most cases being grade 1 and 2. Severe and fatal events were reported in a small proportion of patients. Otherwise, the overall safety profile was consistent with prior clinical trials, and no new safety signals were observed.

The available efficacy and safety data as of this data cutoff date suggest that the potential benefit to patients would be limited in the context of the HR+, HER2-low metastatic breast cancer treatment landscape. We and DualityBio are currently discussing the totality of clinical data for trastuzumab pamirtecan across endometrial and breast cancer within the context of the evolving treatment landscape and areas of unmet medical need, and will determine the next steps. We and DualityBio are discussing plans for BLA submission and will update the markets accordingly. Looking ahead, we are on track for the first interim analysis for gotistobart in squamous non-small cell lung cancer before year-end.

This will be assessed by the IDMC to recommend whether to unblind the trial or continue to the next pre-planned interim analysis. Beyond the various late-stage readouts this year, we also further advanced our late-stage pipeline and initiated six phase III trials. In 2026, we published several datasets from our novel-novel programs with more to come. We executed these earlier combination trials to provide the signal-seeking evidence to inform and potentially de-risk the move of our combination trials into the pivotal stage. This provides the foundation for advancing BioNTech's growing late-stage oncology pipeline towards first approvals. With that, I would like to echo Uğur and thank our exceptional team at BioNTech for their conviction, for their loyalty, and dedication.

Building this company together has been an unforgettable experience, from the humble foundations to receiving approval of the first mRNA-based product, to creating the diversified oncology pipeline we have today. My thanks also go to our partners, investigators, regulators, healthcare professionals, and the patients and their families who have placed their trust in us. Turning the presentation over to our CFO, Ramón Zapata.

Ramón Zapata: Thank you, Özlem, and welcome to everyone joining us. I will start with our third quarter and year-to-date 2026 financial results, then provide an update on our full year 2026 financial guidance and capital allocation highlights. Note that all figures are in euros unless otherwise stated. Beginning with financial performance. Revenues for the third quarter of 2026 were EUR 1.3 billion compared to EUR 1.5 billion in the prior year third quarter. This decline mainly reflects anticipated lower market demand for our COVID-19 vaccine. As expected, revenues of EUR 613 million were recognized in the quarter from our global strategic partnership with BMS related to the co-development and co-commercialization of our next-generation bispecific antibody candidate, pumitamig.

Adjusted R&D expenses for the third quarter of 2026 increased to EUR 579 million from EUR 479 million in the prior year third quarter. The increase reflects greater investment in our prioritized IO and ADC programs, partially offset by lower spending outside of our strategic focus. On an IFRS basis, R&D expenses were EUR 748 million. The additional expenses of EUR 169 million include impairment losses related to intangible assets, which are outside of our strategic focus. SG&A expenses for the third quarter of 2026 on an adjusted and IFRS basis were EUR 179 million compared to EUR 149 million in the prior year third quarter.

The increase was mainly driven by pre-launch activities for late-stage programs and the commercial buildup, as well as our ongoing global initiative to scale processes and ERP infrastructure to optimize operational execution. At the same time, we continue to realize meaningful savings from strategic pipeline prioritization execution and enhanced cost discipline across the organization. Our strong financial position of EUR 16.2 billion in cash equivalents, and security investments at the end of the third quarter provides the foundation to advance our ambition of becoming a global multi-product biopharmaceutical company by 2030. Let's now turn from the third quarter to our nine-month year-to-date 2026 financials.

Comparing this year's performance with the same nine-month period of the prior year, drivers are mostly in line with the factors I have described for the quarter. Revenues were EUR 1.5 billion for the year-to-date 2026 compared to EUR 2 billion in the prior year period. Adjusted R&D expenses were EUR 1.6 billion compared to EUR 1.5 billion. Adjusted SG&A expenses came in at EUR 527 million, up from EUR 407 million. Overall, our year-to-date performance is aligned with our expectations. Our revenue performance in the third quarter allows us to raise the midpoint of our previously provided full year 2026 revenue guidance. Our updated 2026 financial revenue guidance is now EUR 1.7 billion to EUR 1.9 billion.

Our adjusted R&D and SG&A expense guidance for 2026 remains unchanged at EUR 2 billion to EUR 2.3 billion and EUR 700 million to EUR 800 million, respectively. I will now touch on our capital allocation strategy. Our approach remains centered on prioritizing investments towards our highest value opportunities, with a focus on advancing late-stage programs toward potential approvals and launches, while investing selectively in earlier stage innovation. This approach is designed to create diversified revenue streams and lay the foundation for a sustainable long-term oncology business. Our strong balance sheet provides us with the flexibility to complement our portfolio, strengthen our focus areas, and access external innovation where we see strong strategic alignments.

At the same time, we continue to return capital to shareholders. Since the implementation of the share buyback program in June, we have repurchased approximately 5 million shares through September 30th, reflecting our belief in the intrinsic value of BioNTech while maintaining full optionality to advance our pipeline, execute partnerships, and pursue corporate development opportunities. We remain focused on operational efficiency and disciplined resource allocation, optimizing our portfolio, manufacturing footprint, and cost structures to focus resources on our highest value priorities. This is reflected in our recently divested JPT Peptide Technologies business and ongoing manufacturing footprint consolidation, where we continue to assess other areas where we can elevate operational efficiency.

We are also taking steps to simplify our AI operational model and strengthen its integration across BioNTech. We plan to integrate the expertise and capabilities of InstaDeep, our wholly owned AI and machine learning subsidiary, into BioNTech's core business. As part of this initiative, we expect to focus AI development on supporting our strategic objectives, operational processes, and innovation priorities. We believe this more integrated approach will reduce complexity and enable us to deploy AI more effectively. Our conviction in mRNA is anchored by over a decade of translational and clinical research, as well as deep experience in the field.

We continue to advance mRNA cancer immunotherapies and invest in them as a key pillar of our oncology strategy, including novel combination approaches intended to maximize the potential of our diversified oncology pipeline. Irrespective of our conviction in the drug class as such, we assess and optimize the financial structure of our existing collaborations. We have exercised an option in the Roche/Genentech BioNTech collaboration agreement, under which future R&D costs for this program will be reassigned to Roche/Genentech, including assessing the candidate in adjuvant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, or PDAC. BioNTech will be eligible to receive royalties. The decision to exercise the option aligns with our broader capital allocation framework as we optimize operational efficiency.

With this, we aim for an improved financial structure under the terms of the agreement, which does not affect our ongoing clinical program. This means the ongoing phase II clinical trial in PDAC continues as planned, and we are excited to see more data from this mRNA cancer immunotherapy program. Taken together, our strong financial position and disciplined capital allocation approach support our long-term objective of becoming a global multi-product company, addressing the unmet medical needs of cancer patients worldwide. We remain focused on prioritizing investments that advance our pipeline and support sustainable growth while preserving the financial flexibility to respond to evolving opportunities. Finally, discussions regarding Uğur and Özlem's new company and potential contributions from BioNTech remain ongoing.

Any potential arrangement will be evaluated based on its strategic rationale and its ability to maximize value for patients and our shareholders. While there is an opportunity for a deal at this stage, it is optional for both parties and not a necessity. Before I close, since this is the last earnings call that we have with the co-founders of BioNTech, I would like to wish Uğur and Özlem all the best in their new venture. I also want to thank them personally for their vision, leadership, and extraordinary contributions. Together, they built BioNTech from a bold idea into a global pharmaceutical pioneer.

They advanced science that has changed lives, helped patients around the world, and achieved a medical breakthrough which has entered the history books. We are deeply grateful for everything they have done for this company, and the foundation they leave is one we are proud to build on. With that, I will hand it back to the operator to open the call for questions. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you wish to ask a question, you will need to press star one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. Akash Tewari: Hey, thanks so much. And Uğur and Özlem, really congrats on an amazing tenure at BioNTech. Two for you. Özlem Türeci: Akash, I can take the first question. Ramón Zapata: Thank you, Akash. I will take on the second part of your question that is related to mRNA and our commitment to it. That by no means should be understood as a lack of commitment. We continue to be very excited about the PDAC program, are very much looking forward for its next milestones and readouts. Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. Your question comes from Mohit Bansal from Wells Fargo. Please go ahead, your line is open.

Mohit Bansal: Great. Thank you very much for taking my question. Just wanted to understand a little bit about the cancer vaccine program. Özlem Türeci: Thank you, Mohit, for your question. I can give some background to how we see the read-through from colorectal cancer to PDAC. In principle, these are two different questions asked and two different experiments. It is correct that both are cold tumors and both are tumors with tumor mutational burden being more on the lower side. However, these are, on the one hand, entirely different tumor biologies, and also different settings of positioning the vaccine. What I mean with this is that in the colorectal cancer trial, we have used our vaccine in a monotherapy setting as an adjuvant vaccine. In the PDAC setting, it is integrated into chemotherapy and also combined with checkpoint inhibition.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. The question comes from Daina Graybosch from Leerink Partners. Please go ahead, your line is open.

Daina Graybosch: Hi. I also want to echo my gratitude and congratulations for your next steps for Uğur and Özlem. My question is on the TROP2 ADC. Özlem Türeci: Yes. Thank you, Daina, for your question. Annemarie Hanekamp: Yeah. Thank you, Özlem, and this is Annemarie. I will just also add that in line with our strategy, what we shared before on pumitamig, we believe that this next-gen bispecific will be the backbone in different settings and cancer types, and that we're moving this ahead with our partner, BMS, in chemo combinations, but also, to your point, in combination with other assets, and ADCs are a core part of that. We're not only moving those forward with our own portfolio or BMS's, but also, as you've seen during our announcement at ESMO, moving that forward with, in this case, Gilead's ADC. So, we're closely monitoring the field. There's been some interesting data, including in lung cancer.

If you look at our strategic priorities, we're definitely focused with multiple shots on goal in lung cancer, breast cancer, but also GI and GU cancer. We will continue to evaluate, follow the science, and then decide which asset is best combined with pumitamig, where we believe transformational benefits can be delivered on top of the chemo benefit that we're hoping to see in the first wave of combinations with pumitamig.

Ramón Zapata: Hi, Tazeen. Özlem Türeci: Yeah. We have seven global pivotal studies ongoing by end of this year, and these trials are all event-driven, so we cannot predict the exact sequence and timing with confidence. What I would like to do is to point you to clinicaltrials.gov, where we have primary completion dates as posted based on the most current or recent data. According to those primary completion dates, we will see first-line TNBC in China data in 2027, then ROSETTA Lung-02 and ROSETTA Lung-01 around 2029, and then followed by RCC, CRC, HCC, and the other studies. However, the timing, as you know, can move as these studies mature, and dates may change.

The company will update the market when they have enough visibility to do so responsibly. The second question was about, I think, commercial gotistobart positioning.

Annemarie Hanekamp: Yeah. I can take that one. As Özlem already alluded to, we presented an update on the gotistobart non-pivotal part of our phase III study with impressive benefit for patients. As you may know that in this patient setting, for a long time, we haven't seen real improvements. Many shots on goal were tried, but many also failed to demonstrate improvement in overall survival. If the gotistobart part two of the pivotal trial confirms the benefit that we've seen to date, we believe it could address a meaningful patient population, again, where no innovation has been happening for a while.

If you look at the current data, we would estimate around 55,000 patients in second-line squamous non-small cell lung cancer by 2030 in just the G7. With that context, we do view gotistobart as a key asset in our portfolio that can meaningfully contribute to building BioNTech in a multi-product company on the longer term.

Jessica Fye: Great. Thanks. If the first interim passes, would you comment on it one way or the other once that happens?

Annemarie Hanekamp: Yes, we would comment on it one way or another, as we have disclosed that we are expecting this readout. We would also expect if the IDMC would recommend the study to continue, as per Özlem’s earlier comments.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question comes from Cory Kasimov from Evercore ISI. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Cory Kasimov: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking the question, and congrats once again to Uğur and Özlem, and best of luck with the new endeavor. On the heels of the encouraging results with pumitamig plus Elfe-D at ESMO, what are the next steps for this combination, and what tumor types are you most interested in advancing? Then since others are asking multiple questions, a very quick one for you. If iNeST is ultimately successful, what level of royalty would you get from Roche under or post this option you exercised? Thank you.

Özlem Türeci: I can take the first question. Before I do that, I would like to thank everyone on the call, also on behalf of Uğur, for your kind words. It was really a pleasure to work with all of you over these years. Cory, you asked for our plans for Elfe-D plus pumitamig combinations and how we want to go ahead. Yes, we are also very excited about the data we presented for small cell lung cancer, and there is more to come because we have not fully analyzed the other tumor type cohorts, which are still running. We have not decided on a specific indication setting or timing for Elfe-D pumitamig pivotal trials yet.

Our prioritization and decisions will be data-driven based on the large body of data we have produced over the last couple of months in the different indications. This will be part of our 2027 milestones, which we will disclose in a couple of months.

Ramón Zapata: Thank you, Özlem. Hi, Cory. In relation to your question on iNeST, we are not providing specific royalty economics under this option. However, I mean, like, you know, all of this is dependent on successful development and then thereafter commercialization. So these are the tiering of royalties that we currently have. But this is as much as we can disclose at the moment.

Cory Kasimov: Okay. Understood. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question comes from Terence Flynn from Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Terence Flynn: Great. Thanks for taking the question. It might be a little bit early, but Ramón, I was just wondering if you can comment broadly on how to think about 2027 numbers, both top and bottom line, just conceptually. Thank you.

Ramón Zapata: Hi, Terence. It is a little bit premature to talk about 2027. We are currently working these plans, and we will update all of you at a later stage.

Operator: Thank you. One moment, please. Your next question comes from Simon Baker from Rothschild & Co Redburn. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Simon Baker: Thank you for taking my question. Going back to iNeST and FixVac and the development plans, I am keen to get your thoughts on the recent paper in Cell that suggested the potential benefit on efficacy from adding chemotherapy, specifically carboplatin and Taxol. You do have chemo in some of these trials, but I just wondered what you thought about the utility and implications of that early work on future development plans for both iNeST and FixVac. Thanks so much.

Özlem Türeci: Thank you, Simon, for your question. With which compounds we combine our vaccines depends really on the standard of care and backbone, which is used in the respective indication. The data you are quoting shows that combining with chemotherapy is, first of all, feasible, and in fact, can also improve the effect because it supports antigen spreading. We do not shy away, and you can see this in our PDAC study, for example, and also in our studies with BNT116, to combine with chemo where it makes sense from a standard of care and backbone point of view.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question comes from Yaron Werber from TD Cowen. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Tina: Hey, this is Tina on for Yaron. I would like to also add my congrats to Uğur and Ozlem on an amazing tenure, and thanks for taking our questions. I just want to get your broader thoughts on your sense of late-stage pipeline and what you think of the most exciting asset beyond pumitamig and maybe gotistobart. Also, I know that you are in discussions with your partner on T-Pam, but if you will give us any more granularity on how the recent breast cancer results might impact your filing endometrial cancer and your thoughts for that pivotal registrational plans. Thank you so much.

Özlem Türeci: I did not get the question fully. I think one part of it was about what we find interesting in our pipeline or exciting beyond pumitamig and gotistobart. So, actually, all of our assets, pumitamig and gotistobart, are particularly exciting, and we have a large body of data which supports this excitement. However, we are also very excited about our ADCs, in particular also Elfe-D, because again, there, the excitement is supported by data, and which we see across tumors. What was the second question?

Annemarie Hanekamp: I can take that, Özlem.

Annemarie Hanekamp: The second question is about T-Pam and potential filing. As Özlem already mentioned, we are discussing with DualityBio the totality of our clinical data for T-Pam, both across endometrial and breast cancer. We do that, of course, with the mind of making sure that we add both value for patients and shareholders alike. So, we are looking at the context of the evolving landscape, areas of unmet medical need, and then we determine next steps. Currently, we are discussing plans for a BLA submission, and we will update the markets accordingly.

Speaker 16: All right. Thank you so much.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our final question, and the final question comes from Geoff Meacham from Citigroup. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Jarwei Fang: Hi, good morning. This is Jarwei on for Geoff Meacham. Thanks for taking our question. Maybe just a question on pumitamig. I know you guys are testing combinations across several ADCs, but emerging data sets differ maturity, tumor type, and partner assets. I am just wondering what criteria will determine which pumitamig combinations advance most aggressively, and where have the data increased or reduced your conviction so far? Thank you.

Annemarie Hanekamp: I can take this question. Thank you very much. It is first of all, as we mentioned several times for BioNTech, really data-driven. We had a couple of phase I/II combination data sets out there together with our own ADC portfolio and mRNA portfolio. Also, BMS, our partner for pumitamig, is starting combination work, as well as we have several projects now running outside of both BMS's and BioNTech's pipeline. We will await the first data to determine both on safety and early efficacy which candidates and combinations we move forward. But like I mentioned in the previous question, we also continue to monitor the evolving landscape.

The speed of the oncology development over the last decade is continue to accelerate, which is amazing news for patients, but also requires us as sponsors of study to make sure that by the time data reads out, we still address relevant unmet medical needs. It is a constant monitoring of what is evolving, what is in line with our strategy. As we said, we are focused on lung, breast, GI, and GU cancers, and then making sure that the data is in line with those expectations. All in all, to become a multi-product company by the time that we enter into 2030.

Jarwei Fang: Great. Thank you. Also to Uğur and Özlem, best of luck in your next venture. Thank you.

Canva is making significant changes affecting 1,271 people, which is 22 percent of its staff, co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins announced today. “For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs,” says Perkins. “Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today.”

After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough. To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community.

Canva’s changes include bringing its Product, Growth, and Platform teams together into one product organization, “simplifying layers” and “consolidating overlapping responsibilities,” and making Sydney the “primary home for more of our product teams, as well as roles in other Specialties where shared context and close collaboration are especially important.” Starting in January, Canva will also “expect” most hybrid employees to spend 2 to 3 days in an office each week “depending on what makes sense in your area.”

Employees leaving Canva will get benefits including at least six months of salary, twelve months of healthcare coverage, and career support resources.

Yesterday, Squarespace announced layoffs affecting 19 percent of its staff.

#3124. AI Is Making The App Optional

Haz Hubble is the Co-Founder and CEO at Pally (YC S25).

When I started building Pally, an AI assistant that keeps people on top of their messages, I assumed it needed its own app. We built one, with onboarding, settings and a home feed. Fewer than 20% of new users were still active in their second month.

We removed the app and moved the product into iMessage. Users now sign up by texting a number. With the same AI underneath, month-two retention rose to over 70%. That result made me question how much of consumer software exists only to support the app around it.

Every app asks people to do work before they get anything back. They have to find it, install it, create an account, learn where things are and remember that it exists. Some share of users gives up at each step.

The phone they’re installing it on is already crowded. The average user has more than 80 apps, and about 62% of them go unused in a given month. In the U.S., people spend around 80% of their app time in their three most-used apps. A new app is asking for a place that most people have stopped giving out.

The first is new hardware. OpenAI has said it will show its first consumer device, a screenless product designed with Jony Ive, in the second half of 2026. The last well-funded attempt, Humane’s AI Pin, failed. A common explanation is that it asked people to change their habits without giving them enough reason to.

The second is the super-app. WeChat hosts more than 4.3 million mini-programs, and roughly 764 million people used them each day in 2025. People in China order food and pay bills through services they never downloaded, because those services sit inside an app they already open all day. The model depends on one company controlling the platform, which is part of why nothing comparable exists in the U.S.

The third is putting AI inside the messaging apps people already use, such as iMessage, SMS, WhatsApp and email. Language models make this practical because a conversation can now do the job that buttons and menus used to do. The assistant can also message first, so users don’t have to remember to open anything. Of the three approaches, this is the only one that doesn’t ask people to form a new habit.

Satya Nadella made a version of this argument about business software in December 2024. He said, “The notion that business applications exist will probably collapse” as AI agents take on more work. He reasoned that most apps are databases with rules on top, and agents can apply those rules on a user’s behalf.

The same reasoning applies to consumer products. When an assistant can read your messages, check your calendar and act on a request written in plain English, many of an app’s screens become optional. Messaging is where this shows up first, because it’s where people already spend their attention.

Building inside another company’s messaging app means that company can shut you out. Meta did exactly that in January 2026, when WhatsApp stopped allowing general-purpose AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Perplexity on its business platform. After EU regulators intervened, Meta restored access in the European Economic Area in July. As of late July, the ban had not been lifted in the U.S.

Apple’s position is different. In June 2025, a federal judge refused to dismiss the Justice Department’s antitrust case against Apple, and the allegations the court let stand include restrictions on iMessage and on super-apps. Apple has reportedly made several settlement offers to the DOJ this year. While that case is open, blocking third-party assistants from iMessage would hand regulators a fresh example of the conduct they’re already suing over.

That doesn’t resolve the risk. Apple could still change its rules, and no messaging platform has made a lasting commitment to AI developers. Anyone building this way should plan for losing a channel.

1. Within five years, most consumer apps will work mainly as back-ends. Their data and logic will still matter, but people will reach them through an assistant instead of opening them.

2. A phone number will replace the App Store listing as the way many people first try a new product.

3. Screens will be generated when a task needs one, such as signing a contract or reading a chart, and will close when the task is done.

4. Consumer products will be judged by completed tasks. Time spent in an app will start to look like a cost to the user.

5. Regulators will treat AI access to messaging platforms the way they treated browser choice and app store rules, and at least one major platform will be required to open up to third-party assistants in the U.S.

If you’re building a consumer product today, make three changes.

• Track how long a new user takes to get value, counted in messages rather than screens. If the first exchange doesn’t help them, fix that before anything else.

• Build the version with no interface first. Add screens only where text doesn’t work, such as payments or reviewing long documents.

• Keep your data and logic on your own infrastructure, so you can move between iMessage, SMS, WhatsApp and email if a platform changes its rules.

For Pally, this means treating iMessage as our first channel, not our only one. We keep the product’s logic on our own infrastructure so it can run over SMS, WhatsApp or email if Apple’s rules change. We add a screen only when a user can’t finish a task in text, and every new feature has to work without asking anyone to open something new.
