#3123. Knife River (KNF) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Contracting margins compressed as fuel costs and funding delays hit results.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Knife River Corporation (KNF +1.39%) reported that external headwinds, including project delays and high fuel costs, affected performance in the contracting services segment during the third quarter. Management stated the company is implementing the Sharper EDGE program to focus on operational, commercial, and organizational excellence over the next three years. This initiative aims to improve profitability through targeted capital investments in the aggregates business and the modernization of financial processes. The company reported that while some public infrastructure bid lettings have slowed, demand remains supported by historically high state budgets and federal funding initiatives.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Knife River Corporation third quarter results conference call. After today's prepared remarks, we will host a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one to raise your hand. To withdraw your question, press star one again. I will now hand the conference over to Dara Dierks, head of investor relations. Dara, please go ahead.

Dara Dierks: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining Knife River Corporation's Third Quarter Results Conference Call. With me today are President and Chief Executive Officer Brian Gray and Chief Financial Officer Nathan Ring. A question-and-answer session will follow their prepared remarks. Today's discussion will contain forward-looking statements about future operational and financial expectations. Actual results may differ materially from those projected in today's forward-looking statements. For further detail, please refer to today's earnings release and the risk factors disclosed in our most recent filings with the SEC, which are available on our website and the SEC website. Except as required by law, we undertake no obligation to update our forward-looking statements.

During this presentation, we will make references to certain non-GAAP information. These non-GAAP measures are defined and reconciled to the most directly comparable GAAP measure in today's earnings release and investor presentation. These materials are also available on our website. I would now like to turn the call over to Brian.

Brian Gray: Thank you, Dara. Good morning, everyone. On the call today, we will discuss our third quarter performance, characterized by resilience and led by substantial improvement in our aggregates business. We will highlight the actions we are taking to help overcome some near-term headwinds. Most importantly, we will discuss the initiatives underway that position us to drive long-term profitable growth and value creation. While we have made progress on our margins since launching EDGE in 2023, we have been sharpening our EDGE and have identified additional paths to achieve further growth. First, let's start with our quarterly results. Our revenue increased 6% from the same time last year to $1.3 billion.

Adjusted EBITDA was $272 million, and adjusted EBITDA margin was over 21%. We are especially pleased with our record third quarter in aggregates, where EDGE efforts helped drive improved profitability. We focused on increasing aggregate sales to third parties, and we targeted more paving work, which together supported 10% higher volumes year-over-year. We also increased aggregate prices mid-single digits while reducing our per-ton production costs. Combined, these efforts helped us realize a 240 basis point improvement in aggregate gross margin to nearly 30% for the quarter. These results demonstrate what we can accomplish with our EDGE initiatives. We believe there is potential for meaningful margin expansion across all of our product lines, with the largest opportunity still in aggregates.

As we outlined in our September investor update, the external headwinds we faced in the second quarter, market dynamics, project delays, and higher fuel costs carried into the third quarter. The impact has been most pronounced in contracting services throughout the year, which Nathan will address in his remarks. We believe these headwinds are transitory. We have seen similar cycles before and successfully managed through them. Our crews are focused on controlling what they can control, and I'm confident in our ability to manage near-term headwinds while continuing to build for future growth. Meanwhile, we are excited about the progress we are making as we implement new self-help initiatives to improve EBITDA and margins.

Let me discuss some of the results we are seeing and the additional steps we are taking. Since our spin in 2023, we've been putting our EDGE initiatives to work to improve our business across the board. These efforts have contributed to growth in our adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA margin, and product line gross margins, highlighted by the 530 basis point improvement in aggregate gross margins. In addition to these results, the work our pit crews have done the past three years has also given us greater visibility into the substantial new opportunities we have to improve our operations in a meaningful way.

While EDGE 1.0 will continue, our new Sharper EDGE program adds a new set of targeted line-of-sight improvement opportunities across three areas: operational excellence, commercial excellence, and organizational excellence. We have already begun implementing these initiatives, and we expect to meaningfully ramp the program over the next three years, with increased benefits each year. In operational excellence, we're focused on further improving productivity, reducing costs, and making the best use of our assets, and we're seeing results. Starting in aggregates, we improved plant runtime by 4% in the third quarter, and we reduced variable production costs by 5%, contributing to the 29.6% gross margin we achieved.

With Sharper EDGE, we're digging deeper into the day-to-day performance at each plant to unlock greater potential. We are focused on plant reconfigurations and automation, improved mine planning, and optimizing heavy equipment to each operation. We plan to deploy over $125 million of capital on these aggregate opportunities over the next three years. We expect these Sharper EDGE investments will improve aggregate gross profit by approximately $1 per ton. We're also excited about the benefits we expect to see in the first half of 2027 at our aggregates expansion project in South Dakota, which we expect will add over 1 million tons per year to the regional market at highly accretive margins.

These are exactly the type of projects at the heart of Sharper EDGE, and we are pursuing similar organic expansions in other states. In Ready-Mix, we have lowered cement costs by 5% year to date, even as suppliers added fuel surcharges to deliveries. With Sharper EDGE, we will continue managing our cementitious materials, focus on bulk purchasing strategies, and optimizing our mix designs. At the same time, we aim to improve truck utilization, including more effective load and haul configurations to lower costs and increase production. In asphalt, we reduced variable production costs by 7% year to date, despite the inflationary headwinds we faced this summer.

With Sharper EDGE, we continue to optimize mix designs to manage our costs, focus on maximizing the use of recycled materials, and minimizing specialty materials. In Energy Services, our Sharper EDGE efforts include plant automation, modernized rail and loading systems, and increased tank capacity. These efforts are designed to create efficiencies, lower costs, and enable additional liquid asphalt sales. The second focus area is commercial excellence, where the goal is to ensure we are getting the full value for our materials and services. We are focused on three key areas. First, dynamic pricing. We continue to expand the use of pricing and quoting tools supported by real-time analytics.

These tools give our teams better visibility into costs, demand, and market conditions, so we can price each job with more precision. With Sharper EDGE, we are taking this a step further and will be automating dashboards so regional leadership can track pricing and costs to ensure we are delivering on our targets. We expect this to strengthen accountability to our sales targets and improve customer service. Second is the standardized use of advanced technology to optimize pricing, improve profitability, and make Knife River the supplier of choice.

With Sharper EDGE, our priority in this area is the full rollout and adoption of transactional software to give our sales teams greater visibility into pipelines, backlogs, pricing forecasts, and margins in each of our materials product lines. Third is our go-to-market strategy. We are taking a more coordinated approach to pursuing opportunities across our footprint. This includes selling more materials to national contractors and developers. We are also marketing our capabilities across our 15-state footprint to customers who are building large, mission-critical projects, including data centers, power generation, and semiconductor facilities. Our vertically integrated model allows us to offer these customers a single partner with the materials and services they need.

Lastly, we are focusing Sharper EDGE initiatives on organizational improvements to support our operations and reduce SG&A. We have begun streamlining certain administrative processes to remove inefficiencies and speed up decision-making. We started with a financial modernization initiative in accounting nearly a year ago, with the goal of trimming days off our monthly closing process so management gets actionable data more quickly. At the same time, we are focused on evolving our technology. In September, we hired a new executive to lead the AI transformation at Knife River. His team is actively working to become a true solutions provider to our operations in an effort to help drive profit.

They have already delivered an AI bidding agent designed to help our estimators quickly search, score, and rank bidding opportunities, which we rolled out last month. They have several projects underway to automate processes and identify cost savings across our company, both at the back office and in our operations. All of these are tangible initiatives with clear line of sight to improved performance. We believe Sharper EDGE gives us a clear roadmap to build on the foundation established through EDGE 1.0. It is focused on opportunities we have identified, actions we can control, and measurable improvements to the business. Ultimately, it is about driving sustainable growth in adjusted EBITDA, margin expansion, and creating long-term value for our shareholders.

We look forward to providing more detail on financial targets at our investor day in the coming months. Next, I'll turn the call over to Nathan to walk through our product line performance, capital position, and outlook. Nathan?

Nathan Ring: Thank you, Brian. As Brian mentioned, the quarter demonstrated the resilience of our business, led by substantial improvement in our aggregates product line. We delivered higher volumes than last year across our materials product lines, while our commercial and operational initiatives helped offset the headwinds we experienced during the quarter and contributed to higher gross profit compared to the prior year. Starting with the aggregate product line, internal volumes increased 13% as we continue to benefit from additional paving activity and our vertically integrated model. Third-party sales also had a strong quarter, growing 8%, supported by demand from data center and power projects.

Along with higher volumes, we also saw solid pricing, with reported average selling price increasing 4.3% and mix-adjusted pricing increasing 5.9%. Our operational initiatives also continue to deliver results, with variable cost per ton declining in each quarter this year. Together, these improvements helped drive gross margin to almost 30%, the highest level in the company's recent history. Aggregates also became the largest contributor to our gross profit for both the quarter and year to date, demonstrating continued progress toward increasing the contribution of aggregates to our overall business mix. Although we still have work to do, we are pleased with the progress we continue to make on this product line.

For the full year, we expect volume growth of high single digits to low double digits, along with mid-single-digit pricing growth and at least 150 basis points of gross margin expansion. In Ready-Mix, volumes increased slightly during the quarter, supported by contributions from recent acquisitions in Texas and Montana, partially offset by lower residential and commercial demand in the West. Due to third-quarter volumes being below our expectations, we now expect full-year ready-mix volumes growth of high single to low double digits. Pricing also increased during the quarter, supported by our continued focus on sales training and dynamic pricing. Gross margin was lower, reflecting the geographic and end-market mix of volumes during the quarter.

Turning to asphalt, volumes increased during the quarter, with internal volumes rising 10%, benefiting from higher paving activity in our contracting services business. Third-party volumes increased by 5% as we target sales to other contractors for their projects. For the full year, we now expect volumes to increase high single to low double digits. Our operational initiatives also continue to generate efficiencies, contributing to lower production costs at our plants during the quarter. Gross margin was lower than the prior year, primarily due to increased competition for paving work and higher input costs. For liquid asphalt, gross margin was 18.9% in the third quarter, primarily due to lower sales volumes in certain markets, as well as higher material input costs.

While Energy Services has faced margin pressure over the past two years, it remains margin accretive to the overall company. In contracting services, revenue grew by 9% during the quarter, driven by higher paving across our segments. This increased activity generated additional demand for our upstream aggregates and asphalt businesses, demonstrating the benefits of our vertical integration model. The Mountain segment provides a clear example of this benefit, where we shifted our bidding strategy to place greater emphasis on asphalt paving and materials pull-through. Mountain asphalt volumes increased by almost 60%, with more than half coming from legacy operations.

As Brian mentioned, transitory headwinds from competitive market conditions, higher fuel costs, and project delays have had the largest impact on our contracting services business. We saw margin compression as a result of fewer bid lettings in our more profitable markets, like Oregon, and increased competition in others. As such, we focused our bids where we could pull through our higher-margin material sales, as I noted with the Mountain segment, to offset this pressure. Our teams continue to right-size crews and equipment with current market demand and tightly manage variable operating costs, while also broadening the range of work we pursue.

These actions, along with maintaining our disciplined approach to bidding, are focused on improving the quality of our work mix and driving better margin performance over time. For the second half of the year, we expect contracting margin to be 8%-9%. Backlog ended the quarter at $857 million, down from the prior year. The year-over-year change partly reflects the higher level of contracting services revenue recognized during the third quarter compared to last year. As I just mentioned, we have also seen fewer bidding opportunities in certain markets for the quarter, including Oregon and Idaho, where funding delays have contributed to reduced project lettings.

While industry data indicates that DOT budgets are slightly below prior year levels in some of our markets, overall budgets still remain near historically high levels, with approximately 32% of IIJA funding still to be spent in Knife River markets. We are also encouraged by the bipartisan support for BUILD America 250. Reauthorization of the Surface Transportation Bill through 2031 would provide states certainty for their budgets, and we believe a supportive backdrop for public infrastructure investment across Knife River's markets. As we approach our busiest bidding season, our focus remains on disciplined bidding and building high-quality backlog that supports profitable growth across our vertically integrated business.

Moving on to SG&A, expenses continue to track the expectations we shared earlier this year. We saw an increase in $4.4 million during the quarter, including $2.8 million from acquisitions completed over the past year. As we fully integrate these businesses, we expect to achieve greater SG&A leverage over time. As a percent of revenue, SG&A was 5.8% for the quarter, and for the full year, we continue to expect it to be comparable to 2025. Looking ahead, we anticipate SG&A as a percentage of revenue to decline as we execute our Sharper EDGE initiatives. Finally, switching to capital allocation, our priorities remain consistent.

We are investing in our existing operations while pursuing margin-accretive organic and acquisition growth opportunities that offer attractive long-term returns. During the quarter, we invested $37 million in maintenance and improvement capital and $21 million to advance our aggregates expansion project in South Dakota and additional growth investments across our footprint. For the full year, we now expect maintenance and improvement capital expenditures between 5%-6% of revenue, with acquisitions and organic growth investments incremental to that range. We have the balance sheet capacity and liquidity to support our strategic growth priorities. We ended the quarter with net leverage of 2.9x and expect to continue deleveraging through year-end, finishing modestly above 2.5x.

Looking back at the third quarter, our EDGE initiatives continued to deliver improvements across the business, helping us navigate the headwinds we experienced during the quarter. Based on our performance through the third quarter and our projections for the remainder of the year, we now anticipate revenue of $3.375 billion-$3.425 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $475 million-$505 million. This outlook assumes normal weather and economic conditions for the remainder of the year and excludes the impact of potential acquisitions. With that, I will now turn back to Brian to provide closing remarks.

Brian Gray: Thank you, Nathan. I'd like to finish our quarterly recap where we started. We had a solid third quarter in a challenging operating environment, and we remain very optimistic about Knife River's ability to create long-term value. The short-term headwinds certainly had an impact, and I don't want to minimize that, but we should not confuse near-term challenges with the long-term potential of this company. We have multiple paths to achieve EBITDA and margin growth, and we're running at them simultaneously. One is through our self-help efforts, which we continue to expand and improve. We're confident our Sharper EDGE initiatives will drive meaningful growth in EBITDA and EBITDA margin.

At the same time, we have major organic investments moving closer to completion, including aggregate expansion projects in South Dakota and Texas. I mentioned our South Dakota expansion earlier, which includes plant advancements and a rail network to extend our reach into new markets. We're looking at similar investments in our other regions. Aggregates growth is a key component of our Sharper EDGE initiatives and represents an important path to reaching our margin goals. Lastly, our M&A pipeline is active, and the industry in our higher-growth, mid-sized markets is highly fragmented with vertically integrated opportunities. We are well-respected in our markets and often the acquirer of choice.

Whether it's self-help, organic efforts, or M&A growth, we believe we are well-positioned to capitalize on each of these opportunities to improve adjusted EBITDA and margins. While we have made meaningful progress since going public and launching EDGE, we believe there's much more growth ahead of us. Importantly, we know where those opportunities are, and we are actively pursuing them. Thank you for the time today. We will now open the call for questions.

Operator: We will now begin the question-and-answer session. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one to raise your hand. To withdraw your question, press star one again. We ask that you pick up your handset when asking a question to allow for optimum sound quality. If you are muted locally, please remember to unmute your device. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Your first question comes from Brent Thielman with Oppenheimer & Co. Please go ahead.

Brent Thielman: Hey. Great. Thanks. Good morning. Brian, just on the Sharper EDGE initiative, I am wondering if there is particular markets or regions where you see the initiative being more impactful to drive margins higher, I guess, post-EDGE. Wondering where you still see the low-hanging fruit in the business for improvement, regardless of market conditions.

Brian Gray: Thanks, Brent. We are excited to build on EDGE 1.0 with Sharper EDGE. The good thing is it does impact all four of our segments. We have got line of sight, very specific opportunities that we have identified to go deploy that $125 million over the next three years in literally all four of our segments and in all of our product lines. I can tell you that it is very aggregates-centric, and that the majority of that capital is going to be deployed at approximately 23 of our aggregate sites that we have already identified plant improvements and cost-saving opportunities.

So, very aggregates-focused, very operationally focused, but the commercial excellence side of it and the organizational side of the initiative is also very meaningful. And organizational is a little bit new. We've started this about a year ago of really taking a closer look at our internal processes and our systems, and really just trying to find opportunities to streamline those processes to reduce our SG&A, and more importantly, get information out into the operator's hands to make quicker and better decisions. It impacts both back office and out in the operations, impacts all four segments and all of our product lines, Brent. Very excited to share more details, more specific goals and targets at an upcoming investor day.

Brent Thielman: Okay. Thanks, Brian. I guess the follow-up, maybe more specific to contracting services, has been a tougher year, obviously. I understand some of the challenging market dynamics today, and those might continue. But are these initiatives you're undertaking, whether short-term, medium-term, can they return that group to kind of the low double-digit margin performance next year, or-

Brent Thielman: do you need more market cooperation?

Brian Gray: Yeah, the market cooperation, and the good news is that there's demand for our services and the products that we provide, specifically asphalt paving. With the BUILD America 250 Act that we expect to be passed early next year, and the bipartisan support that we have in each one of our states for ongoing funding, there's strong demand for our products and services. We've had a lull that we've seen recently in some bid letting opportunities, specifically in the third quarter in a few of our markets. But we fully expect that is a cycle.

It's a cycle that we've been in before, and it will come out of it, and that we're very well-positioned to go out and capture the work that we do, specifically asphalt paving. The benefit of that is the pull-through of those higher-margin upstream materials, whether that's liquid asphalt, hot mix asphalt, and/or aggregates. We have initiatives underway. We've got some AI tools that are helping our estimators prospect for better leads that could lead to higher margins, where we have the ability to pivot between public and private work. We're still heavily geared towards low-bid, public-funded asphalt paving projects, but we certainly have the ability to pivot and go do more private work when the time is right.

There's opportunities for us to continue to have margin expansion, Brent, over today's backlog and the performance we've had this year. We actually saw sequentially in our backlog, for the first time in five quarters, that our backlog margin went up at the end of the third quarter compared to the end of the second quarter. We do see that we're headed in the right direction at contracting services.

Operator: Your next question comes from Kathryn Thompson with Thompson Research Group. Please go ahead.

Kathryn Thompson: Hi. The first question is more on the near term for the quarter just reported. In particular, an update on the geographic mix and the impact on earnings, particularly on margins. Stepping back, how has this changed over the past couple of years, especially in light of some of the challenges that Oregon has been, and where Oregon is today as an overall mix, and broadly how this impacts margins? Thank you.

Brian Gray: Yeah. Thank you, Kathryn. I mean, region mix has certainly had an impact on our overall EBITDA margins for the year. As you know, Kathryn, Oregon is a very important state for Knife River, so let me just provide some additional context for your appreciation. Oregon's been Knife River's largest state, both from a revenue standpoint and an EBITDA perspective for more than a decade. Its EBITDA margin has been in excess of 20% for the past three years, including this quarter's performance, which is actually higher in the third quarter year-over-year. So, they've been doing a great job of raising their margins, and it's a very important state to Knife River.

But as we've discussed, for the last two years, the state funding has had significant slowdown, and it had a dramatic impact on our revenue and its overall contribution to Knife River's overall portfolio. I do get to be very specific with you, Kathryn. Oregon was about 24% of our total revenue back in 2024, and today it's less than 17%, or a total decline of about 740 basis points as a percentage of our total revenue. So, it's been a challenge. It's absolutely had an impact on our overall EBITDA margin profile, and that has been the challenge. But there's good news in that.

First, that we've been here before with these types of funding issues, and like other states, I've got full confidence, being an Oregonian, that we will get through and they will get through their funding challenges. There's strong public support to improve Oregon's roads. There's strong bipartisan political support to fund it. There are roads and bridges in Oregon that have to get fixed, and I can tell you that we are very well positioned to capture that work when it returns. I think as the third quarter results suggest, our crews, our management team in Oregon are not just standing around waiting for that to happen. They have been actively controlling the things they can control.

They are right-sizing their crews and the equipment pools. They are selling materials to contractors doing other work, including private work. All of this has led to higher margins for the quarter, and again, continued EBITDA margin performance in excess of 20%. I think it is an understatement to say that we are well-positioned in Oregon to capture the opportunities when we come out of this cycle that we are in right now. Oregon has had a big impact on our overall region mix, and obviously our percent of EBITDA margin.

Kathryn Thompson: Okay, great. Thank you.

Brian Gray: Appreciate the question. Yep.

Kathryn Thompson: Yep. Shifting to backlogs. During our quarterly survey season, we heard from a wide variety of companies, private companies, that state DOTs are slowing lettings to create urgency going into the federal highway bill reauthorization, which we are currently on a CR. My question to you is, are you seeing that in the states in which you participate? How would that impact? If so, could explain some of the backlog that you reported in the quarter. Thanks very much for taking my questions today.

Brian Gray: Yeah. Thank you, Kathryn. I think it absolutely explains why our backlog is down 14%. We obviously had strong revenue generation in the third quarter. The fewer bid letting opportunities, yes, we have noticed that. I do not know exactly the reasons. If it is because they are trying to put some political pressure to have Congress pass a long-term reauthorization bill, which we fully expect that they will. It could also be a higher inflationary cost. Our customers, specifically the DOTs, are getting hit with those fuel escalations and oil escalation clauses. So, yes, we have seen a slowdown in bid opportunities. Specifically, we have talked about Oregon. We have seen it in Idaho.

Idaho is down almost 40% in bid lettings for the year. So, we have seen fewer bid lettings in some of our markets in the Midwest. Texas, which is a big state with a massive budget, their bid lettings were down 25% for the year. So, we have seen softness in the bid lettings that has led to a little bit lower backlog. It also has created the market dynamics that we have been talking about for the last two quarters, and frankly, had a fairly large impact on our contracting margins in the third quarter and year to date.

Fewer bid lettings and the same level or slightly more competition is going to create that bid room dynamic that we have been talking about. So, yes, we have seen that. Thank you for your question.

Operator: Your next question comes from Trey Grooms with Stephens. Please go ahead.

Trey Grooms: Hey, good morning, Brian, Nathan.

Trey Grooms: Hey, good morning. On page five, you laid out some of the actions you guys are taking to help navigate some of these near-term headwinds. Just curious, when do you see these actions start to bear some fruit? Maybe apart from EDGE, but just in the absence of a meaningful change in the demand environment, should we start to see some improvement going into next year, or how should we be thinking about the timing there, just given some of those changes you guys have made?

Brian Gray: Yeah. Let me talk about diesel to begin with, and the mitigation efforts that we have been taking. They are bearing fruit. We have recouped the majority of our actual direct impact as it relates to diesel. As we've talked about before, we consume about 25 million gallons of diesel per year. Our third quarter is our largest year, Trey. We saw, you've seen at the pumps that diesel prices went up about 40%. It was a large impact. Because of our commercial excellence teams and the work that our sales teams are doing, we recouped the majority of that direct impact to Knife River through our fuel surcharges and the escalations that we're getting from the DOTs.

What is lagging and what we are not necessarily recovering full recovery on are more of the indirect costs and the impact it is having on our cost of goods sold and our purchases going into some of our heavier bulk materials into ready-mix and asphalt and other product lines. There has been the fruits of our labor, we can see that on the energy costs. The delayed jobs, yes, that has been an impact in the second and third quarter. The asphalt paving specifically that we had budgeted and forecasted and built inventories of aggregates to go out and perform is behind schedule.

But they are paving now, and all that work gets shifted forward into either later this quarter or primarily next year, including the work at Pearl Harbor out on the P-209 project. That was a job that we had forecasted to produce a fair amount of concrete with our on-site batch plant, and that has been delayed for project scheduling reasons into next year. Again, those EBITDA dollars and those impacts that were headwinds for us in the third quarter, we will see those benefits next year. The market dynamics, Trey, is one that, again, we are right-sizing our crews.

I am excited to announce that if you look at contracting services and you look at the things that we can control, we actually were able to lower our cost of labor as a percent of revenue by 120 basis points for the quarter. In other words, the direct labor going out to job sites, the indirect labor that is in the office, as a percent of our revenue, we lowered that. So we are controlling the things that we could control. We are right-sizing equipment pools and crews for the market demand that we have got.

I think the fix to our market dynamics is to get on the other end of this cycle to get certainty with the infrastructure funding at the federal level, to continue to support the states that we are in, to continue to find more funding at the state level, and that quickly fixes itself, and we will see margins expand again there. Not a lot I can do and control on the price of diesel, obviously, or the DOT funding and bid lettings, but certainly are mitigating those impacts, and we are seeing results on those even in the third quarter.

Trey Grooms: Yep. Got it. Understood. Thanks for that. Then, maybe a little longer term or bigger picture just around Sharper EDGE. So, you guys had laid out long-term margin targets of 20%. Again, it is long term, and I understand it is not a straight line to get there, and there are market impacts and whatnot. But my question is, as you look at the things you are laying out here with Sharper EDGE, is that expected to be incremental to that 20% target over the long term? I know we might get more at Investor Day, but just to make sure we are thinking about this right.

Brian Gray: Yeah. Definitely will provide more detail at Investor Day, Trey, in a couple of months. No, I would say that Sharper EDGE is a continuation of our EDGE efforts that we laid out three years ago. Obviously, EDGE 1.0 was very focused on dynamic pricing, and most of the margin expansion that we enjoyed at the beginning of that was related to dynamic pricing and getting the full value of our materials.

We also launched the pit crews out into the fields, and I can tell you that the majority of the work they were doing were quick fixes while they're on site, lower capital-intensive improvements, and certainly saw, and we continue to see, we've had over 500 basis point improvement since launching EDGE in our aggregates margins. Sharper EDGE is a continuation of those efforts and taking some of the work that the pit crews have done, and they have identified very specific larger capital improvement projects to automate our plants, to completely reconfigure facilities, to change our mine planning.

This is where we have announced the $125 million of investment over the next three years that will be very targeted to our aggregate operations. There'll be some money spent in other product lines, but the majority of that's going to be aggregates. It's also going to lead to an incremental dollar per ton over what we're currently doing as it relates to those improvements. That's going to boost our way and help us get to those long-term targets. We've talked a fair amount about the project in South Dakota, the aggregate expansion project in South Dakota. That will be coming online the first half of next year. Those are at margins that are highly accretive to our existing margins.

Sharper EDGE is to look for more projects exactly like that. So very aggregates-centric, very specific capital deployment program to improve all of our operations, but specifically aggregates. Then I've obviously talked about the reduction in SG&A as part of that. Again, that's one of our multiple pathways to get to the long-term targets that we've stated earlier. Does that help you put that in context?

Trey Grooms: Yes. Yes, it does. Thank you, Brian. Best of luck and look forward to Investor Day.

Operator: Your next question comes from Garik Shmois with D.A. Davidson. Please go ahead.

Garik Shmois: Oh, hi. Thanks for taking my question. I wanted to follow up on the backlog. Just wondering how you are thinking about balancing backlog dollars with margin. It is good to hear that margin has improved, but will you be at a point here again in which you might need to trade margin for growing the backlog, just given some of the DOT headwinds that you spoke to?

Brian Gray: Yeah, I think that is a case-by-case, market-by-market analysis. I think you could look at what we did in the Mountain region this last year, and you saw it in the third quarter. They had lower margins, Garik, and we made a very intentional decision to go out and secure additional asphalt paving work, and you can see the benefit. I mean, the overall EBITDA in the Mountain region for the quarter was 10% more than it was a year ago. But we do not have to do that in every market. It will be selective. We will continue to be disciplined, and we will look for the right opportunities to take advantage of our vertical integration model.

I think more work coming into the pipeline of bid lettings will certainly help that a lot as far as margins, and we are well-positioned to capture that. The thing we like about our vertical integration model is that we can have multiple opportunities to win on bid day. We can bid that work, as we have talked about in the past, as a prime contractor.

We can bid that work to go out and do just the specific work that we do as a subcontractor, and maybe that is most likely hot mix asphalt paving for a larger prime, or we will sell our hot mix asphalt to a competitor, or we will sell our aggregates to an hot mix asphalt producer. We have got multiple ways to win, and so that will help offset the margin challenges in the bid room that we are seeing now. I think more work is going to definitely help that situation, Garik.

Garik Shmois: Okay. Thanks for that. Wanted to look ahead to 2027. I know we are not there yet, but I was wondering if you could speak to any preliminary expectations you might have regarding volume and pricing, thinking about aggregates primarily, but any other comments you might have about some of the downstream businesses would be great.

Brian Gray: Yeah, I think the glide path that you have seen us on pricing and enjoying some healthy prices on aggregates is going to continue. I think the demand environment continues to be strong. I think this is a lull in bid lettings that we are seeing. The infrastructure scorecard is still at a D+. There is bipartisan support, and so I think once we get more certainty at the federal level, we will see the public demand continue. Even at today's dollars, most of our DOT budgets are at or near record levels. That is a very important vehicle for us, is DOT funding. We are also seeing good opportunities that is public funding, but not necessarily the traditional DOT.

In our markets that we work in, there is a lot of military spending that we are going on, and we are benefiting from one of those big projects right now in Hawaii, another big project up in Grand Forks at the Air Force base up there. So, there is military spending that we are seeing. Then, obviously, the non-resi side next year. We sit very well in the markets that we are in. These mid-sized markets that we operate in have become attractive areas for developers to build some of these larger warehouses, data centers. We have got some of those in our backyard right now, and we will benefit from that next year.

We are 12 mi from a very large project outside of Bryan, Texas, and there is data centers being built in Wyoming and in Oregon and North Dakota right now. We see that demand environment going into next year continuing to be strong. Our commercial excellence team should allow us to continue to have the pricing momentum that we've enjoyed the past couple years. Then you couple that with our new, very line-of-sight, very targeted initiatives to control costs and improve productivity. I'm excited about what I see in 2027.

Garik Shmois: Okay. Thank you very much. Best of luck.

Operator: Your next question comes from Sherif El-Sabbahy with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Sherif El-Sabbahy: Hi, good morning. I just wanted to put

Sherif El-Sabbahy: a bit of a finer point on the backlog discussion. I understand you're working on prospecting better margin work, but just with to the lower margin that's in backlog this year, how should we think about the impact of that rolling out over the coming few quarters?

Brian Gray: Yeah, I think an important part of that, Sherif, is that I had mentioned that for the first time in five quarters, that we have seen our backlog margin improve sequentially from the end of the second quarter to the end of the third quarter. I think that's something I've been watching very closely, and I think that's a good sign. The other thing that I can tell you is that because we have the ability to pivot and go look at private work and not just public work, and that our crews are very geared to go out and do that type of work, that should also help that situation.

The ultimate solution to this problem is, again, to pass the long-term, reauthorize the Surface Transportation Bill at the federal level and start fixing the roads and bridges that we know that the engineers and the public works directors and the state engineers have said need to get fixed. That is a cycle we've seen before. We lived through this before, and we've seen our backlog fluctuate before. I've got good confidence that we'll continue to rebuild that backlog. We're going into the heart of our bidding season right now. Our busiest bidding periods are from November through April, especially in the markets that we operate in.

Anxious to give more updates on our backlog and where we see that going again as the year progresses next year.

Sherif El-Sabbahy: Thank you. Then I understand you are going into the bidding season, and the federal funding is sort of the key item to monitor. But you mentioned there has been a few more bid opportunities this quarter. What other signs are you watching, or what sign points are you looking forward to see lettings improve here?

Brian Gray: Yeah. So the new AI software called Prospect, it is an internal tool that our team has recently built. That is yielding some new information that we had not seen before. We are broadening our reach and getting data points that are different. I can tell you that some of our states that are slower are looking at adjacent states to go into, specifically Oregon going into Washington and other adjacent states we may not be currently working in. So, we are aggressively pursuing work. We know the importance of our vertical integration model and that the vehicle that the contracting services provides to pull through additional materials is important.

But I would also look at our third-party sales from our materials divisions to our competing contractors on bid day. If we do not get the work as a contractor, I can tell you, if you look at our third-party sales, those have increased, and that is a very concentrated effort that our commercial sales teams are focused on, is not putting all the pressure on bid day to build backlog, but to go out and get the higher margin materials that we benefit from on the material side of the business.

Operator: Your next question comes from Timna Tanners with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.

Timna Tanners: Yeah. Hey, good morning, everyone.

Timna Tanners: I wanted to dig in a little bit more. Hello. I wanted to ask a little bit more about the project delays, and of course, when you talk about some of the measures being transient, it would be helpful to understand what gives you that conviction. From past cycles, when you do see these project delays, have they resulted in eventual projects going forward, or do they result in cancellations at some point?

Brian Gray: No, great question. The project delays that we have talked about, there are three very specific projects. There is the State Highway 6 project in Texas, the State Highway 190 in Texas, and then the P-209 concrete supply project in Hawaii. Timna, we have not seen any projects that are part of our backlog that have been canceled or delayed and/or waiting for funding. These are scheduling delays, weather-related delays, really just phasing of construction activity. We are pouring concrete underwater in Hawaii on the dry dock at Pearl Harbor, and they needed to finish driving the piles before we could pour the concrete.

This is not a matter of funding or uncertainty where we are worried about these projects being delayed. This truly is just construction phasing, just related to permitting, engineering, and those types of events out on the job site. Nothing in our backlog have we seen be delayed or potentially canceled because of any kind of funding situations.

Timna Tanners: Okay. Thanks for that. I wanted to ask also, you talked about continuing to look at M&A, but you are also a little bit outside of your target leverage ratio. So, do you pause M&A until you kind of get back in that range, or how are you thinking about the cadence there?

Brian Gray: I will let Nathan take that one.

Nathan Ring: Yeah. Good morning. Thank you for the question. If we go back to a few quarters. First, let's set the landscape for where our balance sheet stands today. We do have a very strong balance sheet. In fact, our liquidity is at $566 million. Of that, $118 million is cash. One of the first questions we get is, "Are you able to still respond quickly if there's an opportunity?" I think our liquidity position indicates that. From the strength of the balance sheet standpoint, back to your 2.9x, the thing I would remind you is that this is a part of the year to where we start to get back towards net leverage near our target of 2.5x.

We do anticipate being modestly above that. But what I have shared in previous quarters, which is important, is that we would look at going near three times for the right organic project, for the right acquisition project, keeping in mind that we would look at the cash flows, the returns, and margins of that project, that it would quickly get us back to that 2.5x.

So, Timna, I think from a balance sheet standpoint, good liquidity, cash flows this year from a cash flow from operations to EBITDA conversion, probably close to 55%, and then the willingness temporarily to go to that near three times all indicate that if we do have good opportunities come through, we're still in a very good position to pursue them.

Operator: Your next question comes from Chris Ellinghaus with Siebert Williams Shank. Please go ahead.

Chris Ellinghaus: Hi, everybody. How are you today?

Brian Gray: Good morning, Chris. Good, thank you.

Chris Ellinghaus: Brian, you seem confident on the reauthorization, but have you got any concerns that, particularly, we'll see what the election looks like today, and even though it may be pretty universal across parties, maybe that's not necessarily the primary goals initially of the new Congress. Do you have any concerns about the timing of reauthorization at all?

Brian Gray: I don't have any concerns that they're going to get it done, Chris, because they have to, and they know that, and there's full support for that, and they understand the cost of delays. Our industry associations have done a great job at educating legislators in Congress that the longer you wait and kick the can down the road, the more exponentially expensive it gets. They all understand that. Yes, the timing, I would say I'm not going to speculate on that other than the work has been done. There's been a lot of very good work done in the last Congress.

There is full support at the administration and in both the House and the Senate on both the Democrats and Republican sides. I do expect that's going to get passed sooner than later. It's a top priority. I mean, the economy that we've been talking about, and you turn on the news, you hear it every day, a very important part of the economy is to keep freight and people moving and not in congestion, and that you have safe roads and bridges to be driving on, and everybody agrees with that. I'm not going to speculate on the timing, Chris.

I just have full conviction that it's going to get done sooner than later, like it always has, and we'll stay tuned and watch the election results tonight.

Chris Ellinghaus: Okay. Similar lines, have you got any update to your sense of the cadence of when Oregon will address right-sizing its DOT budget?

Brian Gray: Yeah. They're talking about it a lot. They're doing more than talking. I mean, they've got work groups. They're traveling the state. They're prioritizing projects. They are reorganizing the department. They are looking for leadership. There's a lot of activities going on in Oregon. This has been a couple years down the road now. This started early in 2025. Again, Oregonians, both taxpayers and engineers and road masters, know the cost of delaying these projects, Chris, and they become much more expensive to fix and consume a lot more materials the longer you wait. I can tell you there are lots of potholes and cracked roads and aging bridges that have got to get fixed in Oregon. Everybody knows that.

They're working hard on it and fully expect that when the time is right for the legislature to come back into session early next year, that's going to be one of their top priorities.

Chris Ellinghaus: Okay. Appreciate it. Thanks.

Operator: Your next question comes from Ivan Yi with Wolfe Research. Please go ahead.

Operator: Please ensure you unmute. Moving on to Rohit Seth with B. Riley. Please go ahead, Rohit.

Rohit Seth: Hey. Thanks for taking my question. Just on the Q4 guide, you got the range at $95 million-$125 million. You did about $119 million last year. Can you just walk us through the scenarios to get you to the high end and the low end and the midpoint?

Brian Gray: Yeah. I'll talk, kind of the puts and takes on that. We obviously, Rohit, guide to normal weather, and as you know, as we're entering into November, December, that can fluctuate a lot. Last year, we had very favorable weather in the fourth quarter and performed work literally up until a couple weeks before Christmas. If we were to have favorable weather in November, December, that would put us toward the high side of that. If we get some early winter, that really does shut a lot of our operations down, and that would probably be the largest put and take for the remainder of the year.

Obviously, we've talked enough about this, but we are out paving right now, and we have a schedule to go pave in Texas on those two big projects. We've put that as our midpoint of this paving schedule that we've got. There's some hopes that they could expedite and get some additional tonnages out of there yet this year that would put us a little on the high side, but we've also seen a lot of delays for the last six months, and that would put us on the low side.

The other thing that I'd say that this time of year, we're closing out jobs, and there's opportunities to earn a fair amount of quality bonuses for the work that we do. Those incentives, those bonuses get paid typically at the end of the job, and as do some of the fuel escalators and oil escalators. Depending on the timing of us closing out some of the work that we are currently working on, and some of the lags that we have seen of getting the fuel escalations, that could have a positive or negative impact on the fourth quarter. That is also baked within that range. Those would be the large puts and takes for the fourth quarter.

Nathan Ring: The only thing I would add to that.

Nathan Ring: It is an important point you made, Rohit, with the end of the quarter for us as it relates to the bonuses and the incentives that Brian has talked about, we actually see in the fourth quarter for contracting services, and you look over the last four years, historically, that fourth quarter for contracting services actually has higher gross margin than the third quarter and actually the year to date on average. As Brian talks about that, this is something that we do see depends upon, like you said, as those jobs close out. #3122. AI Pods Are Redefining The Unit Of Software Delivery

Alexey Spas is the founder and CEO of Instinctools, a software engineering company focused on AI-powered digital solutions.

For most of the software industry’s history, when a software backlog started growing faster than the team could handle it, a CTO or product leader knew what came next. It was either opening new roles or sending some work to an outside partner.

Whichever the option, the rule of thumb used to be the same: More software to build meant more people needed to build it, until AI put that long-held assumption into question.

A senior engineer working with coding agents can now produce far more raw output than before. That is why software delivery is beginning to reorganize around a different unit: a small senior team surrounded by AI-enabled workflows.

The label is still loose, but the operating idea is easy to picture: An AI pod is a compact, senior-led engineering team accountable for a defined software outcome. Specialized AI agents support the delivery flow from requirements drafting to code generation and testing, while humans keep their hands on the wheel when it comes to business context, quality, security and the final result.​​

And just like that, AI has completely reshuffled the deck for software engineering. An age-old dilemma is now taking on new contours: If companies need a different kind of delivery unit, where should it live? Some organizations will have good reasons to build it in-house. Others may prefer to bring in an external pod. For many, the most practical answer may sit somewhere in between.​

A big part of the appeal of an in-house AI pod is its lean structure, and it’s not hard to see why: Hiring one or two senior engineers supported by AI agents is a very different proposition from building a cross-functional team of five-plus people.

The strongest case for keeping the pod internal, though, may have less to do with headcount than with proximity of in-house engineers to the product, business context and the decisions. Moreover, the lessons learned while building AI-enabled delivery workflows remain inside the organization.

That advantage takes time to build. Giving experienced developers access to coding agents does not immediately produce an effective AI delivery system. Teams still have to determine what can safely be delegated, where human review belongs, which quality gates can be automated and how AI-generated work fits into the rest of the software lifecycle.

There is also the expertise question. A small pod can still draw on a broad range of skills. A modernization effort can suddenly require security input, an AI-heavy feature may call for data engineering or a customer-facing workflow may need experienced UX support. Building all of those competencies internally makes sense when the demand is sustained. It is harder to justify when the need appears for only a few weeks.​

There is no secret AI stack tool available only to software vendors. Anyone can access the same models, coding assistants and agentic frameworks. The advantage of an external pod usually comes from reducing the distance between access to AI and a delivery system that works.

If spinning up a few agents could solve the software delivery problem overnight, things would be simple. In practice, faster generation creates its own downstream load: More code has to be reviewed, tested, integrated and checked for security. The challenge is turning that AI-driven speed into production-ready software.

An outsourced team that has already cut its teeth on different projects can bring patterns refined across more than one production environment: agent configurations, evaluation methods, review workflows, reusable components and quality controls. I know—there’s a lot of skepticism when software development vendors talk about their “unique expertise.” But in this case, uniqueness does not mean exclusive knowledge that nobody else can acquire. It just implies a shorter route through mistakes someone else has already made and experience that has been tested often enough to become adaptable.

There is also a flip side to that breadth of experience. An external pod does not begin with the same institutional knowledge as an internal team, nor is it naturally as close to every product decision. The model makes the most sense when the value of faster ramp-up, cross-project experience or temporary capacity outweighs the benefits of having a team deeply embedded in the product.​

When a company needs AI-enabled delivery capability now but is not yet certain how much of it should become a fixed part of the organization, a hybrid model can be considered. Demand may surge around a product launch, modernization program or backlog push, and then ease again. An external pod can take the edge off this sudden spike without turning peak capacity into permanent headcount.

The same arrangement can also serve a longer-term purpose. A company that ultimately wants the capability in-house can use an outsourced pod as a working prototype for the team it may later build itself.

A “borrow, prove, then build” approach gives leaders a chance to observe which roles they repeatedly need, which workflows survive production, where human judgment remains essential and which metrics genuinely improve. The parts that prove strategic can then move inside the organization with much less guesswork.​

AI pods are making the old build-versus-buy decision more nuanced. For leaders, the choice comes down to a few practical questions: How enduring is the demand? How important is institutional knowledge? How quickly should the capability become operational?

The answers may change as the organization learns. That is probably the main point. AI is reshaping software delivery quickly enough that the operating model that fits today does not have to be the one a company commits to for good.​​

#3120. Hagerty (HGTY) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Written premiums climbed while loss estimates fell, and the full-year outlook moved higher.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Hagerty, Inc. (HGTY +7.17%) reported growth in written premiums and raised its full-year financial outlook following stronger-than-expected underwriting results and loss trends. Management reported that the company's profitability benefited from a $32 million reduction in estimated losses and the ongoing rollout of the State Farm partnership, which has expanded into 41 states. The company closed its acquisition of the United Kingdom specialty broker Bennetts in October, intended to strengthen its international footprint. Management also noted that operational efficiencies, including the implementation of artificial intelligence for member service tasks, contributed to a 20% improvement in employee productivity.

Cars go back into their garages for their winter slumber, and much of the action in the car world moves indoors to the auction room. We saw this with the nine price records Broad Arrow set at The Quail Auction in Monterey during the third quarter, and strong gains at more recent auctions in October with Zoute in Belgium up 35%, and this past weekend at the Concours at Wynn Las Vegas, where sales jumped sevenfold from last year's inaugural auction.

If you have never been to a live auction, I take you inside the room in this quarter's Stockholder Letter, and I hope one day you will join us in person and raise a paddle. You see it in the consistency of our mid-teens written premium growth and the quality of our underwriting over the years. The third quarter of 2026 was our 15th quarter in a row of meeting or beating expectations, shown on slides three and four. Over the first nine months of 2026, written premium grew 18% as we added a record 402,000 new members.

Adjusted EBITDA jumped 43% to $257 million, and net income was $32 million. These profit metrics benefited from our $32 million of lower estimated losses. We have invested significantly in our claims teams, which is almost 40% larger than it was two years ago, and I want to thank them for the great work they are doing. Careful underwriting, members who take care of their special cars, and favorable industry trends also contributed to these results. Given the strength of our year-to-date numbers, we are increasing our full-year 2026 profit outlook, reflecting premium growth, strong retention, and improved underwriting economics.

Patrick will share the details, but the key takeaway is that we are executing well on our strategy and remain on track to reach 3 million policies in force by 2030. One more milestone since the quarter ended. On October 8th, we closed our acquisition of Bennetts, the second-largest specialty motorcycle insurance broker in the United Kingdom. While modest in size, it is an important step for us. Together with Broad Arrow's growing presence there, it gives us a base to bring insurance, auctions, and community together for motorcycle and car enthusiasts in Europe. I would like to give a warm Hagerty welcome to Bennetts employees and their members.

Looking ahead, I see three reasons growth should continue: how we reach members, the next generation of collectors, and what Broad Arrow brings to Hagerty. B2B distribution with large carriers and a network of 54,000 independent agents complement our direct efforts and should support consistent high rates of growth. The State Farm Classic+ rollout is progressing well, with our captive agents now selling Hagerty-powered policies in 41 states. The conversion of State Farm's existing Classic book of 525,000 policies is tracking to plan, with 26 states in process at quarter-end.

As we look to the B2B pipeline for 2028 and beyond, we are making solid progress deepening existing relationships and cultivating new ones, and look forward to sharing updates over the coming quarters. Beyond distribution gains, the market itself can provide tailwinds. While daily driver insurance companies underwrite to depreciating value curves, we underwrite collector cars that are positioned for modest appreciation over time. Collector car values have been moving higher this year, particularly at the high end. Total vehicle sales in Monterey in August across all auction houses reached a record $756 million, up 75% from the prior year. Modern supercars and hypercars accounted for half of all sales, with bidders from multiple continents and generations driving record prices.

I've seen several peaks and troughs over the years, and I would not be surprised to see prices take a breather at some point after the sharp rise in 2026, but I believe the long-term trends on these increasingly scarce assets remains up and to the right. Why do I believe this? Heightened demand is partly the result of the generational shift we are seeing in our quote volume, as Gen X, Millennials, and Gen Z now account for over 60% of our quotes. These younger cohorts are coveting the post-1980s cars of their youth, the same way Boomers coveted 1960s European race cars and American muscle cars. Baby Boomers remain an important driver of our growth.

We recently met a Boomer collector at a September car show who owns an impressive portfolio of 14 British classics, including an Aston Martin DB5, an Austin-Healey 3000, and a Jaguar E-Type, to name a few. The car he chose to bring to the local car event was his newly acquired McLaren MP4. When asked, he told us the reason he loves Hagerty is that we not only protect his vintage collection of 1950s and 1960s cars, but are also able to insure a modern supercar like his McLaren. Broad Arrow is benefiting from the demand across different age groups, with year-to-date auction sales up 83%.

The main driver of our results is the share we have gained since launching five years ago, with the goal of becoming the trusted partner for car collectors. Similar to our insurance business, we are investing in Broad Arrow's capabilities because we intend to continue gaining share over the long run. Auctions are becoming an important channel for future members to first meet Hagerty. A buyer who takes home a car or a seller who trusts us with a consignment can become a policyholder, join Hagerty Drivers Club, and come back for the next sale. Retention of 88% and a Net Promoter Score roughly double the industry suggests those relationships tend to last.

We want to make it easy for any new buyer of a collector car to insure with Hagerty, so we were pleased to see Barrett-Jackson name us as its official insurance partner. That is why we think of Broad Arrow as a customer acquisition and engagement platform for Hagerty, in addition to being a great auction business. Patrick McClymont: Thank you, McKeel, and good morning, everyone. Starting with slides five and six, we delivered written premium gains of 16% in the quarter and 18% during the first nine months of the year. Two-year trends were steady in the third quarter as we compare against higher rates of growth from the second half of 2025. The increase is driven by policy count, not rate, as we continue adding high-retention members attracted by our value proposition. As we described on prior calls, the 2026 GAAP presentation reflects the Markel fronting transition, where under the new structure, MGA commission revenue and the associated ceding commission expense eliminate against each other in consolidation.

That is why reported year-to-date GAAP revenue of $1 billion declined 7%, even as written premium grew 18%. Let me break down the components of our third-quarter revenue. Earned premium grew 42% to $265 million due to written premium gains combined with the increase in our quota share to 100%. Commission and fee revenue for the quarter was $22 million. As noted, this line item is no longer comparable to prior periods given the elimination of Markel-related commissions in consolidation, but is ramping quickly as State Farm conversions progress. Third-quarter marketplace revenue declined 6% to $32 million. Auction growth of 65% was more than offset by lower inventory sales during the quarter.

As a reminder, when we sell a car from our own inventory, we record the full sale price as revenue and the cost of the car as expense rather than just a commission, so revenue can swing more based on the level of inventory sales. Marketplace's third-quarter net loss improved by $3 million year-over-year. Monterey sell-through rates were 85%, with the generational broadening McKeel described helping drive demand at the high end. Membership and other revenue came in at $22 million, with 6% growth in Hagerty Drivers Club paid memberships. Insurance members who are also HDC members retain and cross-purchase at higher rates.

Net investment income was $13 million during the quarter, benefiting from our larger Hagerty Re portfolio and steady returns from the predominantly fixed-income investments. Turning now to profitability, shown on slides seven and eight, Hagerty Re's combined ratio came in at 85.2% during the first nine months, helped by $32 million of lower estimated losses. This includes a $26 million reduction related to our current accident year recorded in the third quarter. This reflects lower physical damage costs and liability claims running below our estimates, and is in addition to the $6 million favorable development of 2025 accident year losses that we recorded in the first quarter.

We believe the substantial investments in our in-house claims capabilities are helping contribute to the lower losses. As McKeel noted, we intentionally grew that team by 40%, including doubling the size of the Material Damage and Special Investigation Units. Industry frequency trends have also been favorable, which has helped as well. One of Hagerty's biggest strengths is how our losses behave compared to daily driver insurers. Our members take meticulous care of their cars, and when a storm is forecast, our team alerts them through our Guardian program. With enough notice, many move their cars to higher and drier ground, whether that's one of the garage spots we reserve for them or an inland parking lot.

High drive-away rates are a big reason our losses have consistently come in better than daily driver CAT models would predict, and why reinsurers and AM Best value this lack of correlation with daily driver losses. Our loss ratios are much more stable than the industry's, with roughly 35% lower volatility since 2010, which is also a compelling story for reinsurers as we formalize next year's program at attractive prices. While we've had an uneventful CAT season for the last two years, the percentage impact that hurricanes can have on our profitability continues to diminish as we scale up. In 2024, Hurricanes Helene and Milton totaled $27 million against adjusted EBITDA of $162 million.

With the growth of our EBITDA since 2024, similarly sized events would have roughly half the impact on current profits. On the technology front, we are making meaningful investments in our platforms and artificial intelligence that should allow us to both serve members better and drive operating leverage. Our member service center is a great example, where we now require just one full-time employee for every 2,800 policies in force. This is a 20% year-over-year productivity improvement across a book of 1.9 million policies. AI-assisted call summaries and workflow automation are handling tasks that previously required manual effort.

This frees up our team to focus on the work only they can do, such as assisting a stranded member with a flatbed for their 1968 Camaro, helping a new member understand the difference between Guaranteed Value and Actual Cash Value coverage, and building the kind of relationship that turns a first-time auction buyer into a 20-year Hagerty member. Our Net Promoter Score remains top of the field, and our members rate their experience 4.93 out of five stars on Trustpilot, and we intend to keep investing in the technology and people behind those scores. In the third quarter, adjusted EBITDA was $97 million, resulting in year-to-date adjusted EBITDA of $257 million, up 43%.

During the first nine months, we have incurred $88 million in new acquisition expenses that were capitalized, of which only $36 million was recognized on the P&L, resulting in a benefit to our adjusted EBITDA of $52 million. In the third quarter, we recorded an income tax expense of $5 million compared to a $33 million benefit in the prior year period when we released a portion of the valuation allowance. The change in tax was driven by non-reversing differences between taxable income and pre-tax book income related to the fronting arrangement, chiefly the ceding commission Hagerty Re deducts on its tax return, but that we eliminate in consolidation.

GAAP net income of $36 million in the third quarter includes $36 million of amortization of deferred ceding commissions for 2025 year policies. Year-to-date GAAP net income of $32 million includes $189 million of amortization related to deferred ceding commissions paid to Markel for policies written prior to January 1, 2026. Net income attributable to Class A common shareholders in the third quarter was $8 million. GAAP basic and diluted earnings per share were both $0.08. Adjusted earnings per share, based on 361 million fully diluted shares, came in at $0.10. Nine-month operating cash flow was $280 million, up 48% from the prior year period, reflecting significantly enhanced economics to Hagerty under the new structure and improved working capital.

As of September 30th, 2026, we had $461 million in unrestricted cash and total debt of $247 million, which includes $103 million from the back-leverage facility for Broad Arrow's portfolio of collector car loans. The balance sheet is in great shape, with ample liquidity to fund high-return investments in organic growth, the Bennetts acquisition, and ongoing technology investments. Let me close with our updated 2026 outlook, which we increased again, shown on slide nine. We anticipate 2026 written premium growth to come in at the high end of our 16%-17% range.

We are raising our expectations for GAAP net income to a range of $48 million-$60 million, and for adjusted EBITDA to a range of $305 million-$315 million, reflecting our year-to-date outperformance and sustained business momentum. This outlook includes the $52 million benefit from capitalizing MGA acquisition costs in 2026, a timing effect that is largely complete as of September 30th and will not repeat again in 2027.
