As we think about just the fourth quarter and then heading into the first part of 2027, I guess, any seasonality you would just kind of highlight in terms of thinking about just PIF growth over the next few quarters?

Patrick McClymont: Yeah, I think we've given our written premium updated guidance, and so you can kind of derive from that what we think the fourth quarter looks like. As you expect, it does slow down seasonally. No comments yet on next year other than. The nature of our business is we're able to. The driving season is the second and third quarters. Typically, the second is going to be the peak, and during the first and fourth, it's typically quieter from a new business standpoint. So we don't expect that to change. Under the new accounting approach, right, there's much less seasonality in the revenues.

You asked that question on the last call or the one before that, and you were spot on. The P&L looks different on a go-forward basis, but the underlying sales cycle is the same.

Operator: One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from the line of Michael Phillips of Oppenheimer. Your line is now open.

Michael Phillips: Thank you. Good morning. You have been clear in the past about talking about investing well ahead of growth, but those costs probably would not go away, I guess, as the business grows. I want to get a sense of, as we look past maybe 2027 and into the longer term, 2028 and prior, and after that, are we approaching a period where the earnings grow, where those investments kind of flow through back into earnings, or do more investment opportunities keep that spending growth kind of elevated?

Patrick McClymont: Well, we have talked about in terms of long term, and I guess we are a year and a half into this or so, but doubling the business by 2030, right? That is in terms of the members that we serve. We do, we are investing to support that growth, and we will continue to do so. If you look at the numbers, we have continued to expand margins since we began that journey sort of in 2023. We will see how this year wraps up, but we will expect that we are expanding margins again this year, which is what we guided to. It is a balancing act, right?

We want to continue to march on a path to what we think is the right long-term margin structure for the business. But because we are deep enough into that path, we do have the flexibility to invest well ahead of growth. That is a balancing act that our leadership team and McKeel and myself, we spend a lot of time on. We are going through it right now for the planning process. If we want to keep growing for the long haul, not just double by 2030, but continue to have this be a growth business, there always will be opportunities to invest to support that growth.

Our job is to strike that balance and kind of give you communications on a year-by-year basis how we think the margins are trending.

Michael Phillips: Okay, Patrick. Thanks. I just want to switch gears to the Enthusiast+ program. I know it is small and it is early stages, but I am trying to get a sense of what the price sensitivity of that book might, or those customers might be relative to your core book. I am curious if there is any differences there, given obviously the soft market that traditional insurance is in. If those folks have more sensitivity to price, does that maybe make the early phases of growth for the Enthusiast+ a little more difficult than what otherwise might be the case?

Patrick McClymont: I think the answer is it is too early to tell. We have been in one market for a year and a half or so now. The other markets are just in the last handful of months. We are learning. We have launched in these markets. We are only doing direct, as we have talked about, direct to consumer. We are not doing anything through agents and brokers. It is out in the wild on a limited basis, and we are learning, but it is too early to draw any conclusions.

Michael Phillips: Okay, thanks. Appreciate it.

Operator: One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from the line of Kevin Wijendra of JPMorgan. Your line is now open.

Kevin Wijendra: Hi. Thanks for taking my question. This is Kevin on for Pablo. There's been some fears on AI disrupting the personal auto market. Is there any impacts you're seeing from AI on shopping trends so far? If so, it looks like 55% of your sales comes through your agent channel. How is Hagerty positioned to deal with AI coming into the market? Thanks.

McKeel Hagerty: Oh, thanks, Kevin. It's the question of the hour, the month, every single conference I go to. The way we look at AI, it's really a layered approach. The investments we're making in AI for our own purposes range from, as was described already in our previous comments, how we can assist our team members and how call flows work, all that sort of thing, whether those come from a direct consumer, whether they come from agents. It's really amplifying the work that our great team members can already do.

There's also the big, great opportunities in the middle of this business, the sort of middleware part of the business, which is how we administer the organization itself, the efficiencies that we can find there. Then, from a real underlying basis, how is this going to help sort of transform insurance? When I say help, I mean really help. Insurance is a business that can really, I think, benefit greatly from the opportunities that AI tool will bring to it, the way you analyze data, the way that you process information, the way that you serve customers. So far, we are not seeing some very different type of customer behavior based on them using AI to shop differently.

We're not seeing it either on the direct or on the B2B side of the house, but we're anticipating it. We know our future quoting engines and servicing engines are going to have to be capable of not only helping people on the other side of the transaction, but also to be able to help agents on the other side of the transaction. We're designing for it, we're building it in, and we're already seeing some benefit with the internal, those kind of three-layer approach that we have. But we're really preparing for that future you're describing.

Operator: One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from the line of Mark Hughes of Truist. Your line is now open.

Mark Hughes: Yeah. Thank you very much. With the better loss experience, sounds like you are doing really well with the internal claims capability. Is there a potential for loss picks potentially to be a little bit lower?

Patrick McClymont: Yeah. We will tell you when we tell you, Mark. We are going through that process now, and we will share guidance on the fourth quarter call. We are pleased with both sort of our internal performance and then obviously the market trends as we have talked about. So, that is part of our consideration set as we do the plan for next year, but nothing to preview right now.

Mark Hughes: Yeah. Okay. Very good. When you think about the improved performance on the liability claims, you just alluded to the fact that you're seeing broader market improvement. I am not sure if it is the liability specifically, but anything you can say about that? Seems significant. Just curious what your experience might be telling you on the liability front.

McKeel Hagerty: Hey, Mark. Good morning, and thanks for being on. Yeah, I mean, a lot of what we talked about in the remarks are how we have been investing in the physical damage side or Material Damage side of the business, and that includes and also on the SIU standpoint. So, we have been boosting our capabilities on Material Damage, which is how we internally adjust for losses and work with repair shops, restoration shops to get our members' cars back on the road. The SIU, which is, of course, Special Investigative stuff, is really meant to make sure that we are managing our results by carefully looking at losses to make sure that there is no fraud involved with them.

You cannot price for fraud in insurance, so you have to be really careful when you identify instances of it. We are really proud of the teams really having millions of dollars of benefit to the business as we are being very, very careful with it. On the liability side, frequency is down. So, it is a unique thing that is happening right now post-COVID when there was a lot of people out driving, a lot of people buying all sorts of cars. Frequency is down, and so that does have a downstream impact, of course, in liability losses.

I would also say, even though the rate increases that we have taken, and as we have described to you in the past, the rates that we have taken, while modest in comparison to daily driver insurance, many of the rate increases were targeted in the lines of liability. Those are the areas that there are a lot of elements to liability claims that are out of our control, whether it is when you are talking about tort-type situations or other legal situations where we just kind of get wrapped up in things.

So, I think we are targeting the right things with the modest rate increases that we take, and we are focused on the other things that we can really control, which is Material Damage and SIU.

Operator: One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from the line of Mitchell Rubin of Raymond James. Your line is now open.

Mitchell Rubin: Hey, good morning. This is Mitch on for Greg. On slide four, you identify refining the Hagerty Drivers Club offering as a priority. What changes are you making, and how do you see its role within the broader Hagerty business evolving?

McKeel Hagerty: Thank you. It is a great question, one I am very passionate about. I think one of the things that differentiates Hagerty is how we treat our members. When we say member, it is not just a throwaway term. It is really welcoming them into our ecosystem as somebody we care about, somebody that we understand. They are not just a car owner, ideally, that insures with us, but they may be browsing on our marketplace, they may be buying a Broad Arrow site, they may be buying a ticket to one of our events, or they are reading our media.

The big thing for us is, how do we bring the maximum amount of people who are already consuming some part of the Hagerty ecosystem, but perhaps not even insurance, and how do we make them a member? The design change will really emphasize how we can bring people in as ideally a free member or a trial member as they come into Hagerty Drivers Club. Then for those who want to pay for the paid levels of Hagerty Drivers Club over time, that is very, very easy for them to do. Ideally, that attaches to an insurance policy. It is great when we insure cars and then also make them a paid member.

But we really need that HDC benefit that we are already investing in and is already being consumed by a lot of people to bring more people in through the door in that free or trial membership basis. That is the design change. We look forward to rolling more of that out next year.

Mitchell Rubin: I appreciate the color. How are the investments in your independent agent channel translating into new business production, and where do you see the biggest opportunity to increase productivity?

McKeel Hagerty: This is really a big investment in the team. We have some incredible new leadership in the insurance side in this channel. Jeff Briglia, who is the President of our Insurance business, has recruited really an A-level team. Adam Van Loon, who comes to us with an incredible career of experience in building out these types of channels. When I think of this side of the business, of course, you have got the big partnerships we have with the big company underwriting carriers, like a State Farm, Allstate, Progressive, on down the line. But we already mentioned we have 54,000 agents that we are working with, that are just many times just Main Street agents with access to great customers.

One of our big jobs there is to be segmenting that business, focusing on the agents that are really growing, where we know that there are opportunities using data resources to help them understand that as the vehicles that we are seeing coming in, say, in the direct channel, are getting newer with younger collectors more interested in these newer vehicle segments, our job is to make sure that we are communicating that to agents. We are helping them understand that there is a lot of that opportunity in their own books of businesses already.

It is a big communications opportunity, a big communications challenge, and it is really, in my mind, the ground war that is going to help us on this path of doubling the business by 2030 and to keep that trajectory strong out past into the 2030s. Very important part of our growth strategy.

Operator: Our last question comes from the line of Tommy McJoynt of KBW. Your line is now open.

Tommy McJoynt: Hey, good morning. When we look at the full-year adjusted EBITDA guide, so it increased by about $35 million at the midpoint. In your guys' own internal projections, was the improvement this quarter entirely driven by the better loss and claims experience in the loss ratio, or was there anything else on the operating expense side or revenue side that allowed you to raise the full year guide?

Patrick McClymont: You talked about the $35 million is the increase, right? $26 million of that is what we released in this quarter. The other $9 million are strong operations within the business. The way that we think about that is a fair bit of that is the fact that there is operating leverage inherent in the business. We are being disciplined, and we are making investments, we talked about earlier on the call, but we are also being disciplined in terms of our cost structure and our headcount. That leverage is working. It is not entirely the reserve releases. There are other benefits in the business that are flowing through.

Tommy McJoynt: Okay, got it. Looking at the balance sheet, the cash balance has ballooned here to $460 million at the end of the third quarter. Is there any seasonality to why that build happened? If not, do you have any plans for how you would think about deploying some of that cash?

Patrick McClymont: It's just a timing thing. We are evolving our investment strategy, as we've talked about. We're modestly moving into riskier assets. That's going to be primarily things like credit investments that are a little bit further down the credit curve from our historical approach. At quarter end, we were halfway through a couple of transactions on that front, so it shows up that it's in cash, but it'll move into investments. So it's not seasonality, it's just literally timing of execution of that strategy.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn it back to McKeel for closing remarks.

McKeel Hagerty: Thank you, operator, and thanks to everyone on the call for your continued support. I want to close by coming back to where we started this morning. People love to drive fun cars. These cars are passion projects, identity markers, and a source of great memories. Our job is to understand what these cars mean to our members and to take excellent care of them. When I think about why this business works so well, I think about the 1967 Porsche 911S that my father and I restored together.

I have heard many similar stories of parents rebuilding cars in the garage with their kids, of a newcomer to the U.S. who saved up to buy a muscle car they first saw on an American television show, of the Gen X buyer who finally found that clean Toyota Supra they could not afford in college. After four decades in the car world, I believe we are just beginning to capitalize on our opportunity. We insure less than 8% of the 36 million vehicle target market in the U.S. today, and there is also a large opportunity for us across the Atlantic.

We are fortunate to operate in a niche that happens to be quite large, and I am optimistic about the road ahead as we keep reinvesting in our members. Thank you to One Team Hagerty. These results are yours. I am proud of every one of you, and I cannot wait to see what this team delivers in the final stretch of 2026. Until then, never stop driving.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect.

#3118. The Guide to JetBlue Seat Selection

JetBlue's seat selection policy is based on the type of fare, so include the selection fee when comparing prices.

Airline miles, hotel points, travel insurance

JetBlue Airways charges more for seat selection than any other major U.S. airline, according to a NerdWallet analysis, so it pays to know when you can pick a seat for free.

The airline offers several seat options, including standard economy seats, extra-legroom seats and lie-flat Mint suites. But whether you can select a seat for free depends on the type of seat and fare you book, as well as whether you have Mosaic elite status.

Here’s what to know about JetBlue seat selection, including the different seat types, how much seat selection costs and when you can choose a seat for free.

JetBlue offers several onboard experiences, ranging from standard economy to lie-flat business-class seats.

JetBlue’s standard economy product is called Main, and there are three types of seats in this cabin.

Main: Economy seats throughout the Main cabin. These seats may be complimentary, depending on the fare type chosen.

Main Preferred: Economy seats located closer to the front of the cabin. They cost extra.

Extra Legroom: Seats with additional legroom that are located over the wing, in front of the Main Preferred seats. These seats also cost extra.

All Main cabin passengers receive complimentary snacks, drinks and Wi-Fi. Each seat also offers an entertainment screen with live television and movies.

EvenMore is JetBlue’s premium economy experience, and the seats are located in front of the Main cabin. These seats offer up to 38 inches of legroom and include priority boarding, priority security (at select airports) and dedicated overhead bin space.

Travelers receive three complimentary alcoholic drinks, unlimited nonalcoholic drinks and snacks, along with free Wi-Fi and a seatback entertainment screen with movies and live TV.

BlueFirst is JetBlue’s new domestic first class, which is expected to start flying on Dec. 8, 2026, on non-Mint aircraft and routes.

Adding a domestic first class product allows JetBlue to better compete for travelers who prefer to fly first class within the U.S., a market currently served by American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines.

JetBlue’s premium business class experience is called Mint, and it is available on select domestic and international routes.

The front row of the cabin also includes Mint Studios, which offer even more space than a standard Mint Suite. Mint Studios also have a large 22-inch television screen, a mirrored vanity, additional storage and a guest seat that can accommodate another Mint passenger during flight.

If a Mint Studio seat is available, it will be displayed on the airplane seat map.

The Mint travel experience also includes a dedicated check-in desk, lounge access (except with Mint Base fares), priority boarding, priority baggage and two checked bags (one with Mint Base fare).

» Learn more: JetBlue boarding groups explained

JetBlue offers three fare categories: Base, Standard and Flex. The table below shows how the categories compare in terms of flexibility.

Base fares are the most affordable but the least flexible.

Main Base fares do not include complimentary seat selection, but travelers can purchase a seat at any time. Those with an EvenMore Base fare can select a seat for free, but only at check-in. If a seat isn’t chosen, JetBlue will assign one automatically before departure. (BlueFirst Base fares include free seat selection only within 24 hours of departure.)

Comparatively, Standard and Flex fares include complimentary seat selection. This also applies to Mint, except for the new Mint Base fare, which charges for advance seat selection; complimentary seat selection is included only with Mint or Mint Flex tickets. Passengers who want to select a Mint Studio will need to pay extra, and the cost of the seat varies. In an October 2026 sample search for a flight from New York to Paris, a Mint Studio upgrade cost an additional $299 on top of the Mint fare.

Seat selection fees vary among airlines. To get an idea of what passengers can expect to pay, NerdWallet analyzed seat selection fees across major U.S. airlines and found that JetBlue had the highest average one-way seat selection fee at $73.

» Learn more: Airlines with the best (and worst) fees in 2026

JetBlue’s elite status is called Mosaic, and there are four tiers, ranging from Mosaic 1 to Mosaic 4. Mosaic members receive complimentary access to certain upgraded seats, with the benefits depending on their status level.

All Mosaic members, plus JetBlue Premier Card holders who book with their card, can get complimentary space-available upgrades to BlueFirst for themselves and one companion. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares aren't eligible.

Main Base fares are excluded from complimentary seat selection benefits, regardless of Mosaic status.

All Mosaic members receive complimentary access to Main Preferred seating, but EvenMore benefits vary by status level. Mosaic 1 members can select EvenMore seats for free starting 36 hours before departure for themselves and up to two companions, while Mosaic 2 and above can select them at booking. Mosaic 3 and 4 members can extend this benefit to up to four companions.

Mosaic 3 and 4 members receive Premium Upgrade Certificates, and starting Feb. 1, 2027, Mosaic 2 members can choose one through Perks You Pick. Mosaic 4 members earn 2 additional certificates for every 100 Tiles earned beyond the Mosaic 4 threshold. Certificates can be used to upgrade eligible Main or EvenMore fares to Mint or BlueFirst (once it starts flying).

» Learn more: JetBlue Mint: your guide to flying business class

You can select a seat during the booking process, or after, through JetBlue’s website or mobile app. During booking, you’ll first choose your fare type (Base, Standard or Flex), which determines whether complimentary seat selection is included.

After you’ve selected the flight, you’ll see a seat map displayed with the available seats and any applicable fees. For example, passengers who purchase a Main fare can choose eligible Main seats for free but will see prices for upgraded seats.

If you purchase a Main Base fare, all advance seat selections will include an additional fee. Mint passengers can select an available Mint Suite at no additional cost or pay extra for an available Mint Studio.

» Learn more: How to navigate costly airline seat selection fees

#3117. The ERP Migration Blind Spots That Technology Alone Can't Fix

Bruno Billy, President & CEO of APGAR North America, advises organizations on the operational reality of data and enterprise transformation.

Enterprise resource planning (ERP) transformations remain high on the agenda for many large organizations. Mergers and acquisitions, consolidation and modernization are driving significant investment. For SAP customers, the approaching end of mainstream ERP Central Component (ECC) support adds further urgency.

But replacing an ERP is much more than replacing technology. It affects nearly everything about how a company does business, from processing customer orders to managing its supply chain and reporting financial results. The scope makes it notoriously difficult and expensive to execute.

The expense creates enormous pressure to get moving. Teams responsible for different workstreams often start before the organization agrees on how the new ERP should represent the business. Often, those differences start with the most basic assumptions about how the business operates.

Here’s a simple question that comes up surprisingly often during ERP transformations: what is a customer?

The obvious answer is the person or organization purchasing your products or services. Simple enough, right? But consider a manufacturer that sells through distributors. For finance, the customer might be the distributor that places the order and pays the invoice. For service, it might be the business actually using the product. Neither is wrong. Both definitions serve legitimate business needs.

An ERP needs to accommodate these nuances through its business objects, relationships and hierarchies. If implementation teams decide how to represent customers independently, they risk embedding conflicting assumptions in data mappings, system configurations and business processes.

Those conflicts may not become apparent until integration testing or financial reconciliation. By then, resolving them can require substantial rework, increase project costs, delay go-live and potentially disrupt business operations.

You won’t resolve every business requirement before an ERP migration begins, but there are three decisions I’d recommend making before the teams get too far into configuration and data migration.

Start by agreeing on how the business will be represented in the new ERP. For each major data domain, define the business entities, their relationships and the hierarchies needed to support operations and reporting.

This is particularly important when consolidating systems following an acquisition. In one organization I worked with, acquisitions had left the business operating six different ERP environments, each with its own representations of customers, suppliers and products. Supplier records in separate systems, for instance, may refer to subsidiaries of the same parent company. The future-state model should preserve those relationships so procurement can understand total spending across the supplier organization and negotiate accordingly.

Before approving the model, test it against actual legacy records. Can the migration team determine what each record becomes, which hierarchy it belongs to and how it relates to other entities? If the answers differ depending on who you ask, more business-design work is needed.

Not every difference needs to disappear. Some reflect legitimate regional or business-unit requirements. Not every local variation is inefficiency. Some may actually reflect a competitive advantage.

A manufacturer may sell the same product in several countries while using different packaging or meeting different regulatory requirements in each market. I find it useful to distinguish between what should be written in ink and what can be written in pencil.

• Write in ink the definitions, identities and relationships that need to remain consistent across the enterprise.

• Write in pencil the attributes and classifications that must accommodate local requirements.

Make these decisions with future rollouts in mind. The first implementation often establishes conventions that subsequent regions are expected to follow. A model designed exclusively around the first region’s needs can become an expensive constraint on everyone else.

Decide which systems are responsible for maintaining master data and, equally important, who has the authority to make decisions about it.

A customer record might originate in the CRM, while finance maintains credit information and payment terms. Authority may therefore need to be defined at the attribute or business-process level rather than assigned fully to one system. For each major data domain, identify who can create records, approve changes, resolve conflicts and authorize exceptions.

Consider a customer changing its legal name. Who determines whether that requires updating an existing record or creating a new legal entity? If CRM and finance reach different conclusions, the ERP can end up with conflicting information even when both systems are functioning correctly.

Establish these governance processes before go-live and sustain them afterward. Customers merge, suppliers reorganize and businesses expand. Without ownership and change management, the fragmentation you worked to eliminate will quickly return.

It is understandable to worry that business-model discussions will slow an already demanding program, but these decisions must be made eventually. The longer they are deferred, the more configuration, mappings and processes are built on assumptions that may need to be revisited.

Making the decisions early reduces rework and gives implementation teams a common foundation. It also creates value beyond the migration itself. The same business definitions and hierarchies can support reporting, analytics, future acquisitions and even AI applications.

An ERP doesn’t merely store your business’s data. It encodes a model of your business. If you haven’t agreed on that model before implementation starts, the implementation will make those decisions for you. ​
