#3102. i-80 Gold (IAUX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Mining delays and processing bottlenecks dented gold output this quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

i-80 Gold Corp. (IAUX -5.80%) reported progress on its hub-and-spoke mining strategy, which centers on feeding refractory and oxide ore from its underground projects to the central Lone Tree processing facility. Management stated that 2027 will be a transition year focused on ramping up mining at Granite Creek and Archimedes while completing the Lone Tree plant refurbishment. The company maintains a target of reaching 150,000 ounces to 200,000 ounces of annual gold production by 2028. Financial results for the quarter reflected higher realized gold prices and increased pre-development expenses as the company advances multiple feasibility and pre-feasibility studies across its Nevada portfolio.

Operator: Hello, and welcome to i-80 Gold's third quarter 2026 results conference call and webcast. At this time, all lines are in listen-only mode. Following the presentation, we will conduct a question-and-answer session. If you wish to ask a question, please press star one. If at any time during this call you require immediate assistance, please press star zero for the operator. I will now turn the call over to Caterina De Rosa, Vice President, Investor Relations at i-80 Gold.

Caterina De Rosa: Thank you, operator, and hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us to review i-80 Gold's third quarter results. Today's company's presenters include Richard Young, President and CEO, Paul Chawrun, COO, and Ryan Snow, CFO. Before we begin, please note that today's discussion will include forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. So we ask you to refer to the cautionary notes regarding these forward-looking statements in yesterday's press release, as well as the company filings. Today's remarks should be reviewed together with the Form 10-Q for the quarter ended on September 30th, which is available at our website, SEDAR+, and EDGAR. I will now turn the call over to Richard.

Richard Young: Caterina, thank you, and hello, everyone. Turning to slide three. We made further progress during the quarter toward our goal of building a multi-asset mid-tier gold producer in Nevada. Each milestone strengthens our track record of execution and brings us a step closer to realizing the value of our portfolio. During the third quarter, we published the Granite Creek Underground Feasibility Study. The study establishes maiden mineral reserves and outlines robust project economics, a higher production rate, and a longer mine life compared with the March 2025 preliminary economic assessment. Paul will discuss the ongoing drilling campaign across the property, designed to support further resource growth and reserve conversion to further extend the mine life at Granite Creek.

At Archimedes Underground, development remains on track to achieve first gold mining by year-end, bringing our second high-grade underground project into production. Metallurgical test work completed during the quarter confirmed strong heap leach recoveries for the greater-than-anticipated oxide material identified earlier this year through infill drilling in the upper 426 Zone. Placing the material on the existing heap leach pad is expected to significantly reduce processing costs over the next few years of oxide mining compared with the Archimedes PEA mine plan. At the Lone Tree plant, the refurbishment is progressing on schedule and largely on budget, with first gold pour targeted for the fourth quarter of next year.

Lone Tree is where our production platform comes together, unlocking the operating efficiencies of our two underground projects, generating stronger margins that is expected to transform our cash flow profile. Our 2026 drill programs across our two underground projects and Mineral Point open pit have delivered strong results, highlighting the potential to expand mineral resources beyond those outlined in the 2025 PEAs. Permitting activities across the portfolio also progressed on track with our development plans.

We also continued discussions with our key stakeholders, particularly in Eureka, the neighboring community of our Ruby Hill property, to advance long-term planning for our workforce, housing, and infrastructure buildup to support planned project growth at Archimedes in the short term and Mineral Point in the medium term. Our team is advancing a clearly defined development plan to increase production and generate stronger free cash flows. Turning now to slide four. We updated our development plan after quarter end. Our near-term plans remain unchanged. This includes establishing our hub-and-spoke mining and processing platform with Granite Creek and Archimedes feeding through the Lone Tree process plant. 2027 will be a transition year for the company.

We plan to continue to ramp up mining at our two underground mines and complete the plant refurbishment to position i-80 Gold to grow from a higher-cost 40,000-50,000 oz per year producer into a lower-cost 150,000-200,000 oz per year producer beginning in 2028. Ahead of Lone Tree's commissioning, we plan on building up refractory and oxide stockpiles during 2027 to support the plant's ramp-up. We are currently evaluating when to begin stockpiling, along with the timing and expected throughput of commissioning next fall. Exploration upside at both Granite Creek and Archimedes supports the potential for longer-term feed base for Lone Tree.

Therefore, Cove Underground has been resequenced later in the development pipeline as an important future source of refractory feed, likely in the second half of the 2030s or later. Our Mineral Point open pit oxide project represents the next major development project, supporting our medium-term production target of 400,000-500,000 oz of gold equivalent production by the early 2030s. Once Mineral Point is operating, we plan to develop the Granite Creek open-pit oxide project, which supports our longer-term target of 500,000-600,000 oz of annual gold production by the mid-2030s. This growth is planned around assets we already own in a top mining jurisdiction we know well.

Our growing team brings proven mine building and operating experience and is focused on continuing to deliver consistent execution quarter after quarter as we build i-80 Gold into a Nevada-focused mid-tier gold producer. With that, I will turn the call over to Paul to walk through each project.

Paul Chawrun: Thanks, Richard. Starting with Granite Creek Underground on slide five. Underground development is on track with nearly 900 m completed year-to-date in the main decline and lateral development to access the ore. This allows for consistent access to approximately 12-15 ore and waste headings at any one time, supporting the mine plan through year-end and beyond. As outlined in the feasibility study, work on a main ventilation raise is planned to begin in late 2026 and carry into 2027 as part of our life-of-mine optimization. Mining continued in the Ogee, Upper South Pacific, and Otto zones, though the total ore tons and material mined were lower than the plan.

This was due to a high volume of contractor workforce turnover during the quarter because of increased competition for skilled underground labor in the region. As a result, material movement was reduced, which delayed access to some high-grade headings. We have since implemented a competitive retention incentive program, and contractor staffing has recovered to a steady state to support planned mining rates through the balance of 2026. We expect both mine grades and tons to improve in the fourth quarter as a result. The total tons mined were approximately 86,000 tons, including 22,000 tons of sulfide ore grading over 8 g per ton and 12,400 tons of oxide ore grading over 9 g per ton.

Approximately 18,400 tons of sulfide ore was processed during the quarter. Limited availability at the third-party facility meant processing lag mining, increasing quarter-end inventories. At the end of the quarter, approximately 6,200 recoverable ounces remain in process at our third party, plus an additional 3,000 oz in finished goods inventory at the facility. Gold production for the quarter totaled approximately 9,100 oz, similar to the prior year period, and higher ounces mined year-to-date. We expect the project to reach the lower half of full-year production guidance range of 30,000-40,000 oz. Unit mining costs were higher year-over-year, reflecting higher contractor and labor costs and lower mining rates. However, we expect to be on budget for the year.

Water management remains under control as the existing pumping infrastructure is able to maintain inflow rates, which remain at approximately 1,300-1,400 gal per minute. Construction of the second water treatment was completed in the quarter and is currently undergoing commissioning for water placement into the RIBs. With the completion of two new dewatering wells this quarter, we expect to reach treatment levels of up to 3,500 gal per minute, which will start to lower the groundwater table and eventually improve the long-term mining conditions of the life-of-mine plan. Moving to slide six. Infill and step-out drilling at Granite Creek Underground progressed to support resource conversion, mine planning, and continued resource expansion.

Since mining commenced, delineation drilling ahead of mining that targets a spacing of approximately 40 ft has consistently defined additional mineralization relative to the block model on individual mining levels. Under a multi-year drilling program expected to begin in 2027, further drilling is planned across five highly prospective focus areas for evaluation: the South Pacific, Range Front, Otto and Ogee zones, and the high-grade CX Zone beneath the historic pit. We believe these programs to grow the existing mineral resource and extend the mine life. The Granite Creek feasibility study published in September strengthened the mine plan through better geological definition with an optimized mine design and increased mining rates due to adjustments to the ore access plan.

Infill drilling improved continuity in the South Pacific zone and converted a significant portion of resources into higher confidence categories. This supported a larger mineable inventory and an eight-and-a-half-year mine life after accounting for more than a year of depletion since the PEA. The updated plan supports higher planned production with less waste development, backed by upgrades to dewatering and water treatment systems and less restrictive ventilation. The study also incorporates stockpiling sulfide and oxide ore in 2027 ahead of Lone Tree's commissioning, allowing more Granite Creek material to benefit from anticipated lower processing costs and reduced reliance on third-party processing. Turning to slide seven.

Progress at Archimedes Underground continues to demonstrate strong execution with unit costs largely on budget, with first gold mine expected in the fourth quarter of this year. This is a highly anticipated milestone that brings our second underground project into operation. Underground operating costs remain in line with the PEA, while capital costs are expected to be slightly higher, reflecting investment in surface and underground infrastructure to support long-term operations at the Ruby Hill property. Favorable ground conditions and contractor productivity supported approximately 2,300 m of development for the nine-month period, well in advance of the plan.

Development during the quarter focused on advancement of the main ramp, completion of lateral access for drilling platforms, and preparation for ore mining this quarter. In addition to the waste development and drilling in the exploration drift, focus for the quarter was on installation of key infrastructure, such as completion of the backfill plant, ventilation raises, and the surface infrastructure. Continued focus on infrastructure will be required in Q4 in preparation for the heap leach, additional ventilation raises, progress in the mine dry facility, and planning and engineering for installation of the main fan assembly area. Permitting activities for Lower Archimedes continue to advance as planned.

As a reminder, the project is permitted above the 5,100-ft level at Archimedes for the start of production mining, which is approximately several years ahead of mining. As part of our updated stockpiling strategy, refractory material from Archimedes is now expected to be stockpiled in 2027 for processing at our wholly owned Lone Tree plant, and once commissioned, rather than processing through a third-party facility. Mine plan optimization for 2027 is ongoing for this increased oxide resource in the upper zone. As Richard discussed, placement of the oxide material on the existing leach pad at Ruby Hill property is expected to begin by year-end. The emerging oxide opportunity at Archimedes has the potential to provide meaningful, low-cost near-term ounces.

Metallurgical test work has been completed for the oxide material, demonstrating excellent leach kinetics and gold recovery at a sizing conducive to the underground run-of-mine feed. We are pleased at how this project has progressed from a construction decision in September of 2025 to the expected first gold in only 15 months. Turning to slide eight. Recent drilling at Archimedes has reinforced the grades and continuity within the planned mining areas from the PEA and extended mineralization beyond the previous resource boundaries. The 2026 infill drilling campaign for the Lower 426 and Ruby Deeps Zones began during the second quarter, with an expected campaign of approximately 55,000 m across 140 holes.

Results of this program will support an updated resource estimate for a feasibility study expected in the second half of 2027. At present, seven drill rigs are operating underground, with drilling expected to be completed in the second half of 2027. The company expects to release ongoing results as this campaign progresses. Looking at slide nine for an update on the Lone Tree plant. We are pleased with the progress on the Lone Tree plant's refurbishment project, which remains on track for first gold pour in Q4 2027, consistent with the execution plan outlined in a December 2025 engineering study. Bulk demolition is complete, contractor mobilization is underway for initial construction, and we are initiating civil and concrete work.

Engineering and procurement continue to advance in line with the project schedule. Management is also preparing for operational readiness, the commissioning schedule, and initial placement of operating personnel during the course of 2027. Construction permits continue to be received ahead of schedule, and the remaining routine operating permits continue to advance in line with the construction schedule. Overall project cost remains largely in line with the $430 million capital estimate. By September end, 74% of procurement packages by value had been awarded, and 44% of total project capital was committed.

While 2026 cash expenditures are expected to be below the original guidance, we still expect refurbishment capital to be near fully committed by the end of the year, as we work towards securing a general contractor in December. Labor costs are running approximately 5%-10% above the original estimates. However, those increases remain within contingency at present. Approximately 20% of total contingency has been used at quarter end, which places us in a great position as we head into the critical phases of the project. Turning to slide 10. As Richard discussed, the Mineral Point open-pit oxide project is our next major development priority.

During the quarter, we completed approximately 26,000 m of core and reverse circulation drilling, focused on converting inferred mineral resources into the indicated category in preparation for a pre-feasibility study. Drilling rates reached steady state during the quarter, with productivity improving significantly as additional rigs arrived. Nine drill rigs are currently active at Mineral Point, bringing the total across the Ruby Hill property, including Archimedes Underground, to 16. Initial infill and step-out drill results to the east and north were encouraging, suggesting potential to extend mineralization beyond the 2025 PEA pit shell.

Of the initial 35 holes reported, 19 tested beyond the existing mineral resource, with all of them intersecting mineralization, and more than half showing gold and silver intercepts exceeding 150 m. 15 of these tested the eastern extension, three to the north, and one to the west. The eastern area shows the greatest expansion potential and has had only sparse historical drilling. Geotechnical drilling for pre-feasibility study is complete. The study is expected in the second half of 2027, subject to completion of the broader drilling program. Early-stage pre-permitting work for Mineral Point continued to advance. Formal permitting has not yet commenced. Turning to slide 11.

At Granite Creek Open Pit, preparation for a pre-feasibility study has commenced, and early-stage pre-permitting activities are ongoing. Technical site investigation and baseline environmental work is anticipated to commence in the first quarter of 2027, with subsequent engineering trade-off optimization studies, followed by completion of a pre-feasibility study technical report, expected in the second half of 2027. We are currently working through operational and permitting needs, followed by an expected EIS, which is currently projected to commence in 2027. Looking at Cove, during the quarter, we continued to advance technical and economic studies for the Cove Underground Project, with optimization of the dewatering capital and a revised mine plan. Federal and state Nevada permitting approvals continue to progress.

A feasibility study for Cove is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2026. As mentioned, recent success at Granite Creek and Archimedes Underground Mines has allowed us to sequence Cove later in our development plan, likely into the 2030s. Now with that, I'll hand that over to Ryan.

Ryan Snow: Thank you, Paul. We ended the quarter with a cash balance of approximately $411 million. This was a reduction from approximately $465 million at the end of the second quarter. Our cash balance remains in line with expectations, if not slightly better. Additional monies are expected under the Gold Prepay with the banks, the Franco-Nevada NSR, the anticipated exercise of warrants, and stockpile facilities.

Together, these sources could provide up to approximately $350 million of additional liquidity over the next 18 months to help fund the completion of the hub-and-spoke strategy and advance the other projects in the pipeline through permitting and technical studies. Other than the NSR, each of these sources is subject to lender approval, definitive agreements, or the exercise of outstanding warrants. Moving to slide 13.

Company-wide gold production and sales for the quarter were approximately 11,700 oz and 7,750 oz respectively, compared to 12,430 and 9,370 oz in the prior year period. Net loss increased for the quarter and nine months, and was primarily due to increased pre-development expenses as we advance the development plan, which we will begin to capitalize as we publish feasibility studies and declare commercial production, non-cash accounting impacts tied to the revaluation of our financial instruments, financing costs related to the recapitalization, all partially offset by higher gross profit.

Adjusted net loss for the quarter and year-to-date increased over the prior year periods. This was in line with our expectations, reflecting the continued ramp-up of our pre-development, evaluation, and exploration activities as we advance several development projects and will continue until we declare reserves at each of the projects. We declared our first mineral reserves at Granite Creek Underground, and as a result, beginning in Q4 of this year, we will be capitalizing qualifying costs associated with pre-development, evaluation, and exploration. Cash used in operating activities for the quarter and year-to-date increased, mainly due to increased development, evaluation, and exploration outflows as we ramp up activities, interest paid on the repayment of legacy debt, all partially offset by our increased gross profit. Overall, sustaining capital, growth capital, and pre-development expense are expected to be at the low end of the guidance range. While the Lone Tree plant refurbishment is on schedule, we are seeing a delay between commitment and invoicing or payment of around four months, rather than the 30 days used in the budgeting process.

Exploration expenses are expected to be below the guidance range, mainly due to fewer feet drilled than planned as a result of the late delivery of rigs to the Ruby Hill property and contractor personnel shortages discussed last quarter. These updates mainly reflect timing of spend, as the company remains on track to meet our development objectives. I'll now hand the call back over to Richard.

#3098. ESR Trust (ESRT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Observatory visits slumped while leasing and debt metrics held steady.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Empire State Realty Trust, Inc. (ESRT +1.20%) reported a third quarter focused on capital recycling, operational efficiency, and executive transition. Management highlighted the completion of the $217.5 million sale of 1359 Broadway, utilizing proceeds to fund share repurchases and strengthen the balance sheet. While the commercial office and retail portfolio maintained high occupancy and positive rent spreads, the Observation Deck segment faced significant headwinds from declining visitation. To address this, the company appointed new leadership to modernize customer acquisition through digital and AI-driven platforms. Financial results were supported by disciplined expense management, with the company remaining on track to meet its multiyear general and administrative cost reduction targets.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Empire State Realty Trust Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce Susanne J. Lieu, Senior Vice President, Chief Counsel, Real Estate. Thank you. You may begin.

Susanne Lieu: Good afternoon. Welcome to Empire State Realty Trust's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. During today's call, management's prepared remarks and responses to questions may include forward-looking statements within the meaning of applicable securities laws. These statements reflect management's current views and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Empire State Realty Trust assumes no obligation to update any forward-looking statement in the future.

The definitions and reconciliations of these measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in the earnings release and supplemental package, each available on the company's website. Now I will turn the call over to Tony Malkin, our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer.

Through disposition and acquisition, we have focused our portfolio on properties and locations, which the market wants. Our decisions to exit the properties we disposed of has proven to be [ present. ] We had a strong quarter across our property portfolio, and our property portfolio represents close to 85% of our NOI. Leasing progress has been good in our office and retail, and we have continued with high occupancy in our residential properties. Our office retail property type at our quality level is limited with no new supply. Our portfolio from office to retail to multifamily, delivered strong operating results.

We achieved our 21st consecutive quarter of positive mark-to-market rent spreads within our Manhattan office portfolio as our commercial portfolio reached 95.6% leased at quarter end. On October 29, we completed the sale of 1359 Broadway. And starting in late July, redeployed the proceeds towards the repurchase of shares, which we believe to be a highly compelling investment. We will also utilize sale of proceeds to pay down debt and maintain balance sheet strength, [indiscernible] remains weak [indiscernible] in conclusion of the search we began in the second quarter. On October 1, Andy Giancamilli joined us as President of Empire State Building Observation Deck in that position he manages the commercialization of the Empire State Building brand as well.

We conducted a comprehensive search with active direct involvement of our Board. Andy's early career between his University of Michigan under-graduate business degree and MBA from Kellogg was at McKinsey and he rejoined McKinsey after his MBA. Andy's last role was at FanDuel, where he served as a central pillar of the leadership team for over a decade. He was VP of Revenue then Chief Financial Officer; and ultimately Chief Operating Officer. He scaled digital consumer platforms, drove customer engagement and monetized customer relationships. During Andy's executive operational watch, annual revenue increased from $490 million in 2019 to $6.96 billion by the end of 2025.

The company also captured and maintained over 40% market share and secured its position as the undisputed #1 sports book in North America. At ESRT, Andy now oversees all aspects, operations, marketing, strategy, brand growth, and monetization for the Observation Deck and Empire State Building brand and reports directly to Christina and me. The Empire State Building is a globally recognized brand with a top-of-tier office building and an iconic visitor experience. We have been clear in prior calls, New York City's destination attraction game has changed and we have work to do.

There's clear opportunity through integrated efforts to maintain the successes of the office building, generate more revenue from the brand, and build back our visitor volumes through new sources. We want to see improved operating performance and cash flow and will update shareholders on our progress. ESRT has achieved a leadership position in and differentiated ourselves through sustainability for nearly 2 decades. Our focus remains on measurable business outcomes, which make money and attract better credit tenants at higher rents. In the process, we reduced energy consumption, improve operational efficiency, support high-performance workplaces for our tenants, and mitigate risk for our stakeholders. ESRT for the second year in a row was the highest-rated GRESB corporate filer.

Hats off to our team for our continued leadership and excellence of our integration of sustainability into all aspects of the tenant experience and property operations. The leadership changes we have implemented are nearly complete. We are already and will be leaner, more agile, and more efficient. For 2026, we remain on track to reduce run rate G&A by approximately 5% to 10% by year-end, consistent with our prior guidance. We will remain on our front foot in all respects. Our current priorities are clear: lease space, optimize Empire State Building observation Deck and brand cash flow drive long-term value through strategic capital allocation and operational efficiency, maintain our balance sheet and achieve our sustainability goals.

These priorities guide every decision we make and align directly with our objectives to drive long-term cash flow growth and value creation. Christina, Ryan, and Steve will provide a little details on our results and outlook. Christina?

Christina Chiu: Thanks, Tony. Following our second quarter earnings call and upon execution of an agreement to sell 1359 Broadway in August, we began to repurchase shares. On October 29, we closed on the sale of 1359 Broadway for $217.5 million. Since July 30, 2026, as of November 2, we have repurchased $85.8 million shares at an average cost of $4.56 per share. We will also utilize sale proceeds to pay down debt such that we maintain balance sheet strength. We have no unaddressed debt maturity until, March 2029.

These capital allocation decisions are consistent with our view that our current share price is not reflective of the value of our assets which has been reinforced by discussions with our investors over the past quarters. Over 5 years ago, Tony, our Board, and I began to execute on a strategy to reposition our property portfolio and allocate capital to enhance long-term growth in cash flow and value per share. Our planned exit from suburban markets and weaker New York City properties resulted in redeployment of capital into higher quality properties. Further, we consolidated building and land ownership at 2 properties, which total approximately 1.7 million square feet and executed substantial share repurchases.

We maintained the strength and flexibility of our balance sheet and implement leadership succession plan and G&A reduction. Inclusive of the year-to-date share repurchases, the company has repurchased approximately $388 million of its common stock since 2020. We also maintain 100% ownership of our assets, which provides substantial optionality. We have spoken for years about how we are on our front foot, and we will continue to find ways to grow portfolio cash flow and quality, maintain a strong and flexible balance sheet, and generate long-term value per share. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Ryan to review our leasing activity.

Ryan Kass: Thanks, Christina, and good afternoon, everyone. In the third quarter, leasing performance remained strong, with volume of 189,000 square feet which includes over 130,000 square feet of new leases. Year-to-date, we have leased 685,000 square feet with 460,000 square feet of new Manhattan office leases, and we continued to grow our lease percentage. Our lease percentage increased to 95.6%, up from 95% in the second quarter on a comparable basis, excluding 1359 Broadway from both periods. This demonstrates strong tenant demand for our top-of-tier portfolio. In this quarter, we achieved mark-to-market spreads of 9.9% in office, our 21st consecutive quarter of positive spreads, which underscores our sustained pricing power.

Tenants continue to expand with us and make long-term commitments, highlighted by our average lease duration on new leases of 9.5 years. Notable leases signed during the quarter include a 29,000 square foot full floor new office lease with Octaura Holdings at 111 West 33rd Street, a 15,000 square foot expansion office lease with Corgan Associates at the Empire State Building, and a 13,000 square foot new office lease with Zenith Advisors at the Empire State Building. Our pipeline of leases and negotiation remains healthy at 250,000 square feet. New York City's leasing market remains strong and provides a favorable backdrop for execution with demand broad based across finance, professional services, TAMI, and consumer products.

Lastly, our multifamily portfolio continues to perform well. Net rents increased by nearly 6%, and our portfolio is approximately 97% occupied. Thank you. I will now turn the call over to Steve. Steve?

Stephen Horn: Thanks, Ryan. For the third quarter of 2026, we reported core FFO of $0.20 per diluted share. Same-store property cash NOI, excluding lease termination fees, increased 50 basis points year-over-year. The improvement is primarily attributed to increases in tenant reimbursement income and insurance recoveries. This was partially offset by operating expense growth and the approximate $2 million year-over-year revenue decline from the previously disclosed FDIC expiration which was pre-leased. Adjusted for FDIC and $1.2 million of positive nonrecurring items this quarter, same-store property cash NOI increased by 1.9%.

Our Observation Deck generated approximately $15.6 million of net operating income during the third quarter as compared to $26.5 million of NOI in the prior year period, with revenue of $26.8 million and expenses of $11.2 million. Our results are consistent with the revised framework we provided last quarter. Visitation was lower by approximately 26% year-over-year and revenue per capita, excluding license fees, increased by approximately 2% year-over-year. We remain committed to a strong and flexible balance sheet. At the end of the third quarter, our net debt to adjusted EBITDA was approximately 6.7x. We maintain ample liquidity of $600 million at a well-lettered debt maturity schedule with no unaddressed debt maturities until March 2029.

We also maintain a predominantly unencumbered portfolio to provide substantial optionality. We reported G&A of approximately $17 million in the third quarter, which is consistent with our prior guidance of a 5% to 10% reduction in run rate G&A by year-end. We remain committed to further reducing G&A and maintaining disciplined cost management across the organization. We have additional cost reduction initiatives underway that could yield at least a further 2% reduction in G&A relative to our year-end 2026 run rate that will benefit from throughout 2027.

Lastly, with no change to our Observation Deck framework we shared in our 2Q earnings release, we increased our 2026 core FFO per share guidance that now stands at $0.77 to $0.80 per fully diluted share. This reflects higher-than-expected year-to-date results from our property portfolio, driven primarily by nonrecurring items which we have explained in our prior 2 earnings calls. In addition to our capital markets activity, which included share repurchases and the sale of 1359 Broadway. This concludes our prepared remarks. I'll now turn the call back to the operator to begin the Q&A session.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first questions come from the line of Manus Ebbecke with Evercore ISI.

Manus Ebbecke: I just wanted to ask if you can touch on your further advertising capacity for additional share repurchases beyond kind of like the 1359 Broadway sales proceeds?

Christina Chiu: Sure. Thanks, Manus. As we mentioned, share buybacks continue to be a strategic part of our capital allocation. So we would certainly evaluate that, and we have been active with the portfolio. As mentioned over the last 5 years, have sold out of suburbs began to look at Manhattan assets on where we've executed the business plan and look at sales and we'll continue to be active. The key objective is cash flow per share as well as value per share. So all those items are on the table, including share buybacks.

Manus Ebbecke: Great. Great. And then I just wanted to touch on 1 of the comments that was just made at the end in terms of further expense reductions on the G&A side. If you could just expand on that a little bit as you go kind of like bridging into '27.

Stephen Horn: Yes. So similar to what we've gone through as far as succession planning in 2026, we'll continue down that path as we look forward to 2027, and also remain committed to reducing this organizational costs and increase efficiency. So we'll look to do more there. It's where the 2% figure comes from. We'll keep the market updated as we continue to execute along those plans.

Operator: Our next question is come from the line of Seth Bergey with Citi.

Seth Bergey: Just maybe following up on those comments, can you just kind of touch on maybe some of the transaction market and how you're seeing that evolve and appreciate kind of the focus on the share opportunities, but maybe just touch on maybe the transaction market and some of the -- what's most attractive to you between kind of the office, multifamily, and retail, if you're looking at anything there?

Anthony Malkin: Well, thanks for your question. We are and continue to be [ nervous opportunivores ] within our food groups of office, retail, and residential, and of course, importantly, share repurchase. I'll let Christina cover any comment with regard to share repurchase. Our view of the market is, transactions are down and cap rates are up. And relative to where any other market would have been 6 years after the commencement of a recovery. That said, we've been able to execute good exits with the right properties to the right buyer profiles at 250 and at 1359. And we will continue to test the market where it's appropriate. And then we look to redeploy as makes sense for growth.

What's the best bargain, what's the best value. So we have 4 very good options. And they're driven by the fact as to whether or not within this lower-volume transaction market, can we continue to do things which we are sensible. And if not, we'll -- we're happy with what we have and we'll move forward. Christina, do you want to make any additional comment there on share buybacks?

Christina Chiu: Sure. As I mentioned earlier, share buybacks are definitely part of the equation. And just to underscore, we have consistently mentioned keeping an eye and prioritizing the flexibility and strength of our balance sheet is key, so that we can operate, invest capital recycle accordingly. So it's both looking at the opportunities and cash flow and value per share as well as having the balance sheet that allows us to navigate all sorts of markets.

Seth Bergey: And then just maybe as a follow-up with the kind of observatory traffic. How much of that do you view as kind of macroeconomic or increased competition from similar Observatory Decks versus levers you can pull? And when do you kind of expect to get more visibility into kind of the progress that you're making on improving performance at the Observatory.

Anthony Malkin: Well, look, this problem did not happen overnight, and it will not be fixed overnight. And so you can be certain we will be transparent with the market and keep you updated on our progress. With regard to our overall perspective. We know how to run an attraction and get reviews, which make us the #1 reviewed transaction in the United States, according to TripAdvisor. With new competition, there are changes in the geopolitical environment, K-shaped economy. We recognize the need to reinvent our customer acquisition program. We need to reexamine our experience and focus on new on the monetization of our brand. Customer acquisition is now largely and will soon be all digital and AI driven.

So I think we just want to point to Andy Giancamilli. We conducted a thorough process with meaningful direct Board involvement and has the right experience and leadership chops for this dynamic environment to diversify our customer base, redefine the revenue model and translate our strengths into improved operating performance and cash flow. So we look forward to the future. We've got opportunity, and we need to go out and monetize on it.

Operator: Our next questions come from the line of John Kim with BMO Capital Markets.

John Kim: I wanted to ask if you can elaborate on what drove the decision to sell 1359 Broadway? I think your other office sales were in slower growth suburban markets. This asset is in place rent of $61. So it seems like there would have been some upside potential as you mark-to-market those rents. But yes, again, if you could talk about why that asset and the exit cap rate that you achieved?

Anthony Malkin: So Christina and I will take that on. I'll say that, look, the sale of 250 West 57th Street was logical to us. as was 1359. We appreciate that they are different from the exits in the suburbs. We also had different outcomes and results. We had very unique opportunity to reinvest in an outstanding asset, which will prove to be very, very good for us at 130 Mercer. We had a unique opportunity to buy the land 111 West 33rd Street and 1400 Broadway and to do so -- and create tremendous value for our stakeholders and shareholders.

So when we look at the choices we made and the choices we make, we try to just determine is there a better for the money for us? Is there a better use for the property for somebody else? And can we make those 2 equations work in a way that with what we do with the proceeds, it's logical. So pay down debt, repurchase shares, these are all part of the mix. Christina, what would you like to add on?

Christina Chiu: I think that covers it. 1359 executed on the business plan, compelling use of proceeds. And this reiterates all the points that we have made if we can recycle towards assets with better cash flow growth prospects or add value if we can buy back shares, if we can maintain a strong balance sheet, all to generate shareholder value, that's exactly what we'll do, and you'll continue to see us actively review the portfolio in that light.

Christina Chiu: If you look at the supp, roughly 7%, you can go through that. But I think a lot of assets in the market. It's very bespoke to the specific situation and tendency in place. So as we've mentioned, a lot of times, the market reverts to per pound and the cap rate do vary quite a bit across the market.

John Kim: Okay. And then as you have improved and repositioned the portfolio, I guess my question is, when do you think we'll see that in improved cash same-store NOI? This quarter, you mentioned it's 1.9% if you exclude the FDIC lease overall, up [ 50 ] basis points. But when can we see that kind of trend closer to some of your peers?

Stephen Horn: Yes. Thanks, John. So we continue to execute leases with that strong mark-to-market growth. And also you saw posting our continued occupancy gains. In isolation, those will generate positive cash NOI returns as free rent periods to amortize. And as you know, we continue to sign leases with shorter periods of free rent, which only help in that regard. So our progress to quickly bring up occupancy and efforts to shave free rent and increased term as benefits outside of cash NOI, and that's within FAD. If you look at our trailing 12-month basis, our FAD increased $64 million or 114% year-over-year. That's on the back of a 5% decline in FFO over that same period.

We see a similar framework, if you look year-to-date, it's a $36 million increase in FAD over a 5% decline in FFO. As said 4 consecutive quarters now of positive FFO to FAD conversion or improvement in FFO to FAD conversion. So it's important to keep in mind that all of these are positive. Those stats are going to ebb and flow as we move through periods of rollover, but the focus on increasing term and reducing concessions has allowed us to benefit further from those positive trends.

Anthony Malkin: And I would just add to that, but we recognize that current investors look for short-term signals. Our actions may take longer and still, they will result in the changes for which investors look, and our focus is cash flow. We can't eat FFO. We can eat cash flow.

Operator: Our next questions come from the line of Blaine Heck with Wells Fargo.

Blaine Heck: Ryan, the supplemental now shows about 174,000 square feet of expected vacates and 68,000 square feet unknowns for 2027. And I think that forecast excludes 1359 Broadway. So can you talk about how much of the improvement reflects good leasing progress or retention progress versus removing that building, and whether any particular tenants or blocks in the remaining rollover could meaningfully change the occupancy trajectory for next year?

Ryan Kass: Blaine, yes, absolutely. So let me start with -- the team has really done a great job throughout the year. They've proactively managed the rent roll. We've been marketing and opportunistically have pre-leased a lot of the 2027 known availabilities. So we'll continue to engage with those tenants, talk about early renewals and market those known vacates to minimize downtime and manage our rent roll. 1359 specifically, roughly 88,000 square feet was removed from a 2027 expiration. Would actually flag in terms of large block, no single tenant within that is greater than 60,000 square feet. And of the unknowns, only 2 tenants are over 6,000 square feet, and lastly, roughly half of our known vacate expires December of 2027.

Blaine Heck: Great. That's helpful. And just to clarify, that 88,000 came out of expected vacates, is that right?

Ryan Kass: The 88,000 came out of a few areas, 30,000 was removed from the tenant vacate, 25,000 from new leases, 24,000 from unknown and 10,000 from renewal and revocations.

Blaine Heck: Great. Very helpful. Second question, Tony. There have been reports of an activist investor taking a position in the company, recognizing you might be limited in what you could share. Can you talk about whether you've had any dialogue with that investor how constructive those conversations have been and whether those conversations led you to executing on any of the transactions during the quarter? Or could, in the future, lead you to consider any changes to capital allocation or a broader strategy?

Anthony Malkin: So first, I'll tell you that all of the actions we took through the quarter going back to the end of the June 30, were already in place and taken without regard to anyone's input. I think importantly, just we note, we have a consistent active engagement with our shareholders and welcome their views on our strategy, performance, and business objectives. Board members participate proactively and in response requests and conversations with meaningful shareholders. Beyond that, we won't comment today on specific discussions or interactions with investors. I would merely say that everything then which we've reported today, began and was put in place and conceived before we had any outreach by this particular investor.

Operator: Our next questions come from the line of Dylan Burzinski with Green Street.

Dylan Burzinski: Maybe going back to, I think, a question that was asked earlier about sort of the Observatory, and Tony, you mentioned the problem with what's happening didn't happen overnight. It won't be fixed overnight. And you sort of laid out some things that you guys are looking at. I guess as you guys sit there and evaluate all those things that you guys are looking at to improve on, I mean, is there a time line in mind as to where you guys will evaluate that and be satisfied or dissatisfied with how long it took to sort of roll out some of these things that you guys are looking at?

Anthony Malkin: So I really appreciate that question. It's super helpful. Andy began on October 1. And he -- well, he definitely did a lot of reading and a lot of awareness building before October 1. He began October 1. We actually look forward to the execution of his plan. He has a process, and he's in his process now. Christina and I, in fact, just met with him yesterday and he gave us the first 1 month update. So from a practical perspective, we have to understand that there are already changes that we have put in place before Andy's arrival.

And through that process, which we began and through Andy's involvement and interaction, we anticipate that we'll begin to see the first opportunities for improvement in the high season in the summer of '27. We may see something before then. And we and he have worked together to prioritize and we start -- at the bottom, we work our way up the tree as far as opportunity.

Operator: Thank you. That does now conclude our question-and-answer session. I would now like to hand the call back over to Anthony Malkin for any closing comments.

Anthony Malkin: Thanks, everybody, very much. Great work ESRT team. At ESRT, we remain focused on a clear and consistent set of priorities, lease space optimize Empire State Building Observation Deck and brand cash flow, drive long-term value through strategic capital allocation and operational efficiency, manage our balance sheet, and achieve our sustainability goals. We look forward to the opportunity to meet with you, our investors and on the sell side in the months to come, and we'll continue, as always, to engage with and listen to our investors. The organization is focused and aligned to drive the business forward. Our high-quality portfolio and strong financial foundation position us to execute in the quarters ahead.

We will continue to take steps to drive long-term growth in cash flow and value per share. Thanks very much.

#3096. How to Make a $50 Holiday Gift Feel Like $100

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Trade time and a little extra thought to enhance gifts this holiday season.

Each month, NerdWallet suggests one wallet win to help you feel more confident about your money. This month’s topic is making holiday gifts feel more valuable, and we’re going to show you ways to elevate a gift without overspending.

Making an inexpensive gift feel fancy is a winter challenge I relish.

As a relatively frugal person who often gets sticker shock when shopping for gifts, I’m always looking for creative ways to save money without diminishing the present. Over the years, I’ve developed a few strategies to make a $50 gift feel like it’s worth at least double that.

In the spirit of the season, I’m sharing these strategies with you. I hope you — and your recipients — find them as celebratory as I do.

What does your gift recipient love to do? It helps if they have a favorite hobby, sports team or other interest.

Let’s say your recipient likes to fish. Giving a gift card to a niche fishing store makes it feel far more valuable than the standard Amazon card because it shows that you considered who they are. And there are specialty stores for every hobby these days.

Maybe gift cards aren’t your go-to. You can easily enhance other gifts, too.

Paying $5 extra to engrave or embroider their name on the gift — whether it’s stationery, jewelry or a backpack — makes the item feel far more valuable than its price tag because it’s customized to the individual.

If you choose a gift that couldn’t have been given to anyone else, it increases its value.

Time required: A few extra minutes to think about your recipients’ preferences and apply them when shopping.

A vintage or thrifted scarf can be a wrapping paper alternative that also functions as a gift. Similarly, you could wrap a gift in tea towels, artwork or online prints that can be reused by the recipient.

Another idea: Wrap a gift in printed sheet music that contains a special meaning for the recipient.

Customizing the presentation of the gift elevates it without adding much to the expense.

Time required: Since you have to wrap the gift anyway, this method doesn’t need to take extra time. You’ll just need to find the cloth or paper you plan to use.

One of my favorite gifts in recent memory involved turning a family photograph into a Jane Austen-era image set on a bucolic English estate with the empire-waisted gowns to match. My mom is a big fan of Jane Austen, so I knew she would appreciate seeing the family in a Regency-style photo.

I hired an Etsy artist to transform my original image, but you may be able to do it yourself with a photo app. Similarly, you could create a custom song, illustration or other form of art made specifically for your recipient.

Adding your own creative spin on a gift shows you spent extra time thinking about the recipient to make something extra special for them.

Time required: Applying your own creativity can be time-intensive, but the process is enjoyable so it goes quickly.

I like to call this technique the hybrid gift approach: You buy something, then get crafty to transform the gift into something one-of-a-kind.

One of my favorite ways to do this is with a photo. I’ll buy a nice but inexpensive frame and then put a photo of the recipient, or the recipient alongside loved ones, inside it.

If the person you’re buying for posts on social media, you might not even have to ask them for a photo in advance. Instead, you can find a favorite one that they already shared and surprise them.

The options are endless, especially with online tutorials to help hone your crafting skills. Adding your own customization to a purchased gift makes it feel special, but doesn’t have to cost much.

Time required: Baking, crafting or creating can take several hours, but again, it’s an enjoyable process.

Experiential gifts tend to go over well, and you may even get to have some fun, too.

One year, I gave my mom a membership to a nearby art museum and tacked on an offer to attend an exhibit with her. We had something on the calendar to look forward to together, and she got the option to visit more times throughout the year.

My parents have given me memberships, too. More recently, they gave me one to a local nature center. It’s great because I can visit on my own or attend kid-friendly events at a discounted rate. It makes me feel part of the community, and I love supporting an organization that helps kids learn more about nature.

Another option is to donate to charity in a loved one’s name and then make plans to volunteer at the organization together.

Experiential gifts help create more family memories together, which is one of my favorite ways to celebrate the holidays.

Time required: Setting aside time to visit a museum or other destination can take an entire day, but it’s time well spent.

The bottom line is that giving a highly personalized gift adds value without eating too far into your own budget. Spend $50. Make someone feel like a hundred bucks.

If you’re following along with us on this monthly financial challenge, start by testing out the tips we shared today over the next few weeks. We’ll be back again next month to learn about setting money goals for the new year. And if you missed last month’s edition, take a look back at how to shop the holiday sales.

#3095. To Defend Against AI Attackers, Start Thinking Like One

Yair Grindlinger is CEO and Co-Founder of Surf AI.

AI is not black magic. It still has to work through real systems, identities, applications and infrastructure, which means its limits are knowable. That matters, because fear is only useful when it’s aimed at the right things.

For enterprises, the right thing to fear is how AI changes the attacker. AI-driven attacks are faster, more persistent and more sophisticated, and they can exploit a single critical weakness or chain together a handful of small ones until they find a way in. ​​

There are several obvious ways AI changes attacks. First is speed. We’re seeing attacks happen in hours instead of days or weeks because AI systems can operate 24/7. The window for defenders is already shrinking. CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report found that the average time it took criminal attackers to move from initial access deeper into a network​ fell to 29 minutes, and the fastest observed breakout took just 27 seconds.

But I think stamina may be even more important than speed. A typical human attacker might spend a few hours trying to get into an organization. If nothing works, they may move to the next victim. AI doesn’t necessarily have that limitation. If you tell an AI system to find a way in, it can keep working 24/7 until it finds something.

Then there is breadth of knowledge. Human attackers are typically good at something, whether it’s social engineering, zero-days or a particular system. AI can have the whole playbook. The same system can work across identity, software vulnerabilities, configurations and other attack surfaces. Because it has both stamina and breadth of knowledge, it can connect those weaknesses together.

That ability to connect weaknesses changes how we need to think about exposure. An attack might begin with an exposed secret, then move to an asset with a risky configuration, a software vulnerability or an identity problem. Each issue might look relatively insignificant on its own. You might classify each one as medium or low risk and decide none is critical enough to demand immediate attention. But together, they can create a critical attack path.

Microsoft made essentially the same point in its July 2026 “Secure Future Initiative“ progress report, noting that attackers can use “frontier models to discover vulnerabilities, chain attack paths, and scale exploitation faster than manual approaches allow.” It also observed that serious security failures can emerge when identity gaps, unmanaged assets and inconsistent configurations sit next to one another.

The Hugging Face intrusion offers a vivid example. In July 2026, the company disclosed that an autonomous AI agent, which had escaped an AI lab’s evaluation environment, carried out an end-to-end intrusion into part of its production infrastructure, with no human directing its steps. The attack moved from code-execution weaknesses to credential harvesting and lateral movement across internal clusters. Hugging Face later reconstructed roughly 17,600 attacker actions as the system searched for a viable path.​ ​Most of those actions failed. The agent simply kept going until something worked.

A human attacker may look for one big open window and move on if it isn’t there. AI will find that window faster, and if it isn’t there, it will patiently look for the little things and chain them together.

Attackers and defenders often see the environment differently. From a defender’s perspective, we frequently manage security in islands. There may be a cloud vulnerability team, an identity team, IT teams and someone else responsible for third-party applications. The attacker doesn’t care about those organizational boundaries. To the attacker, all of those things are part of the same attack surface.

Suppose a team is looking at a cloud vulnerability. On its own, it might not appear urgent. But what if the asset can be accessed by someone whose MFA is misconfigured and who also uses a highly privileged third-party application? If the teams responsible for those areas don’t know the issues are connected, they don’t understand the real priority.

That becomes especially important as AI gives defenders visibility into more exposures. In many cases, these weaknesses were probably always there. We simply know about more of them now. That’s a good thing because defenders can use powerful tools to find the same types of exposures attackers are looking for.

The problem is that organizations will get a lot of results. It will be impossible to manage everything at once. Prioritization therefore has to change. Instead of looking only at how severe an individual vulnerability appears to be, ask whether it is exposed, how it connects to other weaknesses and whether it forms part of an attack chain.

A critical exposure on an important asset still demands attention, whether or not it’s part of a chain. But something that appears lower-risk may also offer a quick win because fixing it breaks a larger chain.

AI has made finding vulnerabilities faster and easier than ever. Closing them still depends on knowing who owns the affected asset, understanding what a fix could affect and getting approval, and that’s where most organizations get stuck. In many of my conversations with CISOs, we never get to attack chains. They have critical exposures they can’t close.

One CISO at a large enterprise told me that 25% to 35% of employees leave or change roles in a given year. Many of them own systems, and the asset inventories meant to track that are almost never up to date. So security teams spend their days chasing people to find out who can approve a fix. That isn’t the job anyone signed up for, and it’s the bottleneck that keeps exposures open. Before you can think in chains, you have to be able to close the basics quickly.​

I see two fundamental requirements for responding to this shift. First, organizations need to know their assets: what they have, who owns each one and what a change could affect. Second, they need automation operating continuously on top of that knowledge.

If attackers are operating at machine speed, defenders cannot depend entirely on human-speed processes. Organizations need systems that continuously collect information, connect exposures and help security teams identify which problems matter most.​​ Then they need to get each fix to the right people, because a prioritized list nobody can act on doesn’t reduce risk.

This matters even for threats no one has seen yet. You can’t patch a zero-day before you know it exists, but you can shrink your blast radius every day by closing the exposures around it, so the next one matters less before it’s even disclosed. And when it does land, you can be ready to answer “are we exposed?” in hours, not weeks.​

For CISOs, my practical advice is to pause and rethink exposure management. The way we have managed exposure until today isn’t necessarily going to work for the AI era. Assign someone, or create a team, whose job is to think about exposure holistically. Then reconsider the people, process and technology required to support that approach.

AI creates real reasons for concern. But the most useful fear is a specific one: attackers are becoming faster, more persistent and more sophisticated. Defenders need to respond in kind: know their assets, shrink their blast radius every day and be ready for the next one.

In other words, we need to start thinking a little more like the attackers.​

To save money on holiday gifts this year, Americans are using these 5 strategies that require coordination with friends and family.

Gift giving can bust a budget, so some Americans plan to have conversations with friends and family this year about setting limits around holiday gifting.

This isn’t as Scroogey as you might think: 55% of holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy that likely involves coordinating with loved ones, according to a new NerdWallet survey conducted online by The Harris Poll.

Money can be a taboo subject, especially among family and friends. But a focused discussion on gift boundaries could be the difference between staying within your budget and piling up debt this holiday season.

What other Americans are doing: 28% of holiday spenders plan to set a per-gift dollar limit with family or friends.

Why this works: It’s simple and easy to remember. Unlike some other ideas on this list, you can probably coordinate this one over text.

For best results: If you’re the one bringing up the topic, you should come with a dollar amount that would be reasonable for everyone in your gift exchange group, so no one feels excluded or overextended.

Your circle of friends and family has a lot of kids.

What other Americans are doing: 23% of holiday spenders plan to buy gifts for children in a family, but not the adults.

Why this works: Cutting out adult gifts altogether can rescue a gift budget that has undergone major “kidflation” as new children join the family.

For best results: If you still want to include adults, give a gift that’s fun for the whole family, like a board game or an experience. And make sure your kid-free loved ones are on board.

You traditionally exchange gifts one-on-one with a friend, but the last few gifts you’ve given — and received — were duds.

What other Americans are doing: 18% of holiday spenders plan to skip exchanging gifts with at least one friend or family member.

Why this works: If you’re feeling gift fatigue, there’s a chance they are, too.

For best results: Frame this as an improvement to the gift-giving tradition rather than a scaling back. Propose an alternative way to celebrate your friendship, like swapping out the $40 gift that’ll probably get shelved for a $7 coffee together.

What other Americans are doing: 16% of holiday spenders plan to do a secret Santa gift exchange, or another game that requires purchasing only one gift.

Why this works: 15% of holiday spenders list buying gifts for more people than they originally planned for as among the reasons they’re most likely to overspend this holiday season. This strategy keeps your list in check, even if the number of people playing grows.

For best results: There are bound to be people in your group for whom the rules to the game are important. If you’re the one organizing, be ready to answer questions — can you trade or steal gifts, for example, and, if so, how many times? Also, this works best for family or friend groups who aren’t likely to go rogue and buy extra gifts anyway.

You have no idea what your college friend’s kids (or spouse) are into.

What other Americans are doing: 12% of holiday spenders plan to give one shared gift per family instead of individual gifts.

Why this works: In addition to saving money, this avoids the awkwardness that comes with uninformed gift giving.

For best results: Presentation is key. Don’t sheepishly give an UNO game you clearly bought on the drive over. You may be cutting back, but enthusiasm is free.

Talking about the holidays and talking about money can be stressful conversation topics. About four in five Americans avoid discussing some money topics with family and friends, according to a 2026 survey by the CFP Board. So discussing both at once may seem daunting. But without a doubt, you’re not the only one thinking about them.

Nearly 9 in 10 (86%) holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy this holiday season. Start with an icebreaker: “Hey, have you noticed how expensive everything is lately? Would you be open to talking about how we can do gifts this year while keeping spending under control?” This conversation might be the thing that’s secretly on everyone’s wish list.

#3091. AMD Forecasts 66% Q4 Growth on AI Chip Demand: Rapid Earnings Reaction

AMD's AI business is growing fast enough to reshape the company, though the quarter's cash flow shows how much that growth costs up front.

AMD (AMD +3.65%) grew third-quarter revenue 45% to a record $13.4 billion as data center sales nearly doubled. Shares rose about 6.5% in after-hours trading. AMD expects growth to speed up to roughly 66% next quarter, but it is spending heavily to get there, and cash hasn't caught up with profits yet.

Data center growth is lifting profits faster than sales. Chip design costs stay fairly fixed, so each extra dollar of GPU and server CPU sales drops mostly to profit. That pushed GAAP operating margin up 7 points from a year ago.

The catch is cash. AMD added about $3 billion of inventory in the quarter as it builds Helios rack systems and Venice chips for its fourth-quarter ramp. It also borrowed heavily, more than doubling its debt since June. If those products ship on schedule, the cash comes back, but if demand slips, AMD is left holding a lot of expensive stock.

GAAP profit also took a $1.1 billion hit tied to warrants AMD issued to certain customers. The charge rises with AMD's share price, so a strong stock can shrink reported earnings. The release doesn't say how many warrants are outstanding.

Track whether fourth-quarter revenue lands near the guided $17 billion and inventory starts turning into cash. Also watch whether adjusted gross margin holds near the guided 55% as rack-scale systems ramp.

#3088. Nokia vs. Verizon: A Contrast in Revenue Scale and Seasonality

Verizon's revenue runs 6x larger, but Nokia's year-end surges reveal a pattern that could signal timing opportunities for contrarian investors.

Nokia Oyj (NOK +2.17%) earns its revenue by supplying extensive network infrastructure, optical routing equipment, and comprehensive cloud services to communications service providers and digital enterprises globally. Between August and October 2026, it completed the planned sale of its fixed wireless access business and entered a separate agreement to develop satellite communications capabilities.

Verizon Communications (VZ +0.42%) generates its revenue primarily by delivering wireless connectivity, high-speed internet access, and specialized business networking solutions to diverse consumer and enterprise customers. Between August and October 2026, it launched a joint venture to eliminate mobile coverage dead zones and finalized the sale of a wireless carrier unit.

Revenue represents the total cash brought into a business before any operating expenses are deducted. This metric helps investors measure a company's overall size, market footprint, and long-term trajectory.

Nokia Oyj vs. Verizon Communications Revenue over the last 8 quarters. Figures: Nokia Oyj shown in U.S. dollars, converted from euros.

Data source: Financial Modeling Prep. Nokia Oyj's figures are converted from euros to U.S. dollars. Data as of Nov. 2, 2026.

Nokia and Verizon are two giants of the telecommunications industry, although both are looking toward capitalizing on the artificial intelligence boom. This could prove transformative to their revenue growth trajectories in time.

Verizon's AI Connect offering is an integrated suite of network infrastructure, connectivity, and data center solutions launched by Verizon Business to help enterprises deploy and scale artificial intelligence workloads.

Nokia formed a partnership with AI giant Nvidia to support the development of AI radio access network (AI-RAN) technology. AI-RAN differs from today's 5G network in that artificial intelligence transforms it from a passive data pipe into one where AI intelligently manages traffic for improved speed, coverage, and capacity.

How these AI endeavors pan out will reflect in revenue totals eventually, if they prove successful. For now, Verizon's income trajectory reflects the stable sales growth inherent in its cellphone service subscriptions, while Nokia’s represents cyclical technology spending. The revenue spikes in Nokia's fourth quarter reflect the use-it-or-lose-it IT spending by its customers, who have to use up their budgets before the end of each calendar year.

#3086. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#3084. Arista Revenue Up 58% as Q4 Outlook Slows: Rapid Earnings Reaction

Arista's own forecast for next quarter calls for far smaller gains than this one delivered. We look at which parts of the profit picture hold up.

Arista Networks (ANET +3.52%) reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58.5% from a year ago and above its own $3.3 billion guide. Shares rose about 8% in after-hours trading. Q3 grew 20.5% from Q2, but the Q4 guide of $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion implies only 7% to 9% more. Growth is set to slow sharply, and gross margin is already slipping.

The guide matters more than the quarter. Arista sells to a few very large customers, and the release's risk list flags that concentration and volatile growth rates. Big customers order in lumps, so growth this fast is hard to hold, and the guide already points to a slowdown.

Gross margin fell because mix shifted toward product sales, which earn less than services. Product was 87% of revenue. Operating margin still rose because operating expenses grew much more slowly than sales. The release gives no gross margin outlook.

GAAP profit includes a $134.5 million gain on strategic investments, which the company removes from non-GAAP earnings. That is why GAAP earnings per share top the non-GAAP figure, and why operating profit is the cleaner read.

Watch whether Q4 revenue lands at or above the top of the $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion guide. Also track whether gross margin stops sliding as product sales keep growing.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates kicked off the week with a drop, but they’re still above 7%.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.
