#3082. A massive trade just happened in surging shares of Snap

Don't call it a comeback yet, but shares of beleaguered social media stock Snap Inc. are up almost 20% this month and options traders are betting it's about to go on a big run.Snap shares have traded under $10 since July 2025 following a near-complete collapse from over $80 at the stock's high in 2021 to a low of $3.81 in April. But now, as excitement swirls over social media giant Meta Platforms' AI agent, traders are pouring into Snap call options on Monday, propelling trading volume to more than four times the month-long average, Cboe LiveVol data show.Almost 140,000 options on Snap traded Monday, including about 64,000 call trades that were likely initiated by buyers, compared to under 7,000 puts. Traders sold more than 12,000 puts, and just over 34,000 calls. The net trade sentiment, as well as net directional bias according to options deltas, was positive, according to Barchart.

Nine out of the top 10 trades by volume were calls, and of the $5.5 million in premium exchanged, $5 million was tied to calls, SpotGamma data show.The most popular contract to buy was the 8-strike call expiring Dec. 18, which traded 26,000 times. That contract costs about 37 cents and needs Snap to rally 30% before expiry to pay off. If that happens, it would be the highest the stock's traded since February.The owner of photo-sharing and messaging app Snapchat also offers augmented-reality `Specs' glasses. Shareholder Blue Duck Capital issued an open letter to Snap's board of directors last week urging the company to raise dedicated capital to support the product, saying it could lead to a $12-$14 share price.

Revenue from the retained automotive businesses, which primarily comprise of royalty income from the franchising businesses, was flat in comparison to the prior quarter. Now turning to all other operating segments. Real estate's Q3 2026 adjusted EBITDA increased by $11 million compared to the prior year quarter.

Food packaging's adjusted EBITDA attributable to IEP increased by $2 million for Q3 2026 as compared to the prior year quarter.

The increase is primarily due to volume-related increases and an increase in price and product mix driven by reduced waste. Home fashion's adjusted EBITDA remained consistent when compared to the prior year quarter, despite softening demand in our hospitality business and continued supply chain disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Pharma's adjusted EBITDA decreased by $4 million when compared to the prior year quarter, primarily due to reduced sales resulting from generic competition in our anti-obesity drug therapy and increased R&D expenses related to our ongoing pivotal drug trials. The TRANSCEND trial preparation for our PAH drug remains on schedule, with four sites active and patient screening underway. Now turning to our liquidity.

We maintain liquidity at the holding company and at our operating subsidiaries to take advantage of attractive opportunities. As of quarter end, the holding company had cash and investment in the funds of $2.3 billion, and our subsidiaries had cash and revolver availability of $582 million. We continue to focus on building asset value and maintaining liquidity to enable us to capitalize on opportunities within and outside our existing operating segments. This concludes our presentation of third-quarter results, and we look forward to our update next quarter. Thank you.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates eased again today, giving buyers modest relief from rates above 7%.

Mortgage rates are continuing to cool off as we head into November.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 6.93% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

A significant drop is eye-catching, but bear in mind that you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. Since September, mortgage rates have been hovering around 7%. That’s a full percentage point higher than they were at the beginning of 2026.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.43% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3078. Block's Adjusted Profit Jumps as Losses Climb: Rapid Earnings Reaction

Block's third-quarter letter shows a payments company growing faster and running leaner, plus two costs its adjusted numbers leave out.

Block (XYZ -1.40%) grew gross profit 22% in the third quarter, ahead of its own guidance, and raised its full-year outlook again. Shares rose about 8% in early after-hours trading. Its smaller workforce is now turning growth into profit, but GAAP results show two costs that the adjusted figures skip: loan losses and a third straight quarter of large legal charges.

Square's growth is real and speeding up. U.S. payment volume growth rose to 10%, and gross profit grew in step with volume as field sales reps and reseller partners won sellers still on older systems. In payments, more volume at steady pricing compounds.

The adjusted jump comes from February's staff cuts, which shrank product spending while gross profit kept rising. The catch is what adjusted results exclude: $435 million of contingency, restructuring, and other charges, mostly accrued legal costs, after similar charges in each of the prior two quarters. The letter doesn't name the legal matter.

Credit is the other cost: transaction and loan losses rose 66%, three times as fast as gross profit, as Cash App Borrow and Afterpay lending grew. Loan fees count in gross profit, while the losses land below it as an operating expense. Management says lending margins held steady with last year.

Watch whether loss growth slows in the fourth quarter, as Block expects, once Borrow limits start rising again. Block also guides gross profit growth to slow to 15% that quarter.

#3076. Yum Brands (YUM) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Pizza Hut sale closed as Taco Bell works through a food safety setback.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Yum! Brands, Inc. (YUM -0.37%) reported the completion of its Pizza Hut divestiture during the third quarter, signaling a transition toward a more focused business model centered on its Raise the B.A.R. strategic priorities. Management reported that the company is prioritizing the acceleration of restaurant unit economics, digital expansion through its Byte platform, and efforts to reach a $5 billion beverage sales goal for Taco Bell by 2030. Despite an industrywide food safety issue that temporarily impacted Taco Bell U.S. performance, the company reported a rapid recovery in same-store sales growth as of October. Management indicated that the company remains on track for a record year of unit development at KFC while maintaining a disciplined approach to capital allocation and debt refinancing.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Yum! Brands Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Matt Morris, Head of Investor Relations and Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

Matthew Morris: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. On our call are Chris Turner, our CEO; Ranjith Roy, our CFO; and Dave Russell, our Senior Vice President and Corporate Controller. Following remarks from Chris and Roy, we'll open the call to questions. Please note that this call includes forward-looking statements that are subject to future events and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from these statements. All forward-looking statements are made only as of the date of this call and should be considered in conjunction with the cautionary statements in our earnings release and the risk factors discussed in our SEC filings.

Please refer to today's release and filings with the SEC to find disclosures, definitions and reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures. Please note that during today's call, system sales and operating profit growth will exclude the impact of foreign currency. For more details on our reporting calendars by market, please refer to the Financial Reports section of our IR website. This conference call is being webcast live on our website and will be available for replay following the call. Our fourth quarter earnings will be released on February 3 with the conference call on the same day. Now I'll turn the call over to Yum!'s CEO, Chris Turner.

Christopher Turner: Thank you, Matt, and good morning, everyone. This was a pivotal quarter for Yum! as we completed the divestiture of Pizza Hut at the beginning of September, while also navigating an industrywide U.S. food safety issue. I couldn't be more pleased with how our teams performed. I especially want to thank the Pizza Hut team members and franchise partners for their many contributions to Yum! and wish them continued success. With the transactions behind us, Yum! enters its next chapter, having a sharper focus on our Raise the B.A.R. priorities, battling for the future consumer, accelerating restaurant unit economics and reaching the full potential of Byte and our digital capabilities.

These priorities will accelerate growth and deliver high-quality, consistent total shareholder returns over the long term. Let me start with an update on Taco Bell's performance. I'm incredibly proud of how the Taco Bell team and our franchise partners have come together with urgency and focus to drive a rapid recovery. From a low point in July, Taco Bell U.S. same-store sales strengthened week after week. And since the end of September, the brand has been outperforming the QSR industry on same-store sales growth. Our progress to date reinforces our confidence in Taco Bell's magic formula and the ability of our team and franchisees to navigate challenges while positioning the brand for sustained long-term growth.

The Taco Bell team is laser-focused on continuing to drive momentum through Q4 and beyond. Stepping back to broader Yum! results, I'll discuss how our teams brought the Raise the B.A.R. priorities to life in third quarter performance. For KFC, Raise the B.A.R. is reflected in the brand's expectation to be the most modern Chicken QSR globally. As we announced last quarter, this initiative will include a refreshed brand identity, a more buzzworthy marketing calendar, an always-on pipeline of innovation, a famous value platform and a broader menu that will feature items such as upgraded tenders, craveworthy sauces and unique beverages. We will scale loyalty and Byte to further accelerate the brand's modernization.

Let me share a few examples of how this strategy is showing up in KFC's third quarter results. KFC, which represents 62% of Yum!'s divisional operating profit, excluding Pizza Hut, delivered system sales growth of 6%, supported by unit growth of 7% and same-store sales growth of 1%. I will now go deeper on KFC's results in 3 parts: KFC International, excluding China, KFC China and KFC U.S. I'll start with KFC's International markets, excluding China. Those markets represent over 60% of KFC's global system sales and approximately 75% of KFC's divisional operating profit.

System sales grew an impressive 9%, with an acceleration in same-store sales growth to 4%, reflecting disciplined value execution, high-impact innovation and continued digital and delivery growth. The Middle East is a great example of how the new strategy is taking hold. Across 7 countries in the Middle East, KFC rolled out a new everyday value platform called Worth It, taking a page from the Taco Bell playbook, KFC balanced its value news with Craveable Innovation, pairing the new value menu with limited time offers such as Hot Honey and Captain Nacho.

KFC India took a similar approach, complementing its value platform with disruptive offers, including a $1 burger meal paired with a locally inspired innovation called the Double Chicken Dynamite. Same-store sales growth in India and the Middle East improved quarter-over-quarter, accelerating 4 and 6 points, respectively. Several other KFC markets focused on combining strong value execution and culturally relevant innovation, including Japan, Thailand, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria and Cyprus. In Canada and parts of Continental Europe, KFC continues to strengthen the consistency of its limited time offers and everyday value propositions. The quarter reflected progress on this effort with value-focused promotions, including Hot Wings in Canada, and summer deals in the Netherlands, generating a stronger consumer response.

We look forward to KFC's global strategy coming together across its international markets throughout 2027. The U.K. is the first market to have most of the core elements in place, and early results in the U.K. have been promising. U.K. same-store sales growth was 6%. Traffic growth outpaced the QSR industry by 5 points and taste satisfaction scores improved meaningfully. KFC expects to continue expanding elements of the strategy across its top 20 markets through 2027. Turning to KFC China, which represents approximately 20% of KFC's divisional operating profit, system sales grew 3%, driven by strong unit growth supported by very attractive paybacks.

Same-store sales declined year-over-year, reflecting severe weather events in August and a difficult prior year comparison driven by delivery platform subsidies. Finally, at KFC U.S., which represents approximately 5% of KFC's divisional operating profit, the brand continues to navigate a competitive QSR environment. The KFC U.S. team is advancing its turnaround strategy. And KFC U.S. saw a strong consumer response to the launch of Popcorn Chicken in the third quarter with the menu items selling out in many restaurants. However, KFC U.S. did not lap the successful Wings and Wedges promotion in Q3 of last year. More work lies ahead, and the team is taking steps to return KFC U.S. to sustainable growth.

Moving to Taco Bell, which represents 38% of our divisional operating profit, excluding Pizza Hut, Taco Bell's third quarter same-store sales declined 4%, with international same-store sales up 5% and U.S. same-store sales down 4%, owing to the industrywide food safety issue. During the quarter, Taco Bell U.S. demonstrated the value and impact of its magic formula. The brand brought back the Decades Menu that included fan favorites from its one-of-a-kind menu archive. In addition, Taco Bell drove brand buzz through exciting menu collaborations with the Mexican music artist, Peso Pluma and iconic chili-lime seasoning brand, Tajín, demonstrating the brand's ability to continually create buzz, stay culturally relevant and give consumers more reasons to engage.

In Q4, Taco Bell is taking its marketing advantage even further, partnering with global pop superstar and longtime Baja Blast fan, Olivia Rodrigo, to launch the first-ever pink twist on the iconic Baja Blast. And just yesterday, Taco Bell hosted the inaugural Live Más Open, an unconventional 9-hole golf tournament hosted by comedian and actor Kevin Hart, which will be streamed to fans later this month. Of course, another element of Taco Bell's magic formula is providing unmatched value. With higher gasoline prices pressuring household budgets, Taco Bell's value architecture remains a critical advantage over its peers. Value leadership is built on giving consumers choice across price points and occasions.

Taco Bell's Luxe Cravings Boxes provide abundant value, while the Luxe value menu offers 10 items for $3 or less and resonates particularly well among lower-income consumers. The brand also brings distinctive innovation to value through limited time offerings and loyalty exclusives like the Build Your Own Luxe Box, Taco Bell's most ordered digital item. Altogether, Taco Bell can deliver the affordability consumers expect without sacrificing the craveability, innovation, and choice that make it distinctive. Most importantly, franchise partners are very supportive of the value strategy. In fact, over 90% of the system offers all 10 Luxe value menu items for $3 or less. Internationally, Taco Bell is building relevance and scale.

I'm pleased with the strong performance across Taco Bell's largest markets, and I'm very excited about the opportunity ahead as the team starts to leverage Taco Bell's iconic cult favorite products. As a recent example, in the U.K., Taco Bell rolled out Baja Blast at the end of June, becoming the first market outside of North America to offer this exclusive beverage. Since launch, the U.K. market has maintained double-digit same-store sales growth. We are exploring additional markets for Baja Blast while continuing to launch fan favorite cult classics like the Quesarito. Moving to Habit Burger & Grill. The brand delivered 3% system sales growth driven by unit growth.

The team is sharpening its near-term priorities to drive traffic and improve top line trends. For the balance of the year, this includes the launch of the new $10 Dipping Trio Box and the MyHabit Exclusive Value Menu featuring $2, $4 and $6 offerings, while driving cultural buzz and focusing development in markets with the greatest opportunity to scale. Loyalty is central to our Raise the B.A.R. priority of battling for future consumers who seek more personalized, relevant and seamless experiences. It also helps us build deeper, more direct relationships with them. We witnessed the power of our loyalty programs in Q3.

At Taco Bell, following the initial sales decline from the industrywide food safety issue, loyalty users returned to the brand 2x faster than non-loyalty users. Taco Bell's U.S. loyalty program also grew meaningfully throughout Q3, contributing to 25% growth in total membership year-over-year. KFC is also rapidly expanding loyalty with plans to have loyalty programs in 18 of its top 20 markets by the end of this year. Like Taco Bell, KFC sees strong engagement with 48% growth in global loyalty members, excluding China. Across all of our brands, loyalty represents an important step in deepening consumer relationships and creating more opportunities to drive engagement and frequency over time.

Another important way our brands are battling for the future consumer is the launch of an expanded beverage lineup to meet their evolving preferences and enter new occasions to give them more reasons to visit. The new KWENCH by KFC beverage platform is live in more than 1,000 restaurants across over 10 markets, including 6 of KFC's top 20, and is on track to reach 2,000 restaurants by year-end. The team has plans to double that count by the end of 2027, continuing to scale across Australia and Canada before expanding into some of KFC's largest markets around the world. At Taco Bell, we're excited by results from Live Más Café.

The Taco Bell team is focused on delivering an amazing consumer experience while minimizing build costs and optimizing labor models. Further learnings will come from a new flagship location that is set to open this month in Las Vegas. What is clear at this stage is that the concept is serving as a fantastic innovation platform. Since launching Live Más Café has introduced more than a dozen new beverage innovations that have expanded to the full Taco Bell U.S. system. Each sip, test and learning is helping inform Taco Bell's broader beverage strategy as the brand works toward its goal of reaching $5 billion in beverage sales by 2030.

Now I would like to share highlights on the people and culture front. People and culture remain a competitive advantage for Yum! and are foundational to how we grow iconic restaurant brands globally. Two weeks after completing the sale of Pizza Hut, we brought together Yum!'s top 150 leaders at our Global Leadership Summit to align around our recipe for good growth, our Raise the B.A.R. priorities and the actions required to deliver on our bold ambitions, all in the context of a more focused Yum!. Bringing our global leaders together in person is an important way we strengthen connections, reinforce our culture and build the alignment needed to move our business forward.

And as we drive growth, we never lose sight of how we show up in the communities we serve. In September, we celebrated our Food and Futures in Action Month, bringing our teams together to help more people access food and build brighter futures. Through volunteering, our employees helped provide the equivalent of more than 106,000 meals and positively impact more than 86,000 lives. As we look ahead, our Raise the B.A.R. priorities are clear and we are energized about this next chapter for Yum!. With iconic brands, significant global white space and multiple levers to accelerate performance, we are well positioned to capitalize on favorable consumption trends within our categories.

We will remain disciplined in execution, investment and capital allocation with a clear objective of delivering dependable results and sustained long-term shareholder value. With that, Roy, over to you.

Ranjith Roy: Thanks, Chris, and good morning, everyone. I'll begin by reviewing our third quarter results. Our reported numbers and year-over-year trends for this past quarter reflect 2 unique factors. First factor, the successful completion of the Pizza Hut divestiture during the quarter, which resulted in a onetime gain and only a partial quarter being reported for Pizza Hut. And the second factor, the impact of an industrywide food safety issue over the summer, which affected Taco Bell U.S. results in particular. With that in mind, during the third quarter, excluding Pizza Hut, Yum! grew units 7% and grew system sales 3% and grew Core Operating profit 1%. Year-to-date, which includes the first, second and third quarter, excluding Pizza Hut, Yum!

Core Operating profit growth was 6%. In the third quarter, Taco Bell achieved restaurant level margins of 20.2%, demonstrating strong restaurant level execution despite the impact of temporarily lower sales in equity stores, particularly in the more heavily impacted Midwest region, investments in compelling value offers and investments in store level labor. KFC restaurant level margins were 12.3%, down 140 basis points year-over-year, primarily from mix change from 2025 to 2026 as we added 15 test stores under the Saucy brand that were operated with lower margins.

Ex-special G&A, excluding Pizza Hut, was $235 million in Q3, up 8% year-over-year with 3 percentage points of the increase in G&A, consisting of costs associated with Yum!'s biennial Global Leadership Summit held in Q3 this year and the corporate costs associated with continuing transition services to Pizza Hut, the offsetting fee income for which is reported in other income. Finally, the completion of the Pizza Hut transactions resulted in a pre-tax gain of approximately $1.7 billion. Moving to development. Excluding Pizza Hut, Yum! opened 955 gross new restaurants during the quarter. KFC opened 878 gross new restaurants and surpassed an impressive milestone of 35,000 restaurants globally.

We reached this milestone less than 3 years since eclipsing 30,000 units, underscoring the strength of KFC's development engine. Yum!'s world-class franchise partners remain very committed to growth, particularly in large parts of the world with significant white space, markets such as China, India and Brazil and whole regions like the Middle East and Asia ex China. We currently expect 2026 to be a record year for new unit development in KFC with record gross openings in KFC International as well as KFC International, excluding China. Taco Bell opened 73 gross new units during the quarter, including 36 in the U.S.

Despite the temporary sales impact in the U.S. over the summer, Taco Bell U.S. development pipeline for next year and beyond remains robust, and our view of its growth opportunity remains unchanged. Internationally, Taco Bell opened 37 gross new units, the team recently opened its first restaurant in Germany and in Croatia, with Germany receiving an incredible reception as hundreds of fans lined up for hours to experience Taco Bell. We are encouraged by Taco Bell's near-term expansion plans in countries such as Poland, Denmark and Prague. These planned market entries further build on the brand's existing momentum of having expanded into 6 new markets since the third quarter of last year.

Strong and increasingly consistent international same-store sales growth from quarter-to-quarter reinforces our view of Taco Bell's long-term potential outside the U.S. Across Yum!, we are focused on sustainable unit development, grounded in accelerating unit economics, which is the A in raising the B.A.R. Having great unit economics makes our franchisees' businesses stronger today and opens up more trade areas for our brands tomorrow. An early example would be that over the past year in Saudi Arabia, our team ran a comprehensive program across sourcing and supply chain to drive a significant improvement in future restaurant paybacks.

As we apply a similar lens to other markets around the world as part of raising the B.A.R., we expect to focus on shorter paybacks on new stores over time, thereby broadening our new store pipeline and bulletproofing our unit development engine. Moving to technology. Reaching the full potential of Byte is the third pillar of Raise the B.A.R. With our unmatched scale, proprietary technology platforms and world-class talent, Byte by Yum! is creating better consumer experiences, simplifying operations and providing greater value to franchise partners. We will continue to further develop our technology suite and to deploy it in additional markets around the globe.

A strong example of technology development is the new Byte Kitchen Display System in our Smart Ops bundle, which upgrades the capabilities of KFC restaurants and is now beginning to roll out in the U.S. with plans to expand it to additional markets over time. The system enables team members to manage kitchen demand more efficiently and execute with greater consistency. In the limited portion of the U.S. system where it is currently deployed, prior to a broader rollout, we are seeing measurable operational gains, 8% faster drive-thru speeds, a 12% reduction in refunds and a more than 20-sec reduction in delivery driver wait times.

Our brands are also using our digital capabilities and AI to battle for the future consumer by delivering more personalized experiences. Our marketing teams are regularly testing millions of permutations across consumer communication channels to improve the efficacy of messages to consumers. When focusing on the team member experience and consumer experience, more than 900 Taco Bell restaurants now use voice AI in the drive-thru and the team expects to expand it to more than 1,500 restaurants by year-end. In locations where voice AI has been deployed, the brand has seen a 6% improvement in overall drive-thru satisfaction, approximately 1.5% sales uplift driven by higher check and sustained improvements in team member retention compared with our control group.

Looking ahead, our AI pipeline is focused on shifting from AI testing to adoption and then to scaling impact ensuring that the capabilities we develop translate into measurable improvements in restaurant operations, consumer experiences and franchisee economics. Next, I'll provide an update on our balance sheet and liquidity position. During the third quarter, we completed the divestiture of Pizza Hut to LongRange Capital and Yum! China, for which we received approximately $2.4 billion in net proceeds. We paid off our revolver balance of $675 million and repurchased $543 million of stock. Cumulatively, during the first 3 quarters of this year, we have returned $1.8 billion to shareholders through share repurchases and dividends.

We ended Q3 with $2.1 billion in cash and cash equivalents. And when including our undrawn revolver, we had total available liquidity of approximately $3.6 billion. Our balance sheet remains robust, and our asset-light franchise business model provides flexibility to invest in growth opportunities and return substantial capital to shareholders. Now turning to our outlook for the rest of the year. I'll start with unit growth, where when excluding Pizza Hut, we expect to exceed our 5% long-term algorithm for the full year. With respect to our expectations for Taco Bell sales in Q4, as Chris shared, same-store sales in the most recent period are once again outperforming the QSR industry.

Same-store sales are up approximately 1% quarter-to-date and up roughly 3% over the trailing 4 weeks through last Friday. Contributing to this momentum has been a relentless focus on what makes Taco Bell special: brand buzz through big brand moments and disciplined approach to value, which have helped attract new consumers to the brand and accelerate loyalty registrations. At this time, we see consumer visits by heavy users of the brand has rebounded fully, while visits by medium and light users are tracking to 95% of prior levels.

During the remainder of Q4, we intend to continue focusing on the fundamental drivers of Taco Bell with a view to 2027 growth, including creating big brand moments and leaning into value with a disciplined manner with targeted initiatives. These actions will be taken in our equity stores and with the partnership of the Taco Bell franchise base. We have franchise partners who are willing, capable and committed to investing with us during good times and difficult times. As a result of these actions, we expect Q4 restaurant-level margins in the range of 21.5% to 23.5% representing a sequential improvement from Q3 and also reflects continued sales improvement and easing year-over-year inflation on beef input costs.

We expect Q4 ex-special G&A to be in the range of $285 million to $305 million, which includes approximately $2.5 million per month of Corporate G&A previously allocated to the Pizza Hut Division. We expect offsetting transition services fees to be recorded in other income in Q4. The fee revenue is expected to taper off by mid-2027 as the transition services obligations fall away. As mentioned previously, we expect to mitigate the associated corporate G&A costs over time. Turning to interest expense. We expect Q4 net interest expense of approximately $130 million to $140 million, excluding the impact of any financing activities.

Please note, between now and the first half of next year, we expect to address $1.6 billion of maturing debt. I would also like to note that beginning with our 2027 Q1 results, Yum! will transition its U.S. brands and select international markets from a period-based reporting convention to a calendar-based reporting convention, aligning the financial reporting close dates across our entire organization. This change will provide greater consistency and comparability in our financial reporting, streamline internal processes and better enable us to leverage our global scale. To support comparability and provide a clear historical baseline, early in 2027, we intend to provide certain historical results recast on a calendar basis.

In closing, we are encouraged by the strength of our business as we enter this next chapter focused on executing our Raise the B.A.R. priorities and delivering durable financial growth. Yum!'s asset-light model and strong cash generation give us the flexibility to invest behind our highest return growth opportunities while also delivering dependable capital returns to shareholders. With that, operator, we are ready to take questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of David Palmer from Evercore .

David Palmer: Congratulations to the Taco Bell team for navigating what must have been an extremely difficult quarter, and it does seem like you're going to be outperforming the industry for this year in spite of that. It's very impressive. So congrats to them on that. I want to ask a question about KFC. I think one of the things that people appreciate about what you're doing is that you're not -- that you're essentially trying to Raise the B.A.R., as you say, with the international business there.

And you mentioned the U.K. market in the mid-single-digit comp outperformance there and the fact that you're going to be rolling out elements of what you're doing there into your top 20 markets by the end of '27. So I wanted to maybe double click on that a little bit. What elements have really driven the outperformance? It looks like you've been doing well there for much of '25 and now into '26 with accelerating 2-year. So what is particularly helping there? And how much of that do you think could really help these other markets and when?

Christopher Turner: Yes. Thanks a bunch, David. Like you said, we are really proud of the Taco Bell team and our franchise partners for the rapid recovery they've driven. So I appreciate that comment. When you think about the KFC Global business, we remain really optimistic about the long-term opportunity to accelerate our growth. The third quarter same-store sales performance was broadly encouraging across our international markets. So if you take KFC Global, excluding China, that leaves about 80% of the division's operating profit, and we had 3% same-store sales growth, which was an acceleration from the prior quarter. In fact, all but one of our international markets outside of China had positive system sales growth during the quarter.

So to your point, how is raising the B.A.R. coming to life? We think about raising the B.A.R. at KFC, it is about getting to a sharper value proposition. It's building greater relevance with consumers through the new brand identity, elevating our tenders, elevating flavors through sauces in a market-relevant way, bringing loyalty to life, bringing the beverage platform KWENCH to life, and of course, making moves to leverage our scale to improve unit economics and deploy Byte.

So all of those things are a part of the plan and the KFC leadership team, is actually together right now for one of their regular GM meetings, and they are talking about how do we bring this to life across our markets. Now it will take time. We've got 150 countries. So it won't translate to sales overnight, but this is part of building the brand over time. But we are seeing those proof points. So you mentioned the U.K. market. Same-store sales were up 6% during the quarter. This is a really competitive market in the U.K.

Our transaction growth there outperformed broader QSR by 5 percentage points and it reflects the sharp focus we've got on value, really compelling innovation and a continued drive around store economics in that market. If I go beyond that, every market has examples of where Raise the B.A.R. is starting. I'll highlight 4 of our markets that you see had double-digit system sales growth. So Asia was plus 12% system sales growth. I visited Korea and Japan a few months back. What you see there are things like elevating the innovation through flavors. In Korea, we've got a range of sauces. We've got great tenders. You're seeing us modernize the assets, and that's improving unit economics.

If you go to Latin America, plus 11% system sales growth. Brazil is a place where our franchise partner has really modernized the menu. That's helping to transform the consumer perception of the brand there. This is a great example in Latin America of accelerating unit economics. Our franchise partner has really distinctive supply chain capabilities that give them a competitive advantage no one else could match. Middle East, plus 25% system sales growth. We talked about value, elevating food innovation and flavors in that market. That's another place where loyalty. We're actually a leader in loyalty there, a massive loyalty program that's been built in the Middle East.

India, plus 20%, value platform and food innovation are at the core of what's happening there. You take those 4 markets, that's 28% of KFC system sales, and we're not fully rolled out in terms of raising the B.A.R. there, but you're seeing those early proof points come to life. So we're excited to continue the strategy. We think the opportunity ahead of KFC is really big.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Chris O'Cull from Baird.

Christopher O'Cull: It sounds like Taco Bell sales recovery is tracking roughly in line with your expectations. Does what you're seeing give you confidence the business can return to mid-single-digit comp growth? Or has maybe something changed in the consumer environment that makes that trajectory harder to achieve?

Christopher Turner: We are really pleased with the rapid recovery at Taco Bell. The recovery to date, I think, has been one of the fastest, if you look at sort of the history in the restaurant industry recovering from an event like this. And that recovery was really driven by the magic formula and the elements of the magic formula. We may have changed the emphasis at various times. The first phase of the recovery was about getting our heavy core users back. You saw us do those Tuesday Drops, which leveraged our loyalty program, leveraged incredible value. That brought our fans back in droves. Now it also resulted in us actually growing the loyalty membership base faster than normal.

So we got a long-term benefit that came from that. As we shifted into the next phase of the recovery and what you're seeing in Q4, is us speaking to those medium and light users and ensuring that they're coming back. We're not fully recovered on that front. But you saw things like the Olivia Rodrigo collaboration with Pink Baja Blast. You've seen the My Usual Meals with Paris Hilton, Doja Cat, Kevin Hart, which match craveable innovation under our Craveable Menu with real value plus that cultural buzz that Taco Bell is known for.

The really exciting thing as you think about this is the consumers that we've acquired since the disruption, they're actually spending 5% more and visiting 6% more frequently than the consumers we lost. So we're not just bringing folks back. We're bringing a really attractive consumer set to Taco Bell. So we're pleased with the recovery to date, but the team is leaning in and continuing to play offense through the end of the year and into the beginning of 2027.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Dennis Geiger from UBS.

Dennis Geiger: I wanted to ask a little more about the strength of the global unit development despite presumably macro pressures globally. Can you talk a little more about how the 2 brands and the franchisees are effectively managing challenges to open restaurants at such a solid rate? And is there anything else, as you talk about continuing to strengthen those payback periods? Anything else that you could offer on the visibility of development looking ahead, how that pipeline looks and anything more on the development side of things looking ahead?

Christopher Turner: Yes. Look, our development trajectory remains strong. We shared on the call from a KFC standpoint, we expect to set multiple records this year in our development trajectory, driven by strong unit economics. So that raising the B.A.R., if you think about accelerating restaurant economics, the KFC leadership team has specific initiatives and specific targets that they are pushing for across markets that are aimed directly at how do we get paybacks down. And of course, paybacks are the lifeblood of development in our industry. Those come through leveraging our scale. And of course, they also come from the sales growth benefits that we get from battling for the future consumer.

If you go into KFC, our development leaders in the quarter, China, obviously, India, South Africa, Thailand, Korea, were all at the top of the list in KFC International. We've entered 6 new countries over the past year: Germany, Croatia, Ecuador, Moldova, Serbia and Sweden, and we've got more new market entries planned. And as the Taco Bell brand continues to become more well-known and more relevant in each of these markets, we expect that momentum to continue. So we're excited about the development path on both.

Ranjith Roy: I'll also add, look, the thing we take real comfort in is Yum! what we call 3C partners, where our franchisee base, the qualities we look for are 3Cs: capable, committed and well capitalized. We feel very comfortable with the network of franchisees we have. And so they are leaning into growth and excited to develop more restaurants. When you think about the payback periods, as Chris mentioned, paybacks are the lifeblood of development. We see an opportunity to broaden the range of development we have in terms of the number of markets because right now, as you think about it, it's logical, the fastest developing markets today are the ones with the most attractive paybacks.

If we can reduce paybacks, that will broaden the number of markets that are accelerating and we certainly intend to do that in the years ahead, and our franchisee base is ready and willing.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of John Ivankoe from JPMorgan.

John Ivankoe: I ask this question often, but as we have more time to kind of think about the longer-term model and opportunities from both an efficiency and effectiveness perspective to look at G&A as a percentage of system sales. And I understand that would be net G&A as a percentage of system sales. How do you think over the next couple of years, given your priorities, given opportunities with AI? I mean, I guess at this point, assuming you're going to be a 3-brand company, including Habit, how that might evolve?

And if I may, to continue on that, how we're thinking about -- if we're thinking about CapEx as a percentage of EBITDA, just longer term, any way to kind of anchor that CapEx number in the model longer term as that does become an increasingly important part of the model overall?

Ranjith Roy: John, thanks for the question. I'll start with the CapEx question. Look, historically, we've always mentioned we have a very good capital allocation framework, which means the first item in our capital allocation framework is to invest in the business for growth. You should assume that historically, we've never starved any of our brands when we have high return opportunities. And so from a CapEx standpoint, we currently don't see any dramatic change in the amount of CapEx we need to invest to drive our Raise the B.A.R. strategy. Of course, we're always looking for more opportunities to invest. You talked about the -- the first part of your question was around -- I think you mentioned G&A and productivity.

And look, what we say is on the G&A front, we've always been disciplined on G&A, and we'll continue to do so. From an AI perspective, we do expect AI to be transformative to the business and the productivity gains are primarily in empowering our people to deliver the best hospitality experience possible, which results in accelerating business growth. And so first and foremost, that starts with Byte. It gives us a unique advantage to deploy AI at the front lines of the business, and to drive growth. Voice AI is a great example of that. Across marketing, we previously talked about A/B testing in the drive-thru.

We've also talked about personalized messages that we can send to consumers, and we're doing that at scale now using AI. And from an operations perspective, we're excited about developments on the horizon as part of Byte Coach that would help GMs and regional leaders identify and fix restaurant level issues more effectively when AI is teamed up with Byte Coach. AI usage is at this point -- if you just take a step back, at this point, AI usage is about 40% up across our enterprise, reflecting a shift from where people use AI as a tool to just assist day-to-day tasks to embedding AI truly within the capabilities of our organization.

But coming back to first principles, we expect to be highly focused on G&A and maintain discipline on G&A. And we fundamentally think of ourselves as a hospitality business, which involves people and franchise partners. AI is coming to life in a way that empowers our people to deliver a great experience for consumers and drive faster business growth.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Zach Fadem from Wells Fargo.

Zachary Fadem: Now that the Pizza Hut transaction is complete, could you talk a bit more about the long-term financial vision for Yum! in terms of profit growth outlook? And any additional color you could offer on plans to offset the Pizza Hut dilution and stranded costs would also be helpful. And while we're at it, maybe also thoughts on deploying the $2 billion of cash on the balance sheet.

Christopher Turner: Yes. I'll start with the long-term view of our strategy. Yum! exits the Pizza Hut divestiture as a more focused company. Our 3 brands have massive white space ahead of them. We have big growth opportunities, and we could be more focused on capturing those. I'm not going to get ahead of any potential long-term guidance or updates to our algorithm today. But we see massive opportunities to strengthen our growth profile on the path to creating long-term shareholder value. And that's what Raise the B.A.R. is really about. It's about raising our aspiration and ambition and we do that through battling for the future consumer, accelerating restaurant economics and reaching the full potential of Byte and our digital capabilities.

If you take KFC, if you think about the white space, we still believe there should be 75,000 KFCs around the globe. So the 35,000 milestone that we hit in this quarter is still less than halfway on that journey. Taco Bell, we laid out a very clear strategy, getting to $3 million AUVs and the Taco Bell team is laser-focused on doing that. And Taco Bell International, we've tripled our system sales in Taco Bell International since 2018. So we've had a tremendous growth trajectory there, and we look to continue that. So you sum all of that up, we are very bullish on Yum!'s long-term growth opportunity.

Ranjith Roy: To cover your questions around G&A. Look, as I mentioned in an earlier question, that we're going to be tremendously disciplined on G&A as disciplined as we've been in the past. Just to keep in mind on -- particularly on the Pizza Hut and you mentioned stranded costs. When you think about it right now, we completed the divestiture of Pizza Hut. We are still executing on the Transition Services Agreements, and we will continue to do so for the next several months. We have about 74 TSAs in place for the Pizza Hut transaction.

The fees for which are in other income, but the costs and those costs are people, effort, facilities, infrastructure, subleases and third-party contracts that are pass-throughs, those costs sit in our G&A. As those agreements roll off by mid-2027, we'll continue to evaluate the cost structure on an ongoing basis to ensure it is appropriate to our business. I do want us to be clear eyed on timing. It is not practical for us to line up cost management perfectly with when the TSAs roll off.

So you can imagine we will have a clean 2028, but there may be certain temporary periods in parts of 2027 where our P&L is exposed to some portion of the approximately $2.5 million per month of TSA support costs. I don't like it, but it is manageable, it is contained and it is temporary. We're going to continue to be very thoughtful and disciplined as we go about this work on maintaining a disciplined approach to G&A. And regarding the return of capital to shareholders and the proceeds of Pizza Hut, look, our -- we're going to -- as we said in the past, we're going to apply our capital allocation priorities to this.

Our historical guidance is to maintain approximately 4x net leverage over time. We're currently running materially below that threshold as we're carrying cash on balance sheet from the Pizza Hut divestiture. Our expectation is to return excess capital to shareholders. And from a prudent standpoint, we will do that after we address near-term debt maturities, primarily through upcoming refinancings. Our capital allocation framework is unchanged, and we expect substantial return of capital to shareholders.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Danilo Gargiulo from Bernstein.

Danilo Gargiulo: Great. I just have one question more near-term oriented and one more bigger picture. So in the near term, we are seeing a range of protests arising in Europe. So I was wondering if there is anything to call out regarding how the operators are facing challenging times in Europe. And then if we take a step back and think about the longer-term picture, during this call, a couple of times you mentioned we are accelerating the growth. So does it mean outpacing the growth you've achieved in the past 3 years or maintaining the trajectory you've achieved in the past even without Pizza Hut?

And in the case you are accelerating, meaning like going ahead compared to the past 3 years, which part of the algorithm do you feel more confident you could be accelerating and how?

Christopher Turner: Thanks, Danilo. Let me start with the second part of the question first. Our view is we come out of the Pizza Hut transaction, as I mentioned before, is that Yum! is a more focused company. We're focused on the big opportunities ahead of our business. And as I said earlier, raising the B.A.R. is about having a higher ambition as we look to the long term. We've got so many structural strengths behind each of our businesses. Taco Bell being a category of one in the U.S., KFC International in most of those markets, we are the only scaled chicken-focused player. So we've got real competitive advantage there.

And Taco Bell International as it grows, it should have those same strategic advantages as it builds a foothold in each market. So we think the opportunity is significant and raising the B.A.R. actually addresses all elements of the algorithm -- battling for the future consumers should help us support continued improvements in sales growth, accelerating restaurant economics. That's the lifeblood of development. And of course, the digital capabilities underpin both of those. So we're looking to Raise the B.A.R. on all elements over the long term. If I turn to Europe, it's a broad range of countries in Europe. We believe we've got significant white space opportunity.

If you compare the size of KFC to our competitors in most markets in Europe, our competitors are significantly bigger. We've seen where we get really focused and we get unit economics to an improved place like in Italy, we can see a real expansion and change in trajectory in our growth in Europe. So the team there is working hard, but we think over the long term, there's a big opportunity there.

Matthew Morris: We have time for one more question.

Operator: Your final question comes from the line of Jacob Aiken-Phillips from Melius Research.

Jacob Aiken-Phillips: You gave some useful data on like the uplifts from voice AI and the better employee retention. But from a franchisee's perspective, how does that translate into incremental restaurant profit after the technology costs? And what determines the pace of adoption beyond the locations targeted for year-end? And maybe if you could expand that to the broader Byte modules as well.

Ranjith Roy: Look, that's a great question. Look, drive-thru voice AI is one of the many AI initiatives we have across Yum!, and it is particularly visible given its direct impact on the consumer and the team member experience. In our prepared remarks, we did talk about some stats where of the uplift we're seeing at the restaurant level, which benefits -- directly benefits the team members and our franchisees. Voice AI allows restaurant team members to focus more of their attention on delivering a great experience for consumers at the drive-thru window. The biggest thing when you think about deployment, what we like to think about is deployment is one axis of growth for voice AI.

But it's important to differentiate the digital products we have at Byte because they're not static products like just putting up a menu board or putting up LED lighting in a restaurant. These are products which alongside deployment growth, they have the potential for constant new feature development. So in voice AI, for example, the team is already thinking about loyalty integrations, multi-language support, multilane drive-thru support, new operator dashboards to better integrate the human factor in the restaurant with the AI that's helping the human, all of which makes the product more compelling over time. The reason we are able to do that in a broader Byte context is because of 3 factors.

We have a connected technology ecosystem, which we have spent years integrating, which is a competitive advantage. We have the scale of our brands, which is a competitive advantage, and we have the talent at Yum! to go after these opportunities in technology, but also in -- across all of our digital ecosystem. So on the voice AI front, we're seeing uplift right now. We are focused on executing against the 1,500 deployments in Q4 and getting those right, but the opportunity is much bigger, we believe, both in terms of number of deployments as well as the impact we can have in each deployed location.

Christopher Turner: All right. With that, thanks, everyone, for making time to join the call. If you step back, Yum! is focused on raising the B.A.R. Taco Bell, really proud of the recovery to date, but the team is still leaning in and playing offense very aggressively as we look forward and the magic formula is resonating with consumers as it always has. #3072. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.
