#3071. Lindblad (LIND) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record quarter arrives alongside a major acquisition push.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Lindblad Expeditions Holdings, Inc. (LIND -10.64%) reported record quarterly performance and achieved a significant strategic expansion through the acquisition of a majority stake in White Desert and Echo Charlie. Management stated that the integration of these brands transforms the company into a multi-industry experiential travel platform capable of transporting guests by sea, land, and air. The company reported its third consecutive quarter with occupancy exceeding 90% and raised its full-year guidance for the second time in six weeks. Management indicated that the core strategy focuses on expanding booking curves and implementing cost innovation initiatives to drive operating leverage and mitigate macroeconomic headwinds.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Lindblad Expeditions third quarter 2026 financial results. After today's prepared remarks, we will host a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one to raise your hand. To withdraw your question, press star one again. I will now hand the conference over to Rick Goldberg, Chief Financial Officer. Rick, please go ahead.

Rick Goldberg: Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us for Lindblad's third quarter 2026 earnings call. With me on today's call is Natalya Leahy, our Chief Executive Officer. Natalya will begin with some opening comments, and I will follow with details on our Q3 results and expectations for the full year before we open the call for Q&A. As always, you can find our latest earnings release in the investor relations section of our website. Before we get to all of that, I'd like to remind everyone that the company's comments today may include forward-looking statements.

Those expectations are subject to risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results and performance to be materially different from those expectations. The company cannot guarantee the accuracy of any forecast or estimates, and we undertake no obligation to update any such forward-looking statements. If you would like more information on the risks involved in forward-looking statements, please see the company's SEC filings. In addition, our comments may reference non-GAAP financial measures. A reconciliation of the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures and other associated disclosures are contained in the company's earnings release. With that out of the way, I'll turn the call over to Natalya.

Natalya Leahy: Thank you, Rick. Well, this has been a fun and exciting quarter for us. We welcomed two extraordinary brands, White Desert and Echo Charlie, to our global experiential travel platform, expanding our ability to take guests to some of the world's most remarkable places by sea, by land, and now by air. At the same time, we continue to deliver strong business momentum. Combined, these developments gave us the confidence to raise our guidance mid-quarter and again today. We delivered another outstanding quarter with double-digit growth in both revenue and Adjusted EBITDA. Total company revenue reached $269 million, up 12% from a year ago, while Adjusted EBITDA increased 12% to $64 million, despite fuel prices rising approximately 50% year-over-year.

We also generated approximately $27 million in net income available to stockholders. Our year-to-date revenue, Adjusted EBITDA, and net income are all at record levels. These results are especially meaningful against the backdrop of a challenging geopolitical environment and significantly elevated fuel prices. They demonstrate the strength and resilience of our business model, the effectiveness of our strategy, and our team's ability to execute. I'm incredibly proud of what we continue to accomplish and very confident in the opportunities ahead. Occupancy increased 310 basis points to 91% on a 4% increase in capacity. It was our third consecutive quarter with occupancy above 90%, consistent with our long-term stated goal.

Net Yields increased 6% year-over-year to $1,398 per guest night, the highest third quarter net yield in the company's history. Lindblad segment revenue increased 12% to $153 million, and our Land Experiences segment revenue increased 13% to $116 million. Our disciplined commercial execution, revenue management, and improved marketing strategies continue to drive strong bookings momentum. I'm pleased to share that our 2027 bookings continue to outpace the prior year for both our expedition and land segments, and our 2027 booked position is at record high. Our 2028 bookings are also pacing ahead of 2027. Given our continued momentum, we are raising our 2026 full-year guidance again.

Specifically, we're increasing our revenue guidance to a range of $870 million - $885 million from our previous guidance of $850 million - $880 million. We now expect net yields for the full year to increase in the range of 6% - 7%, and we are updating our full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $142 million - $148 million. Before I walk you through our three strategic pillars, I wanted to highlight the significant growth opportunity ahead of us and how our increasingly diversified experiential travel platform positions us to capture it. We continue to benefit from powerful macro trends as affluent travelers increasingly seek authentic, immersive experiences in extraordinary places.

Expedition cruising is one of the fastest-growing and most under-penetrated segments of leisure travel. While expedition capacity has more than doubled over the past decade, it still represents less than 1% of total cruise capacity, with fewer than half a million guests traveling on expedition cruises annually. To put the broader opportunity in perspective, our approximately 60,000 annual guests across eight brands represent less than 0.1% of global travelers with financial means to experience our journeys. This gives us an enormous runway for growth. And importantly, with the addition of White Desert and Echo Charlie, we have further strengthened our position as a truly global experiential travel platform.

Our eight complementary brands now offer extraordinary experiences by sea, by land, and by air, creating more opportunities for guests to explore the world with us across multiple brands and destinations, while further diversifying our portfolio and expanding our addressable market. I believe this combination of strong market tailwinds, an exceptionally large untapped opportunity, and our expanded platform positions us extremely well for sustainable long-term value creation. Now, let me walk you through the progress we made across our three strategic pillars. First, maximizing revenue through higher occupancy pricing and deployment optimization. Second, optimizing financial performance through cost innovation and fixed asset utilization. And third, pursuing accretive growth opportunities. Beginning with our first pillar, maximizing revenue.

We continue to execute against several revenue levers we have discussed previously: dynamic pricing, improved marketing communication, maximizing sales channels, and optimizing revenue management. These initiatives continue to deliver on their objectives, as evidenced by our results and forward-booked position. We stated several times that one of our goals over the past 18 months was to expand booking curves, which drives better revenue predictability and stronger price elasticity. I'm happy to share that our average booking window increased from 9.5 months - 11.9 months. We also continue to see strong momentum in onboard and extension revenues, delivering 27% growth year-to-date.

With a robust pipeline of initiatives ahead, I believe we have significant room to further unlock the full potential of this revenue stream. Moving to our second pillar, cost innovation and fixed asset utilization. We have a culture of continuous improvement, and we continue executing several efficiency initiatives across the company. To give you a few examples, we outsourced our warehouse operations and completely overhauled our accounts payable processes. We're also building out our supply chain and inventory management capabilities and exploring AI to drive further efficiencies.

Fuel costs remain a significant headwind, but I'm particularly proud of the partnership between our shoreside and shipboard teams that worked together to deliver year-over-year improvements in fuel consumption this quarter, despite 4% capacity growth. We have a strong pipeline of process improvements and cost initiatives, and we see more opportunities ahead to capture efficiencies and improve margins. That brings me to our third pillar, accretive growth, which I am most excited to discuss today. On our last few calls, we talked about evaluating opportunities to add to our portfolio of brands. On September 15th, we announced the acquisition of a majority stake in White Desert and Echo Charlie.

It is the largest transaction in the company's history and the beginning of an incredible new chapter in our 60-year legacy of exploration. If you aren't yet familiar with White Desert, you're in for something truly special. Founded in 2005 by the record-breaking polar explorer Patrick Woodhead, White Desert flies guests deep into the interior of Antarctica on private aircraft to otherworldly camps in places very few people will ever see. One-of-a-kind bucket list itineraries range from a journey to the geographic South Pole to a visit with emperor penguin colony of more than 20,000 birds.

When I experienced White Desert, I immediately felt a shared spirit of curiosity and innovation, and a mutual desire to keep pushing the boundaries of what travel can be. White Desert adds a distinctive new offering to our platform that we're actively working on growing, including the addition of a fourth camp. I'm equally excited about what Echo Charlie brings to our portfolio. Echo Charlie is a new expedition travel brand we're launching together with Patrick. It combines White Desert's aviation expertise with our knowledge of extraordinary places to create journeys into some of the world's most remote regions, the kinds of adventures many of us grew up reading about, dreaming about, and never stopped hoping to experience ourselves.

We see a strong long-term value creation opportunity here. We just introduced three inaugural 2027 itineraries, each offering multiple departure dates exclusively to our past guests, and we're planning to launch publicly over the coming days. Echo Charlie gives past guests of Lindblad and White Desert new reasons to travel with us. Our Chief Expedition Officer, our Head of Corporate Development, and I just returned from Cape Town, where we spent time with White Desert team brainstorming our future together. What an amazing group of people. They are incredibly innovative, talented, and let me tell you, really fun.

I came away even more convinced that we are a great cultural fit and even more excited what we can build together and the growth opportunities ahead. We're also very pleased that Patrick Woodhead will serve as a strategic innovation advisor to Lindblad. This acquisition reinforces our view that Lindblad experiential travel platform provides an exceptional opportunity to drive value creation by enabling affluent travelers to explore by air, land, and sea. As we talk about our why and commitment to sustainability, I would like to highlight that White Desert shares the same commitment to our mission.

White Desert flies hundreds of scientists to research stations across Antarctica each season, and it has long been a trusted partner for the scientific community. Additionally, White Desert recently announced the first commercial agreement in Africa to supply sustainable aviation fuel in partnership with Sasol. This will help lower the carbon emissions of our flight and support our carbon offset program. Before I turn the call over to Rick, let me leave you with three key takeaways. First, our revenue maximization efforts are working. Net yields increased 6%, occupancy rose to 91%, and our 2027 and 2028 bookings continue to pace ahead.

Second, we are becoming a more efficient organization, and that discipline is showing up in Adjusted EBITDA margins and growth. Third, our accretive growth initiatives give us multiple ways to capture a large and still under-penetrated market. With White Desert and Echo Charlie, we have added air to our cruise expeditions and land journeys, making us a comprehensive experiential travel platform. Lastly, this year has had its share of challenges, from geopolitical risks to significantly higher fuel prices. I'm very proud of our operating results in the face of them, and I want to thank every member of our team for their focus, their resilience, and their unwavering commitment to the guest experience.

To our new colleagues at White Desert and Echo Charlie, we're delighted to have you with us. With that, I am turning it to you, Rick.

Rick Goldberg: Thank you, Natalya. I'm pleased to report that the third quarter was another record-setting quarter for Lindblad Expeditions, with our highest-ever quarterly Adjusted EBITDA and net income, and our third consecutive quarter with occupancy above 90%. Reflecting the strong performance and continued booking momentum, we're raising our full-year guidance for the second time in just six weeks. Before diving into the details, I'd also like to recognize the acquisition of White Desert and Echo Charlie, our largest acquisition to date and an important milestone in Lindblad's growth. I'm particularly proud of the team's work to bring this transaction to completion, reflecting the capabilities we've built to identify, evaluate, and execute strategic acquisitions.

With that, let me walk through our third-quarter results in more detail. Total company revenue for the third quarter was $269.2 million, an increase of $29 million, or 12.1%, compared to the prior year. Lindblad segment revenues were $153.4 million, an increase of $15.8 million, or 11.5%, compared to the prior year. Despite a 4.3% increase in available guest nights, occupancy increased 3.1 percentage points from 88.1% to 91.2%, and Net Yield per Available Guest Night increased 6.4% to $1,398, the highest Q3 net yield in company history. Land Experiences segment revenues were $115.8 million, an increase of $13.2 million, or 12.8%, compared to Q3 2025, primarily driven by a 12% growth in guests.

Turning now to the cost side of the business. Operating expenses before stock-based compensation, transaction and reorganization expenses, and depreciation and amortization increased $22.1 million, or 12.1%, versus Q3 2025. Specifically, cost of tours increased $11.6 million, or 9.3%, driven by additional voyages and trips, as well as higher fuel costs. Despite higher fuel prices, revenue growth outpaced the increase in costs, resulting in gross margin expansion of 130 basis points to 49.5%. We remain focused on reducing fuel consumption through technology and operational improvements while preserving the flexibility for our captains and expedition leaders to adjust itineraries in real time to optimize the guest experience. These efforts are delivering tangible results.

Despite a 4.3% increase in capacity, we reduced total fuel consumption year over year. However, higher fuel prices resulted in a $1.3 million, or 22% increase in fuel expense, with fuel costs representing 4.9% of Lindblad segment revenue compared to 4.5% in the prior year quarter. Selling and marketing costs increased $7.7 million, or 25.5%, primarily due to the final royalty rate step-up under our National Geographic agreement. General and administrative costs, excluding stock-based compensation, transaction-related expenses, and reorganization costs, increased $2.9 million, or 10.2%. Approximately two-thirds of this increase, or $1.8 million, was attributable to a one-time employee retention tax credit benefit recognized in the third quarter of 2025.

Excluding this prior year benefit, G&A as a percentage of revenue declined approximately 1% year-over-year, reflecting disciplined cost management and improving operating leverage as we scale the business. Adjusted EBITDA for the quarter was $64.1 million, an increase of $6.9 million, or 12%, compared to the third quarter of 2025. Lindblad segment Adjusted EBITDA increased $4.3 million, or 13.2%, to $37.1 million, while Land Experiences segment Adjusted EBITDA increased $2.5 million, or 10.3%, to $27 million. Despite higher fuel costs and the final royalty rate step-up under our National Geographic agreement, we maintained Adjusted EBITDA margins of 23.8%, consistent with the prior year quarter.

Net income available to stockholders reached $24.2 million, or $0.36 per diluted share, compared to a slight loss in the prior year quarter. Importantly, this represents the highest quarterly net income in our company's history, a significant milestone that underscores the progress we're making in driving profitable growth. Through the first nine months of the year, net income available to stockholders totaled $28.8 million, or $0.44 per diluted share. Turning to the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with total cash of $308.2 million, an increase of $18.4 million since year-end 2025. This reflects strong operating cash flow of $111.3 million, driven primarily by solid business performance and increased bookings for future travel.

Cash used in investing activities totaled $73.4 million, including $18.8 million in capital expenditures, primarily for maintenance of our own fleet, and approximately $54.6 million for the acquisition of 60% controlling interest in White Desert and Echo Charlie, net cash acquired and subject to customary post-closing accounting reconciliations. Year-to-date Free Cash Flow reached $92.5 million, an increase of $32.1 million, or 53%, compared to the prior year quarter. Following the acquisitions of White Desert and Echo Charlie, net leverage stood at 2.5x at quarter end, compared to 2.2x at the end of the second quarter.

Our balance sheet remains strong, and we believe we are well-positioned to continue pursuing accretive growth opportunities, including fleet expansion through new builds, acquisitions, and charters, as well as additional Land Experience acquisitions. Turning now to our full-year outlook. When we announced the acquisition of White Desert on September 15th, we raised our full-year guidance to reflect both the addition of White Desert and the continued strength of our core business. Since then, our core business has continued to demonstrate strong momentum, and I'm pleased to share that we are once again raising our outlook.

As Natalya mentioned, booking momentum remains strong, with continued strength in booking for travel during the remainder of 2026, and both 2027 and 2028 are pacing ahead of the prior year. Reflecting this momentum, we now expect Net Yield per Available Guest Night to increase 6%-7% year-over-year, up from our previous guidance of 5.5%-6.5%. We are also raising our full-year revenue guidance to a range of $870 million-$885 million, compared to our prior range of $850 million-$880 million. While higher fuel prices continue to present a headwind, the strength of our underlying business is helping offset these pressures.

Accordingly, we are raising the low end of our full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance by $2 million, resulting in an updated range of $142 million-$148 million, compared to our previous range of $140 million-$148 million. In closing, we're proud of the progress we've made this year, delivering record financial results while continuing to invest in the long-term growth of our business. With strong booking momentum, a healthy balance sheet, and an expanded portfolio of differentiated travel experiences, we're more confident than ever in Lindblad's future. Thank you for your interest in the company. With that, Natalya and I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.

Operator: We will now begin the question-and-answer session. Please limit yourself to two questions. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one to raise your hand. To withdraw your question, press star one again. We ask that you pick up your handset when asking a question to allow for optimum sound quality. If you are muted locally, please remember to unmute your device. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Your first question comes from the line of Steven Wieczynski. Your line is open. Steven Wieczynski: Okay. Just to be clear, there you are kind of saying as we think about next year, like a mid-single digit yield would be pretty fair at this point.

Rick Goldberg: Nope. I think you covered it, Natalya.

Steven Wieczynski: Okay, guys. Appreciate the color. Thank you so much.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Ian Zaffino with Oppenheimer. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Ian Zaffino: Hi. Great. Thank you very much. Glad to see demand is so strong here. Question would be just on Q4 and maybe EBITDA guide. Can you maybe help us understand the bridge there? Is this kind of mostly related to fuel? Because I'm just looking at the year-over-year comp, and is that all fuel? Anything else going on there? Anything else you could do to mitigate that? Thanks.

Rick Goldberg: Yeah. Thanks so much, Ian. What I'd say with Q4 is, as we shared previously, we expect capacity to be down mid-single digits in Q4 due to the timing of dry docks and repositionings. We're continuing to expect full-year capacity to be up 4.5%-5%, but there always is some fluctuations between quarters in terms of dry docks and repositioning. So you're seeing that in Q4. In addition, we have fuel price, which remains a headwind for the business. Despite that, we're continuing to see strong in-year bookings, which is helping to offset and mitigate those factors.

Ian Zaffino: Okay. Then just maybe sticking on fuel for a second longer. I know you kind of mentioned a few things to mitigate fuel costs, but any thinking on surcharges or pursuing hedges or anything like that? Or maybe any other kind of mitigating steps that you think that you could take to offset some of that? Maybe even like dynamic pricing. I don't know if that factors into any of that at all. If you could give some color there. Thank you.

Natalya Leahy: Ian, let me cover your surcharges and dynamic pricing question, and we can comment on hedging. The pricing, and I firmly believe in that, has to be driven by consumer. So our job is drive demand there and develop capabilities. First of all, develop an outstanding product and guest experience, and that will be supported by our marketing tools to generate pricing capabilities. We are doing that in a very, very strong way, which obviously helps to offset any kind of cost fluctuation, including fuel or investments in our food and guest experience.

I don't think you can, I don't believe you can just add the surcharge for fuel, and I think it needs to be supported by guest experience and natural organic demand. I'll let Rick comment on hedging.

Rick Goldberg: The company has never hedged fuel consistent with some other public peers, and our focus is really on looking at ways that we can control fuel prices. We talked about a little bit on the call the steps that we're taking to reduce consumption. We're also looking at how and where we purchase fuel in order to help us limit the impact of these price increases that we're seeing in the fuel markets.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Chris Woronka with Deutsche Bank. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Chris Woronka: Hey. Good morning, guys. Thanks for taking the questions. I know that you've always talked about the importance of availability of airfare, particularly adequate number of first-class seats from some key feeder U.S. markets. As you kind of look out to 2027, just given airlines keep kind of playing around with their schedules in response to fuel, is there anything on the good side or bad side that you see schedule-wise in terms of, or do you think there's going to be enough first-class capacity in the major airlines and the major feeder markets to your markets internationally? Thank you.

Rick Goldberg: Yeah. Thanks so much, Chris. We're not seeing anything in terms of air routes that we expect to impact demand for our 2027 or 2028 itineraries at this time.

Natalya Leahy: I think, Chris, remember, we have, with all the growth that we have for our company, but we only have 60,000 guests traveling with us annually across all of our brands.

Chris Woronka: Yeah. That's a great point. Thanks, Natalya. And the follow-up question is, I mean, look, we've seen in the last quarter, we've seen one of the major cruise companies do this newer land-based strategy with the joint venture. I know that's not something you guys would necessarily look at in that kind of size or scope, but is there any thought to hotel operations in certain markets if there's the right opportunity that kind of fits your demographic?

Natalya Leahy: Chris, I think this is very much related to our main topic of this call is we are and have been building a truly experiential travel platform. We are not per se in a hotel business. We are in experiential travel business. Our goal is to grow our portfolio by delivering very high to replicate exceptional experiential guest experience in most unique destinations. We had portfolio of land companies that take people by feet, by bicycles to most exceptional destinations and close to the nature and culture.

Now we are at White Desert, we are launching Echo Charlie, and all of these brands play in this experiential travel segment, allowing our guests to transition from brand to brand as they experience this world.

Chris Woronka: Okay. Understood. Very helpful. Thanks, Natalya. Thanks, Rick.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Anthony Berni with Jefferies. Your line is open. Please go ahead. As a reminder, please unmute your device locally.

Natalya Leahy: Anthony, if you are speaking, we cannot hear you.

Rick Goldberg: Maybe we will go to the next question, and if Anthony comes back on, we can bring him back into the queue.

Operator: Okay. Your next question is from Eric Des Lauriers with Craig-Hallum Capital Group. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Eric Des Lauriers: Great. Thanks for taking my questions, and congrats on another very impressive quarter here. Both my questions focus on the Land Experiences growth opportunities. We saw some increased ownership stakes this quarter. Just wondering what capacity remains for increased ownership stakes across some of your various Land Experiences brands or companies here, and then ownership stakes aside, how should we think about the organic growth opportunities within your existing Land Experiences portfolio? Thanks.

Rick Goldberg: Yeah. I will start with the second half of that question, Eric, which is we continue to see tremendous opportunities to grow our Land Experiences portfolio businesses organically, and you can see the results over the last year of those businesses, and we remain very bullish on them. In terms of the increased stakes, we did earlier in the year purchase a little bit of the outstanding stakes for Natural Habitat Adventures as well as Classic Journeys. However, over the last year, all of the founders of our Land Experiences businesses have signed extensions to continue to lead those companies into the future, and we remain very excited and enthusiastic about those partnerships.

Eric Des Lauriers: Great. That is it for my question.

Operator: Again, we have Anthony Berni with Jefferies. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Anthony Berni: Hi, good morning. Can you hear me now?

Natalya Leahy: Good morning. Yes, we can, Anthony.

Anthony Berni: Hey, sorry about that before. Thank you for taking our questions. Congrats on a great quarter. Apologies if this was asked before, but just following up on the capacity question, I think I heard charters will increase cruise capacity by mid-single digits next year. Is that correct? Are there any other factors to consider? On the land side, appreciate that you can flex your capacity up and down with demand pretty easily, but can you give us any color on how much volume you expect next year in that segment as well? Thank you.

Natalya Leahy: Well, I think, Anthony, we are going to provide the next year guidance in upcoming calls, so I'm not going to share exact numbers. But you are hearing correctly the fact that we will continue to grow our charter business in some of the most unique destinations. We expanded our Amazon offerings. We have Greg Mortimer expanding our Alaska business and growing, and we continue to develop this long-term partnership. You heard about European river cruises, et cetera. Yes, that will continue to be our moderate capacity growth lever. Yes, our Land Experiences businesses are growing both in geographies that they are offering, but also in adding additional departures or various different products within their current destinations.

Last time we talked about Off the Beaten Path launching a new Grandslam product in Alaska that sold out within days. We continue to innovate in places where we already are strong.

Anthony Berni: Perfect. Last one from me. In the past, you've called out dozens of cost innovation initiatives that you have available. Can you quantify how much you intend to save with those and which cost buckets you think should see the biggest benefits?

Natalya Leahy: Rick will answer more detailed questions. What I want to stress here, we continue to see dozens on cost innovation initiatives. What I would say, while we have seen significant results translate into margin this year, we're still in pretty early innings on that work, given some of the investments in technology we are making and capabilities. I mentioned today inventory management as one of the areas that I think we're going to really see some results coming in upcoming years, given our investments in technology and people and capabilities in that space. Rick, anything to add?

Rick Goldberg: Yeah, I'd just say that of the initiatives that we have launched here in 2026, we won't see the full benefit of those hit the P&L until 2027, just given the long lead time that many of them have. If you think about what lines on the P&L are most impacted, it's cost of tours, it's G&A, and it's CapEx.

Anthony Berni: Great. Thank you very much.

Operator: Your last question comes from the line of Stephen Grambling with Morgan Stanley. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Stephen Grambling: Hey, thank you for taking the questions. Maybe a good segue from that last question on technology is actually just thinking about the potential impact of agentic bookings. I know that you're mainly direct in terms of your business, but curious how you make sure that as more people use agents and/or LLMs in how they're researching their vacations, how you ensure that you'll be kind of in the top of the heap, or even maybe see opportunity to improve the awareness and pricing capabilities. Thank you.

Natalya Leahy: Yeah, thank you, Stephen. It's great to hear from you. We talked a little bit last time, you and I talked about that. I think we are all learning here. What I would say in terms of, yes, people use AI to get them information, and therefore, as we think about our storytelling and demand generation, what plays a bigger role than ever is areas like public relations or organic-generated opinion on things like Reddit, et cetera, where what we can do there is, one, is we are investing in our public relations and storytelling capabilities. We just welcomed a new PR leader into our organization last quarter.

We also will have to continue deliver exceptional guest experience that generate organic comments that are feeding AI agents as they're providing recommendations. So, hopefully it helps.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Rick Goldberg for closing remarks.

Rick Goldberg: Thanks so much. Really appreciate everyone taking the time to join today's call and your continued interest in Lindblad Expeditions. Thanks so much, everyone. Bye now.

#3068. Marzetti Company (MZTI) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Freight costs and a cyclospora outbreak weighed on margins despite new Bachan's sales growth.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

The Marzetti Company (MZTI -0.95%) reported a decline in fiscal first quarter earnings as a regional health outbreak and elevated logistics expenses offset gains from its recent acquisition of the Bachan's brand. Management stated that a cyclospora outbreak primarily affected results in the Great Lakes region, where the company maintains its highest market development, accounting for 30% of its overall business. Despite these headwinds, the company integrated the Bachan's business and reported market share gains in its frozen dinner roll and garlic bread categories. The company is implementing new pricing actions in its frozen segment to mitigate ongoing transportation inflation and expects financial performance to improve as the health outbreak impact moderates.

Operator: Good morning. My name is Kelly and I will be your conference call facilitator today. At this time, I would like to welcome everyone to The Marzetti Company's Fiscal Year 2027 First Quarter Conference Call. Conducting today's call will be Dave Ciesinski, President and CEO; and Tom Pigott, CFO. [Operator Instructions] And now to begin the conference call, here is Dale Ganobsik, Vice President of Corporate Finance and Investor Relations for The Marzetti Company.

Dale Ganobsik: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today for The Marzetti Company's Fiscal Year 2027 First Quarter Conference Call. Our discussion this morning may include forward-looking statements, which are subject to the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements are subject to a number of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially and the company undertakes no obligation to update these statements based upon subsequent events. A detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties is contained in the company's filings with the SEC. Also note that the audio replay of this call will be archived and available on our website, investors.marzetticompany.com later today.

For today's call, Dave Ciesinski, our President and CEO, will begin with the business update and highlights for the quarter. Tom Pigott, our CFO, will then provide an overview of the financial results. Dave will then share some comments regarding our current strategy and outlook. At the conclusion of our prepared remarks, we'll be happy to respond to any of your questions. Once again we appreciate your participation this morning. I'll now turn the call over to The Marzetti Company's President and CEO, Dave Ciesinski. Dave?

David Ciesinski: Thanks, Dale, and good morning, everyone. It's a pleasure to be here with you today as we review our first quarter results for fiscal year 2027. Our fiscal first quarter, which ended September 30, presented challenges for our business as the cyclospora outbreak and the sharp increase in freight costs adversely affected results. Consolidated net sales declined 2.4% to $481.5 million while operating income decreased $17.8 million to $41.4 million. Excluding noncore sales attributed to the TSA, adjusted net sales declined 0.3%. Cyclospora drove double-digit declines in the affected categories and the impact was concentrated in the Great Lake region where our Marzetti dressings, dips and croutons have their strongest market development.

Retail segment sales grew 2.0% to $252.7 million as $17.8 million in incremental sales from Bachan's, our newly acquired Japanese barbecue sauce brand, along with strong growth from our Texas Roadhouse dinner rolls offset the impact of cyclospora. Foodservice sales, excluding noncore TSA sales, decreased 2.6% as strength from select national chain restaurant accounts and a modest level of inflationary pricing were offset by the impact of the cyclospora outbreak. Other areas of our business continued to perform well during the first quarter and the impact of the cyclospora outbreak has moderated in recent weeks.

Circana scanner data for the quarter ending September 30 showed continued strong performance of the Bachan's brand with sales up 10.7%, total distribution points or TDPs increasing 7% and velocity up 13% as the brand continues to grow share in the barbecue sauce category. Texas Roadhouse rolls continued the strong path of growth in the frozen dinner roll category with sales up 21.3%, TDPs up 79.6% and a market share gain of 270 basis points. When combined with our Sister Schubert's brand dinner rolls, we finished the quarter with a category-leading market share of 64.2%.

Our New York Bakery brand also continued to perform well with sales up 5.1% in the quarter resulting in a market share gain of 250 basis points for a category-leading share of 46.6%. I'll now turn the call over to Tom Pigott, our CFO, for his commentary on our first quarter results. Tom?

Thomas K. Pigott: Thanks, Dave. Overall, we encountered substantial headwinds this quarter that impacted our results more significantly than was anticipated. While some portions of the business performed well, the cyclospora impact to our Retail segment and our input costs for fuel were both higher than we initially forecasted. First quarter reported net sales decreased by 2.4%. The key drivers were a decline in organic volume and product mix of 460 basis points primarily driven by the impact of the cyclospora outbreak, a pricing contribution of 80 basis points, the addition of Bachan's sales, which added 360 basis points of growth. These items were offset by the discontinuation of noncore temporary supply agreement or TSA sales that we have previously discussed.

This discontinuation unfavorably impacted revenue by 220 basis points. Excluding the TSA sales, adjusted net sales declined by 30 basis points and we estimate the cyclospora impact to have reduced revenue by approximately 300 basis points. Consolidated gross profit decreased by $8 million or 6.8% versus the prior year quarter to $110.8 million. Reported gross margin declined by 110 basis points. The gross profit decline was driven by the reduced sales volume attributed to the cyclospora outbreak and the associated impact to our production facilities, higher freight costs due to increased diesel prices and higher linehaul rates and incremental expenses related to the capacity expansion at our sauce and dressing facility in Atlanta.

Incremental sales from the Bachan's acquisition and our cost savings programs contributed to partially offset these items. Going forward, we expect a higher level of productivity contribution. Selling, general and administrative expenses increased by $10.9 million. The increase was primarily driven by the addition of Bachan's core SG&A expenses and a modest increase on the base business. We also incurred $2.4 million in noncash amortization expense for the Bachan's intangible assets. Consolidated reported operating income decreased by $17.8 million or 30.1% due to the reduced gross profit and higher SG&A expenses. Our tax rate for the quarter was 24.4% compared to 22.4% in the prior year quarter.

We estimate our tax rate for the remainder of fiscal '27 to be 23%. First quarter reported diluted earnings per share decreased $0.64 or 37.4% to $1.07. The drivers of the decline were the lower operating income, higher interest expense and a higher tax rate. Turning to the balance sheet and cash flow. The company delivered operating cash flow of $51 million. That cash was deployed into payments for property additions of $17.8 million as well as debt reduction, share repurchases and dividend payments. Our full year forecast for capital expenditures remains at $90 million. A quarterly cash dividend of $1 per share paid on September 30 represented a 5% increase from the prior year's amount.

Our enduring streak of annual dividend increases stands at 63 years. The company finished the quarter with less than $200 million of debt on the balance sheet with an effective interest rate of approximately 5%. So to wrap up my commentary, our results reflected the impact of significant headwinds we encountered during the quarter. As the impact of the cyclospora issue has largely moderated, we are focused on improving performance while continuing to invest to grow the business and returning funds to shareholders. I will now turn it back over to Dave for his closing remarks. Thank you.

David Ciesinski: Thanks, Tom. Going forward, The Marzetti Company will continue to leverage the combined strength of our team, our operating strategy and our balance sheet in support of the 3 simple pillars of our growth plan: to one, accelerate core business growth; two, to simplify our supply chain to reduce our cost and grow our margins; and three, to expand our core with focused M&A and strategic licensing. As we look ahead to our second quarter and the remainder of fiscal year 2027, in addition to the incremental sales attributed to Bachan's, we expect Retail sales will benefit from new items that we've recently launched or have planned for introduction later this year.

In the Foodservice segment, we expect sales to remain supported by select quick service restaurant customers in our mix of national chain restaurant accounts. We continue to anticipate a moderate level of commodity cost inflation along with significantly higher freight cost, which we expect to substantially mitigate through inflationary pricing and our cost savings programs as we remain focused on margin improvement. On the sales front, I have some exciting news to share regarding our largest Foodservice customer and trusted partner, Chick-fil-A. Beginning November 16, Chick-fil-A is introducing a new spicy version of their popular Chick-fil-A sauce produced and supplied by Marzetti.

The new sauce will be available in their restaurants nationwide and is planned to be a permanent addition to their sauce offerings. The sauce combines the iconic Chick-fil-A sauce with mustard notes and a smoky tang balanced with subtle sweetness and infused with spicy peppers. We greatly value our long-standing relationship with Chick-fil-A, which dates back to 1983, and we look forward to further strengthening our partnership and supporting their continued growth through this important initiative. Before I finish up, I also want to take a moment to welcome Mark Christenson as the new President of our Retail business. I'm very excited to be adding Mark to our executive leadership team.

Mark is a proven brand builder with a track record of creating sustainable growth in highly competitive categories. His background includes more than 20 years of relevant leadership experience, most recently serving as Chief Revenue Officer of Wingstop where he led brand strategy and customer-facing commercial activity for the company's U.S. business. Prior to Wingstop, he spent 20 years at Procter & Gamble in roles including Senior Vice President of Global Feminine Care, Vice President of North American Baby Care and Vice President of Global Fabric Care. I'm confident Mark's experience and leadership will help us accelerate organic growth in Retail, strengthen our brands and innovation pipeline and deepen our customer partnerships.

In closing, I extend my sincere thanks to the entire Marzetti Company team for all their hard work this past quarter and their ongoing commitment to grow our business. This concludes our prepared remarks for today and we'd be happy to answer any questions you may have.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Alton Stump of Loop Capital.

Alton Stump: Dave, I just wanted to kind of touch on what I thought was interesting comments about the outbreak was having a bigger impact because you guys have a very strong presence in the Great Lakes region. So given that as you kind of see things get back to normal hopefully in coming quarters, should we see sort of an outsized recovery for you guys because of that regional presence that you have that was obviously impacted most heavily by the outbreak?

David Ciesinski: Yes. Alton, I think it's an important question. I appreciate you asking it. If you look at sort of market development by brand throughout the various regions and you look at the Great Lakes, it represents 30% of our overall business versus all of the other regions. So it's a very high concentration. It's 3x most of our other competitors there. And as you pointed out, those were the areas that were most significantly impacted. So if you went to sort of the center of when this thing was and part of the impact, it was sort of early August and that impact ran until the very end of August. So case in point here, if you look at croutons.

Croutons as of that first week in August were actually down 30%, believe it or not. By the end of August, they had recovered 18%. If you look at shelf-stable salad dressing, it was down 17% for the entire month of August. And then if you look at produce dressing, which is I think again an area where we're very developed, it was down 23% as a category for the first week of August and it remained down 20% as of the last week of August. So bringing it around, when it does recover, we would expect to see an outside benefit. Now as for the recovery, what we're seeing is that it's trailing.

The category, as you remember, was a little bit soft going into this. So we're still seeing a modest decline there, but it's substantially recovered over where it had been before. And what I would also add is as we were in the throes of the situation, we and other peers elected to turn off our marketing because it really didn't make any sense to be spending consumer advertising while the category was going through this. We do have that advertising expected to come back online in the back half. We're going to do it around January 1, which is the historic beginning of salad season and new Year's resolutions around eating healthier and attacking light food.

Alton Stump: Got it. That's some great color. And then I guess just one other one and then I'll hop back in the queue. Obviously we are several months now into your Bachan's acquisition. Clearly based on sell-through data, it's off to a very good start. I'm curious kind of if you have had any sort of material learnings now that you've owned the business for several months as far as maybe upside potential that maybe was even better than what you had thought heading into the deal.

David Ciesinski: Yes. I would say, look, the brand and the team have met and exceeded all of our expectations and maybe I'll start by talking a little bit about the brand. As you heard in the comments, we're continuing to achieve double-digit growth. We're continuing to expand TDPs. And one of the metrics that I'm particularly excited about is that we're actually growing our velocity faster than we're growing the sales overall. So it isn't just by virtue of new distribution that we're achieving growth, but really it's the underlying velocity or sales per TDP of the existing items, which is driving the product. So I would say on core item, we continue to be very excited.

We're driving awareness and trial in households and it's manifesting in the velocity. Now if you look at sort of the other pillars of the overall growth plan. The team has done a fabulous job developing mayo and selling it in and so far, the sell-in has gone very well. It's already available in the natural channel at Whole Foods where they were a lead customer and you could expect to see it in the remainder of retail as we go into the next calendar year. And then they have other items in their pipeline as well. And so the team continues to do a great job. What's the learning?

I think probably the biggest one, Alton, is that Bachan's on the label says Japanese barbecue sauce, but nearly 3/4 of the occasions actually are everyday meals where consumers are looking for fresh, flavorful, quick meal solutions and Bachan's really plays well there. And I think that learning for both us and Marzetti and the team at Bachan's is informing how we think about marketing communications to drive that versatility message. I think that's going to be important in the future of the business. Maybe one other quick passing comment is the business is actually growing faster in Canada than it is in the United States right now. So that's been a nice surprise on the upside.

Operator: Our next question comes from Jim Salera of Stephens.

James Salera: Tom, I wanted to start on the gross margin side. If I kind of piece everything together, it seems like the primary variance in 1Q was the freight cost and kind of the incremental transport cost. So can you just maybe break that apart and give us a sense for how we should think about freight costs for the remainder of the year? And please correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe in the 4Q call, you guys talked about kind of 100 basis points give or take of gross margin expansion through the year. Are we still thinking about something in that range or maybe a little bit less given where 1Q came in?

Just some puts and takes on gross margin would be great.

Thomas K. Pigott: Sure. So you're right, the higher freight costs significantly impacted our first quarter margins. We calculated an impact of about 120 basis point headwind from that. In addition, the higher cyclospora impact on revenue impacted our ability to drive cost savings as well as the mix was unfavorable. That was an additional 40 basis point headwind for the quarter. Now as you go forward, the freight headwind remains through Q2. So as we look at our Q2 outlook, we anticipate being able to get to flat margins, but not grow margins in the second quarter.

But as you look at the second half, we expect to be fully back on algorithm and to be able to drive some nice margin growth. So the full year outlook we've adjusted down to be growing between 25 basis points and 75 basis points really driven by growth in the second half. Now what I would say is that our forecast is based on the market outlook for diesel fuels, which does anticipate some moderation in the second half. So it's something that we're going to continue to monitor and continue to work to offset.

James Salera: Great. And then shifting gears and just talking about innovation, exciting to hear the new opportunity at Chick-fil-A. You guys also had a press release out yesterday announcing new collaboration. Can you just give us a sense for how much incrementality innovation outside of Bachan's should contribute this year and just maybe the sequencing of when those things start to [ emulate ] kind of an initial ramp for Chick-fil-A, but just how quickly we should see the uptake in market and sort of quantify some benefits?

David Ciesinski: Maybe I'll hit them in the order of which you covered them, Jim, and I'll begin first with Chick-fil-A sauce. So as was discussed in the script, we're thrilled. It goes in market on November 12. They're going to be starting their advertising before too long to drive it and we're super excited about it. It's a major initiative for them that's been in the works for quite a long time and we look forward to supporting with them and participating in the growth. As you might imagine, it's going to be a contributor to Q2 for Foodservice and a contributor for Q3 as well.

And as the item becomes a permanent part of their sauce portfolio, I think we're going to remain I think optimistic about what the overall impact is going to be. And I'm going to switch to Retail, if I may. Swinging around to that portfolio, the current plan is to launch that product in Retail in the spring launch window of next February. So it's not going to come out right now on the heels of the restaurant launch. They want to use the restaurants as a means by which to shoot the advertising and drive it as an LTO, but we have plans in place already to bring it into Retail, but it's going to be launching next year.

As far as the current pipeline of activity that we have this year, I would characterize it as building. Our bakery items are already out in the marketplace with New York Texas Toast behind the focaccia bread and loaf. They're both doing very well. We launched a new SKU of Texas Roadhouse that's driving TDP growth and I think you saw consumption was up about 20% in the period. As we move around to sauces where we've spent a lot of energy recently, what you're going to begin to see is a host of new items, the first of which we mentioned in the press release, which is a really exciting partnership with Tajin.

You can consider this sort of licensing 2.0, where we believe we found a very, very consumer-relevant brand platform that connects with both younger consumers and consumers out West. It's growing very rapidly in a range of different areas and it naturally lends itself to things like ranch dressing. So we have several items that we have planned to come out into the marketplace this year in February with that, we're selling those in right now. And then we also have a range of activity in flight with our own Marzetti brand where we're looking to bring new items into the refrigerated section.

The intention is not for these to be salad dressings per se, but really for them to be more versatile sauces that you can use to dip, drizzle or to dress. Those products are also in the process of being sold into the market. So you can expect to see those February-ish and as retailers begin to prepare to reset their shelves.

Operator: Our next question comes from Scott Marks of Jefferies.

Scott Marks: First thing I wanted to ask about is if we look at underlying organic growth trends, right, if we strip out the impact from cyclospora, it looks like organic volumes were still down across both Retail and Foodservice. So wondering if you can just help us understand a little bit what are the main drivers behind that and how should we think about those factors contributing or helping going forward?

David Ciesinski: Yes. It's an important question. If you pull them out, Scott, like you indicated if you adjust for cyclospora, what you're looking at on the base business continues to be a low single-digit decline. And what I would point to is a couple of things. One, despite or in spite of cyclospora, really it's the dressings category is probably the softest piece. Other than that, we feel like our categories are generally healthy. We're continuing to drive growth in our bread business and really all eyes and focus are on continuing to build on our strength in sauces and really fix and then grow what we have going on in the dressings space.

And it may be an opportunity now to talk about some of what we have going on. You read recently that we appointed a new leader of our Retail business. David Ciesinski: So maybe I'll start with the first because it's a really important point. The first one went into effect right on the heels of the beginning of June. The next one went at the end of June. They all since flowed through and that includes all customers.

And those conversations, as you might expect were -- they were full conversations, but we were resolute that we could see clear line of sight to how the commodities were flowing right through to our products. Even though when you look at the segment makeup of the 2 businesses, you can see that the margin -- maybe I'll step back. Our Foodservice business is largely a customer pickup business on outbound.

Having said that, when we're looking at diesel running in the $6 range across the United States and $8 in Canada, what's happening now is we're seeing that diesel not just in outbound, but we're seeing it inbound on all of the ingredients and all of the packaging that's coming to our plants. Todd Brooks: Okay. Great. Very helpful. And then I want to talk on the frozen bread side of the house. Any early reads on the performance of the new York Bakery items? Matthew Curtis: Okay. Great. And then one more on Bachan's. I think you've previously talked about more than $100 million in revenue from that brand this year. I assume that's still achievable. Matthew Curtis: Sure. No problem. I think for Bachan's, you mentioned about $100 million in revenue that you're expecting this year with some $18 million in the first quarter, I was just wondering if you're expecting a fairly steady ramp-up in that figure as we go forward?

#3066. Douglas Dynamics (PLOW) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management flagged uneven commercial demand and a tougher fourth quarter ahead.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Douglas Dynamics, Inc. (PLOW -8.05%) reported its highest nine-month adjusted earnings in company history, reaching record performance levels for both the third quarter and year-to-date periods. Management attributed these results to robust preseason demand for snow and ice control equipment following an above-average snowfall winter and the successful integration of the Venco Venturo acquisition. The company raised its full-year 2026 guidance across all key financial metrics, citing visibility into the fourth quarter and strong municipal demand. Operations remain focused on expanding capacity through new facilities in Missouri, Iowa, and Ohio to capitalize on growth opportunities while maintaining disciplined cost management in commercial markets where demand remains uneven.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Douglas Dynamics Third Quarter of 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the call over to Nathan Elwell, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Nathan Elwell: Thank you. Welcome, everyone, and thank you for joining us on today's call. Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the comments that will be made during this conference call, including answers to your questions, will constitute forward-looking statements. These forward-looking statements are subject to risks that could cause actual results to be materially different. Those risks include, among others, matters that we have described in today's press release and in our filings with the SEC. Please note the quarterly fact sheet can be found on our IR website. Joining me on the call today is Mark Van Genderen, President and CEO; and Sarah Lauber, Executive Vice President and CFO.

Mark will provide an overview of our performance, followed by Sarah reviewing our financial results and guidance. After that, we'll open the call for questions. That said, I'll hand the call over to Mark. Please go ahead.

Mark Van Genderen: Yes. Thanks, Nathan, and welcome, everyone. What can we say? So far, 2026 has been a great year for the company. This quarter also includes the contributions of Venco Venturo, which we acquired last November. One number I will point out is the almost 24% adjusted EBITDA margin we produced year-to-date in the Attachment segment, which stems from higher demand, throughput and strong product mix.

Now this is just one data point, but it clearly shows that when we see the demand, our team steps up, executes our plans and our margins follow, putting us right in the wheelhouse this quarter of the mid-20s margin we have been targeting for the Attachments segment. Now we aren't expecting these results every quarter going forward, but it's a great sign of the progress we've been making. Our teams did an excellent job delivering the second half of our preseason orders. Based on the ordering patterns we've observed and our most recent dealer checks, it is clear that dealer inventories earlier this year were substantially lower than where they have been in recent years.

The orders we've seen this year have likely helped to replenish dealers' stock of snow and ice control equipment. Even so, our plans include building more finished goods inventory compared to last year so that we have enough product available and ready to ship when the winter weather arrives. When it comes specifically to parts and accessories, the results are even more outstanding. As we explained last quarter, after achieving record P&A sales and shipments in 2025, we've already surpassed that level in the third quarter this year, significantly exceeding our expectations.

They've responded with a tremendous effort to increase production and ship the equipment, parts and accessories as quickly and efficiently as possible. During the years when constrained chassis availability limited our throughput and efficiency, our municipal teams invested significant effort in continuous improvement initiatives, operational efficiencies and process enhancements that are paying dividends today as volumes increase.

DDMS, or the Douglas Dynamics Management System is the foundation for the innate drive to get better every day. While our continuous improvement efforts may not have been front and center recently as we focus on our strategic initiatives, make no mistake about it, DDMS projects and the philosophy in general remain a crucial part of Douglas Dynamics. So, collectively, these highly cost-effective investments strengthen our capabilities and position us to capitalize on the growth opportunities we see across our markets. In response, we have better aligned our cost structure with current conditions, preserving profitability wherever possible while maintaining the flexibility to capitalize on opportunities. And although fleet demand remains relatively subdued, we are beginning to see an increase in smaller orders, which bodes well for next year.

Taken together, the strength of our municipal operations and the resilience of our commercial business position us to deliver another year of solid performance that remains near the record levels we have achieved in recent years. And over the past year, we've seen growing recognition across the industry and potential partners of what we are seeking to accomplish through our Activate strategic pillar. As a result, we've engaged in a broader range of compelling conversations. And that said, while activity levels have increased, our approach to M&A remains disciplined. We will continue to be highly selective and focused on opportunities that are strategically aligned and capable of creating long-term value.

And we're just getting started. We're building on the momentum with a compelling strategy for future growth, and we are confident in both the course we are charting and our ability to execute it in the years to come. And there is a lot we aim to accomplish. With that, I'd like to pass the call to Sarah.

The stronger-than-average snowfall we experienced last winter has been an important underlying factor contributing to our record 2026 performance.

Assuming snowfall patterns return to historical averages this winter, our early view suggests that under the right operating conditions, we are positioned to replicate our anticipated 2026 performance again in 2027. In closing, we executed effectively and are very pleased with our exceptional year-to-date results. We feel well prepared, and we will be monitoring reorder patterns closely as winter weather approaches. With that, we'd like to open the call for questions. Operator?

#3065. One Possession: Marcus Smart does Marcus Smart things against Celtics

One Possession: Marcus Smart does Marcus Smart things against Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Boston

Two 3s. Two steals. Two flops. Two middle fingers.

The Celtics got the full Marcus Smart experience on Monday night in Houston and — if we're being honest — it made us a bit nostalgic.

Sure, it was a lot more fun when the uniforms were flipped back in December 2017. That night, Smart busted out his entire bag of Smart tricks, including baiting James Harden into a pair of offensive foul calls as the Celtics improbably rallied to take down the Rockets at TD Garden.

Being on the other side of Smart's chaos-inducing playbook is decidedly less endearing.

Smart left his fingerprints all over Houston's late-game takeover. It started in the final minutes of the third quarter when Smart sold a shove from former teammate Jayson Tatum, earning Tatum his fourth foul and sending him to the bench with 1:39 to play in the frame.

The Celtics were down just five at that point, but Boston trailed by 16 by the time Tatum returned to the floor with 7:02 to play in the final quarter.

Smart hit 3-pointers on consecutive trips early in the fourth frame to help build that lead. Then, somewhat inexplicably, he threw his middle fingers in the air running back up the court. He would later suggest to reporters in Houston that it was "pent-up" emotions and some feedback to a Boston bench that had been previously vocal about his shot selection.

Before that, he 1) Tried to encourage referees to give Jayson Tatum a first-half technical as he vented about a whistle, 2) Nearly drew a Payton Pritchard charge before the play was overturned on video review, and 3) Did one of his familiar kip-ups to celebrate after nearly drawing that charge on Pritchard.

That's serious nostalgia for everyone who watched Smart in his nine seasons with Boston from 2014 to 2023. You might not always miss his shot selection, but no amount of analytics could quantify the Smart chaos quotient.

Every good team needs an agitator. The type of player that gets under your skin and never lets you get too comfortable. After tough stops in Memphis, Washington, and even with the Los Angeles Lakers, it's gotta be refreshing for Smart to be back in a situation where he can aid winning with his antics.

This was only the third game Smart had played against Boston, and the other two were otherwise forgettable, with Smart tallying three points in 41 minutes during games with Memphis and Los Angeles.

But the Celtics got a reminder of Smart and his penchant for winning plays on Monday night. To quote the great modern philosopher Ric Flair, "You don't have to like me, but you'll never forget me."

Record sales, thin margins, and a cash problem that's growing with the business.

Watch whether operating cash flow turns positive as these receivables come due. Also check that the final quarterly filing matches, since the release calls these figures preliminary and unaudited.

#3060. Why are there no NBA games today? League promotes the midterm vote

In a push to get more people out to the ballot box, for the fourth time in five years, the entire NBA will go dark.

The league did not schedule any games Tuesday, Nov. 3, the day of the fiercely contested 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Because the first slate of polls close on the East Coast at 6 p.m. ET, with many more at 7 p.m. ET, holding games would severely interfere with the ability for people who choose to vote in person to do so.

It's one of the three days that the NBA typically avoids scheduling games, joining Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve.

The NBA has also published a website with several resources for fans interested in voting to learn more about their polling sites, ballots, and the league even has a link to check voter registration status.

Although the entire league is off Tuesday, each team played Monday, Nov. 2. And at each of those 15 games, players wore T-shirts that said "VOTE" across the chest.

"No games have been scheduled for Election Day (Tuesday, Nov. 3) as the league will encourage fans and the broader NBA community to make a plan to vote and to participate in the civic process," the NBA said in August when it issued its official release announcing the schedule.

Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr spoke on the importance of voting before their game against the Phoenix Suns on Monday, Nov. 2.

"I hope everybody votes," Kerr said. "I voted today, dropped my ballot off in a ballot box near my house, and, you know, I always encourage everybody to get out there and vote. And sometimes there's a tendency to stay away in the midterms and only vote in the presidential elections, but there's a lot of really important issues here in California.

"I hope everybody gets out there and cast their ballot.  That's what democracy's about."

The NBA first began the initiative of not scheduling games on Election Day in Nov. 2022. At the time, the league also encouraged its teams to promote voting initiatives. The NBA also declined to schedule games on Election Day 2023 and 2024.

And since Tuesday will be an off night, the league will return to action in full force Wednesday, Nov. 4, with a slate packed with 14 games.

Navitas is shifting toward power chips for AI data centers and has just bought another business to support that move. Its fourth-quarter outlook shows what that costs.

Navitas Semiconductor (NVTS +7.95%) grew third-quarter revenue 38% to $14.0 million, its first year-over-year gain since 2024. Shares rose about 5% in after-hours trading. The growth is real. Fourth-quarter guidance, though, has costs rising much faster than revenue, so losses should widen before they narrow.

Fourth-quarter guidance puts non-GAAP operating expenses about 50% above this quarter, and the release says that includes the newly acquired Claros business. An acquisition adds its costs on day one, while its revenue usually takes longer to arrive. Revenue is guided up much less, so the non-GAAP operating loss should grow at the midpoint.

The jump in GAAP gross margin is mostly an accounting effect. Some acquired technology finished amortizing, which cut a charge that sits in cost of revenue. On a non-GAAP basis, gross margin barely moved, at 40%.

Cash more than doubled since year-end, but the release has no cash flow statement, so it does not show where the money came from. Weighted shares outstanding are up 23% from a year ago.

Watch whether fourth-quarter revenue lands in the guided range while non-GAAP operating expenses stay near $25 million. The release also gives no current AI infrastructure revenue figure, so check whether that share is on track for the 40% target.

#3057. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3054. Celtics’ shooting woes got the best of them — as did Marcus Smart

The Boston Celtics already had their hands full on Monday night. No Paul George. No reprieve on the second night of a back-to-back on the road. Then came Marcus Smart.

Former beloved friend of the program, Smart embraced his new Houston Rockets uniform. Like a gray wolf circling wounded prey, he watched his former team struggle through a miserable 38.6 percent shooting performance before sinking his teeth in at every opportunity. Whenever the Celtics tried to put out the fire, Smart poured kerosene on it, leading Houston to a 109-93 victory and bringing Boston's Eastern Conference-best five-game winning streak to an end.

"He woke up everybody's ass," Rockets teammate Alperen Şengün told Ryan Hollins postgame.

It didn't take long for Smart to make his presence felt.

HOUSTON, TX – NOVEMBER 2: Marcus Smart #36 of the Houston Rockets shoots a three point basket during the game against the Boston Celtics on November 2, 2026 at the Toyota Center in Houston, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Logan Riely/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

After noticing Jayson Tatum expressing his frustration with referee Matt Kallio with 3:11 left until halftime, Smart immediately fled Houston's bench and instigated, urging the official to issue Tatum a technical foul. He was all laughs, while Tatum — considerably less amused by the antics — remained visibly frustrated as he stared Smart down for a brief second and walked back to Boston's bench.

Smart was still all smiles, as he put his arm around Mike Conley and began plotting his scheme.

In the third quarter, Smart got Tatum again. He drew a charge on Tatum, handing him his fourth personal foul. Seconds later, Tatum was whistled for a second straight offensive foul, bringing his total to five and forcing Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla to remove him with 1:39 remaining in the frame. Tatum, visibly frustrated once again, made another unhappy trip to Boston's sideline.

Payton Pritchard also fell for Smart's bait, earning a third-quarter offensive foul himself. Smart did his signature Shawn Michaels-inspired kip-up to get back on his feet.

By then, it was official. Smart's plan was in full effect.

Much like the menace who wore No. 36 for nine seasons in Boston, Smart reminded the Celtics why it's great to play alongside him and a pain in the ass to compete against him. He went scoreless in the first half and missed his first seven shots before finally making Boston pay.

Rockets head coach Ime Udoka kept Smart on the floor to begin the fourth quarter, and the 13th-year veteran rewarded that decision with two timely shots.

Smart drained back-to-back 3-pointers, extending Houston's lead to 90-79 with over eight minutes remaining. He raised both middle fingers in celebration, later claiming the gesture was directed at a select few seated on Boston's bench.

"Just a lot of pent-up, I guess you can call it emotions," Smart told reporters. "Plus, certain guys on the (Boston) bench was talking. Didn't know who. I just heard them say something, so I let them hear it back."

Smart finished with eight points, four rebounds, four assists, and two steals in over 19 minutes.

"You always wanna do good against your former team," Smart added, "and show them that you still can go out there and do what you do, right? So it definitely felt good. Energy was there. They know what I can do, and I reminded them again tonight."

The energy Tatum once benefited from having alongside him had finally come back to haunt him. Smart's swagger was contagious, and everyone in Houston fed off it.

The Rockets shot 40 percent from three and 54.4 percent overall, having their way with Boston.

Meanwhile, the Celtics couldn't get anything to go.

Boston's top outside-shooting threats — Pritchard, Derrick White, Sam Hauser, and Baylor Scheierman — combined to go 4-for-21 from beyond the arc. Luka Garza, coming off the bench to play over 17 minutes, was the Celtics' leader in 3-point makes (four), although that contribution was largely overshadowed by the rest of the team's shooting woes.

They were a hair better from three (29 percent) than they were 24 hours earlier (27 percent) against the Orlando Magic on Sunday night.

Tatum went 1-for-7 from distance and 5-for-16 overall, finishing the night with 19 points and a season-high five turnovers in Houston.

It's difficult enough to play two games in two nights, especially on the road, but Tatum believes the Celtics didn't do themselves many favors either throughout the game.

"Everybody plays back-to-backs," Tatum told reporters, per NBC Sports Boston. "We're not the only team that's gotta travel and play a back-to-back. Are they tough? Yeah. But a lot of us been doing this for a long time. There were moments where we cut it to six or seven (points) and couldn't get a rebound, and they hit a three. It's moments like that where we gotta dig deeper a little bit."

It's been three years since the Celtics traded Smart, originally sending him to the Memphis Grizzlies. In the years since, the 32-year-old has struggled to make his former team pay, whether because of his on-court performance or availability. But Monday night in Houston, Smart finally got his get-back, and Boston felt it.
