#3034. Is Palantir Stock a Buy After its Latest Earnings Report?

Revenue nearly doubled, but a slowdown in contract growth has investors on edge.

I've liked Palantir Technologies (PLTR -1.65%) stock for a long time and even predicted earlier this year that it would reach $220 before the end of 2026.

Unfortunately, after the company's third-quarter earnings report, it appears that prediction won't come true. But I'm still holding my shares.

Despite another quarter of outstanding revenue growth, Palantir shares fell more than 5% following the company's Q3 report and are now 16% below their all-time high. Investors appeared concerned about a slowdown in the company's total contract value (TCV), which increased just 6% year over year after jumping 49% in the second quarter.

Does that mean Palantir's remarkable growth story is starting to lose steam? Not necessarily.

Palantir's third-quarter revenue was $2.31 billion, up 96% from a year earlier. U.S. commercial revenue grew 148% to $984 million, while U.S. government revenue increased 96% to $953 million. For the first time, Palantir generated more revenue from its U.S. commercial customers than from its U.S. government business.

I've long argued that Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) is revolutionary because it helps companies put AI to work in their actual operations. Rather than simply generating text or answering questions, AIP allows businesses to connect AI models with their existing data and use them to make decisions and improve efficiency.

And the results suggest that businesses are increasingly willing to pay for those capabilities. Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count increased 29% year over year to 686, while the company closed 212 deals worth at least $1 million during the quarter.

The company also raised its full-year revenue guidance to between $8.53 billion and $8.534 billion, representing approximately 91% growth.

Those aren't the numbers of a company whose business is losing momentum.

There's a legitimate reason investors are paying attention to Palantir's contract numbers. Total contract value measures the potential value of contracts signed during a period, including certain contract options. It's an important indicator of future business, although not all of that value represents guaranteed revenue.

Palantir's third-quarter TCV reached $2.92 billion, increasing just 6% year over year. That was a sharp slowdown from the 49% growth reported in the second quarter.

CFO Dave Glazer explained on the company's earnings call that Palantir signed several large contracts that were shorter than usual as customers began adopting its new Sovereign AI capabilities. The company expects those agreements to grow in size and duration as customers expand their use of the technology.

That makes sense, but it's still something investors should watch. Shorter contracts can reduce reported TCV even when customers are spending more on Palantir's software.

Meanwhile, Palantir's total remaining deal value increased 55% year over year to $13.4 billion, suggesting its existing business continues to expand.

Still, Palantir's premium valuation leaves little room for disappointment. The stock has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 108 times and a forward price-to-sales multiple of 51 times. If contract growth remains sluggish, investors may begin questioning whether the company's extraordinary revenue growth can continue.

I've been bullish on Palantir for years, and its transition toward a larger commercial business is one of the biggest reasons.

Government contracts provide an important foundation, particularly as Palantir expands its work with the Pentagon through programs such as Maven. But the commercial market offers opportunities across industries, from manufacturing and healthcare to financial services. AIP gives Palantir a compelling way to pursue those opportunities.

My $220 price prediction for 2026 will probably miss the mark. I'm not thrilled about it, but I can accept it. But Palantir remains one of my cornerstone holdings because I believe the long-term opportunity is much larger than any single year's stock-price target.

A disappointing quarter for contract growth deserves attention. It doesn't erase the company's progress in turning AI into a practical business tool -- or my conviction in Palantir's long-term prospects.

#3033. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

#3032. Wizards defense cracks down on Magic in stifling third quarter

The Wizards entered last night's game at the Orlando Magic ranked 10th in defensive rating (points allowed per 100 possessions). They then put the Magic into a figurative chokehold — limiting Orlando to 28.2% three-point shooting, 94 points in the game, and just nine points in a stifling third quarter.

It's the second consecutive game that the Wizards opponent scored less than 100 points. Washington managed that feat just three times all of last season. And the Wizards did it without Alex Sarr (out with a sore knee) and Justin Champagnie (broken foot).

Kyshawn George played a strong all-around game in the Washington Wizards win over the Orlando Magic. | Getty Images

The Wizards' record is now 4-3. The last time they had a winning record this deep in the season was 2021-22.

Comparisons with last season are for illustrative purpose only, by the way. Washington was trying to lose last year. This is a different squad with a different purpose, and it shows. And it's fun to watch.

Against the Magic, Kyshawn George was excellent on both end all night. He took good shots except when the only shots were tough ones — and he shot well. He defended, rebounded, set up teammates while avoiding turnovers and fouls. He finished with 22 points, 4 rebounds, 5 assists, a steal, a block and a turnover. That's a helluva good game.

Anthony Davis dominated inside, scoring 27 points and grabbing 9 rebounds and 3 steals. He did get a bit sloppy at times, which showed in his five turnovers. Still, another strong game from the team's best player.

In what might well be a sign, I thought AJ Dybantsa had a relatively rough outing. A few times in the second half, he had some trouble finishing through contact and managing against Orlando's physicality. He shot just 7-17 from the floor. And yet, he finished with 21 points, 5 rebounds, 2 assists, and 3 steals. His PPA was 148, and the team was +10 in his minutes. Reminder: this is a 19-year-old rookie.

Bilal Coulibaly was disruptive on defense. Bub Carrington gave the team 19 productive minutes. Trae Young was kinda meh for him, and he still generated 9 assists and grifted free throws.

So why am I still at "want to believe" status? One big reason is the likelihood that they're benefitting from opponent shooting luck. One of the lessons of statistical analysis is that defenses don't have much effect on opponent three-point shooting. The fact that Washington's opponents are shooting below 30% on threes is great. But over a small sample, it's probably just luck. When opponent shooting regresses to the mean, so will Washington's defense.

I say "probably" because they're doing a lot right on that end. Their effort is NBA level, which is something the franchise hasn't had in a few years. They swarm, they pressure, they scrap, they chase and deflect and challenge shots. I see that and appreciate it while the analyst part of my brain keeps saying, "Tap the brakes. It's not that hard to look good when opponents are shooting 28% from three-point range."

The Magic targeted Young and had success, even on a bad offensive night. Young's defensive effort is as good as it's ever been across his entire career. My sense from watching him this season is that his (relative) defensive strength is as a help defender or jumping passing lanes. His point-of-attack defense is weak and will be a target as the Wizards play more meaningful games.

I'm not sold on Dybantsa's three-point shooting stroke. There's something about his arms and the location of the ball as he's shooting that's not sitting right with me. It's something like the ball spending too much time at eye level and a flat trajectory.

The Wizards are huge and have a couple of elite athletes — Dybantsa and Coulibaly.

Despite being tall, mobile, and athletic, Deandre Ayton has very little presence as a rim protector. In the second quarter, I jotted a note that Orlando guard Jase Richardson had found his ideal victims — Young at the point of attack and Ayton in the paint.

Once again, Washington's first offensive play was for Dybantsa. They set screens for him, and got him the ball on the move, which helped him drive to the room. He missed through contact that probably should have been called a foul.

Once again, Young's ability to threaten defenses with his passing set himself up for an open layup.

Head coach Brian Keefe used essentially a nine-man rotation. Sarr and Champagnie were out with injuries, but Khris Middleton got a DNP-CD, and Will Riley played just four minutes.

Below are the four factors that decide wins and losses in basketball — shooting (efg), rebounding (offensive rebounds), ball handling (turnovers), fouling (free throws made).

eFG% (effective field goal percentage, which accounts for the three-point shot)

TOV% (turnover percentage — turnovers divided by possessions)

FTM/FGA (free throws made divided by field goal attempts)

PPA is my overall production metric, which credits players for things they do that help a team win (scoring, rebounding, playmaking, defending) and dings them for things that hurt (missed shots, turnovers, bad defense, fouls).

PPA is a per possession metric designed for larger data sets. In small sample sizes, the numbers can get weird. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better and replacement level is 45. For a single game, replacement level isn't much use, and I reiterate the caution about small samples sometimes producing weird results.

POSS is the number of possessions each player was on the floor in this game.

ORTG = offensive rating, which is points produced per individual possessions x 100. League average so far this season is listed in the Four Factors table above. Points produced is not the same as points scored. It includes the value of assists and offensive rebounds, as well as sharing credit when receiving an assist.

USG = offensive usage rate. Average is 20%. Median last season was 17.7%.

ORTG and USG are versions of stats created by former Wizards assistant coach Dean Oliver and modified by me. ORTG is an efficiency measure that accounts for the value of shooting, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. USG includes shooting from the floor and free throw line, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers.

+PTS = "Plus Points" is a measure of the points gained or lost by each player based on their efficiency in this game compared to league average efficiency on the same number of possessions. A player with an offensive rating (points produced per possession x 100) of 100 who uses 20 possessions would produce 20 points. If the league average efficiency is 115, the league — on average — would produced 23.0 points in the same 20 possessions. So, the player in this hypothetical would have a +PTS score of -3.0.

Players are sorted by total production in the game.

#3029. Should You Buy Qualcomm Stock Before Its Nov. 4 Report?

Is the chipmaker's 11% one-day drop a chance to buy ahead of earnings?

Qualcomm (QCOM +1.45%) shares slid 11% on Oct. 30 to close at $164.79. The company didn't release any news of its own that day. Instead, it was caught in a broad chip sell-off after Intel forecast less revenue in the fourth quarter than in the third and warned the PC slowdown might last until at least mid-2027.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index lost about 7% in the same session.

Shares sit near $167 as I write, about a third under the $251.02 record close they set on May 29. That peak came after the stock more than doubled from its early-April low, so shares have swung a lot in a short time.

Now Qualcomm releases fiscal fourth-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, Nov. 4. Is the stock worth buying before the report? I'd say the September quarter matters less than what management says about the December quarter.

Qualcomm's handset business has been slipping all year. Handset chip revenue was still up 3% year over year in the three months ending Dec. 28, 2025, Qualcomm's fiscal first quarter of 2026. Then it dropped 13% in the March quarter and 20% in the June quarter, to $5.1 billion.

Memory is the biggest issue. Qualcomm's latest quarterly filing says it expects tight memory supply, and the price hikes that went with it, to hit demand from several phone makers.

Apple (AAPL -1.90%) is the other drag. Qualcomm now expects its share of new iPhone launches to come in well below its earlier 20% estimate, a gap management linked partly to its own supply constraints. And it forecast Apple revenue dropping around 50% from the September quarter to the December quarter.

PCs are a smaller part, but Intel's warning still matters. Qualcomm's PC chips are in its internet of things (IoT) category, where revenue rose 9% year over year in the June quarter. A softer PC market might slow one of the chipmaker's growing businesses.

In all, Qualcomm guided for $9.7 billion to $10.5 billion in fiscal fourth-quarter revenue and $2.05 to $2.25 in non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share. At the midpoints, that's around 10% and 28% under the year-ago quarter.

The more interesting piece of Wednesday's report will probably be the outlook. Qualcomm has custom chip deals with two very big cloud computing companies.

Revenue from both should begin in the December quarter, according to chief financial officer Akash Palkhiwala. "As you know, the December quarter is right there. And so we do have POs from these engagements, and so we've already started wafers," he said on the July earnings call, referring to purchase orders.

Management targets over $15 billion in data center revenue by fiscal 2029. Of course, that's a target.

But the auto business shows what a ramp can look like. Automotive sales hit $1.6 billion in the June quarter, a record and 61% higher than a year before. This growth rate climbed from 38% in the March quarter and 15% in the December quarter.

Profitability is the trade-off. Qualcomm's chip segment had a pre-tax margin of 31% in the December quarter. That slipped to 27% in the March quarter and 26% in the June quarter, 4 percentage points lower than a year earlier, because higher wafer and memory costs came before Qualcomm's price hikes could catch up.

Wednesday's guidance for the December quarter should show if Android growth and the first sales from the two custom chip deals can make up for the Apple drop. That figure might matter more to the stock than anything Qualcomm earned from July through September.

At around 17 times expected fiscal 2027 earnings, Qualcomm trades a little under the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio of about 19. That multiple arguably doesn't assume much data center success. If anything, the market seems to be pricing Qualcomm more like a phone-chip maker that's losing Apple's business.

Even so, the two data center deals haven't shown up in reported revenue yet. Purchase orders and wafer starts are promising, but I'd rather judge the business by the December quarter's actual sales from those deals, which Qualcomm won't report until early 2027.

I'm in no rush to buy before Wednesday. If the stock gets cheaper as I wait for those sales numbers, I'm OK with it.

#3028. Suns’ fourth-quarter mistakes overshadow promising first half

You watch the Suns, and you feel like Bob Wiley following the guidance of Dr. Leo Marvin. Baby steps. Baby steps. If this team is going to get better, they have to start taking baby steps. And on Monday night against the Golden State Warriors, it felt like some of those steps were finally being taken.

After all, the Suns got off to their best start of the season, building a 17-point lead in the first half. It was easily the most impressive opening stretch we've seen from this team thus far. But as we've learned through the early portion of the season, Phoenix still has plenty of work to do. Nothing comes easy for this group. Everything has to be earned.

If they want to earn another victory this season, they're going to have to clean up multiple aspects of their game. One thing we've been waiting to see is whether this team can actually close out a basketball game. On Monday night, that question remained unanswered. They simply couldn't close.

Down one point with two minutes remaining, Devin Booker missed a wide-open 12-footer. On the next possession, Booker turned the ball over. The possession after that? A turnover by Jalen Green. And then, to complete the sequence, Booker was called for an offensive foul.

Was it a flop? Probably. When you have no room for error, it ultimately doesn't matter. What does matter is execution, and that continues to evade this team, particularly when it matters most. They've yet to put together a complete game, and every time it feels like they're ready to take a full stride forward, they stumble.

Those baby steps were certainly present on Monday night. At times, the defense looked locked in. At times, the offensive sets were functioning the way they're supposed to. There were stretches when you could see what this team is trying to become. But in the NBA, when you have a roster that feels like it's fighting against itself because of how poorly it's constructed, when you can't consistently rebound the basketball or prevent opposing teams from generating extra possessions seemingly at will, baby steps might be all you're capable of taking.

Perhaps that's the most frustrating part of watching this team right now. You can see the progress, recognize the improvements, and appreciate the effort, but none of it matters much when the same mistakes continue costing you games. The Suns are learning how to compete, yet they haven't figured out how to win. And while Dr. Marvin might applaud the baby steps, the NBA standings certainly won't. At some point, Phoenix has to learn how to walk.

Collin Gillespie's double-double off the bench, where he went for 16 points and 10 assists, earned him his first Bright Side Baller of the season. 52% of the vote went his way, with Miles Bridges (38%) and Dillon Brooks (5%) getting some love as well.

#3027. Hagerty: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Hagerty's claims team grew 40%, and its member service staff now handles 2,800 policies per employee, a productivity gain that bears on long-term loss control.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 3, 2026, Hagerty (HGTY +7.17%) raised its full-year earnings guidance after generating $257 million in adjusted EBITDA, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, through the first nine months of the year. The specialty insurer added 402,000 new members while scaling its high-margin distribution partnerships and auction platform. Three things management said stand out.

Gen X, Millennials, and Gen Z account for the majority of new-quote volume as younger buyers collect post-1980s vehicles. This demographic shift expands the addressable market beyond older collectors of classic automobiles.

Growing the internal claims team by 40% helped reduce physical damage costs and liability claims below expected levels. Specialty underwriting and proactive storm warnings keep loss ratios more stable than standard auto insurers.

Partnerships with large carriers and 54,000 independent agents deliver a steady stream of new business. The rollout with State Farm alone includes converting 525,000 existing classic-car policies to Hagerty-backed coverage.

Workflow automation and scaled distribution are strengthening the company's competitive advantage while driving operational efficiency. Management is maintaining pricing discipline and leveraging its partner network to capture market share.

Long-term value creation rests on converting auction attendees and car enthusiasts into multi-year policyholders across an underpenetrated vehicle market.

#3025. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3024. 3 Key Takeaways From Upstart's Latest Report

Investors shrugged off Upstart's earnings, but the stock could be a big winner in 2027.

Upstart (UPST +0.28%) came into Tuesday's third-quarter earnings report, trading around a two-year low.

While the company has delivered solid growth on the top and bottom lines in recent quarters, investors have been skeptical of the loan origination specialist's ability to deliver strong results in a challenging macroeconomic environment as interest rates are elevated, inflation remains sticky, and the cost of living keeps going up.

Revenue jumped 34% in the quarter to $371 million, ahead of estimates at $363.7 million, and earnings per share rose from $0.23 to $0.33, beating expectations at $0.23.

However, originations growth has slowed to be flat sequentially, and the company raised guidance slightly for the full year for revenue from fees but lowered it on adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), due to pressure on the balance sheet from the macro climate.

Investors essentially shrugged off the results, as the stock was up around 2% in afternoon trading. While the report didn't spark a big reaction from investors, it did signal progress for the company in a number of ways. Here are three takeaways from Upstart's Q3.

Most of Upstart's business still comes from unsecured personal loans, but its secured loan business in home and auto loans is growing much faster, and it represents a much larger market, in the trillions of dollars in loans in aggregate.

For the first time in the third quarter, its secured loan business was profitable with a contribution margin of 17%.

Originations in the secured segment nearly tripled to $587 million, but Upstart CEO Paul Gu, in an interview with The Motley Fool, said, "We've been almost exclusively focused on profitability as the goal for the secured products before we're turning our attention to growth," meaning the company could accelerate top-line growth in the secured category now that it has flipped to a contribution profit.

Upstart's core objectives come down to screening applicants for credit-worthiness as accurately as possible and marketing its product to bring in new customers and grow the business.

Gu credited improvements in technology and marketing for driving contribution profit up 48% to $218 million. Contribution profit is the metric the company uses as its "north star," and it strips out much of the noise in its financial reports. Contribution profit at Upstart is made up of revenue from fees minus costs from acquiring and servicing borrowers, and 48% growth in that category shows the company is executing its strategy effectively.

Acknowledging the macro headwinds facing the company, "I'm just so much more confident in the long term of the business, and that's because ultimately the macro kind of comes and goes, but these technology and marketing wins that stack, that we're making the rate at which we're delivering them, those things are durable."

On a price-to-sales basis, Upstart stock now trades at a multiple of 1.5, making it the cheapest it has ever been, with the brief exception at the end of 2022.

Back then, Upstart's revenue was tumbling as interest rates rose and the business was in disarray. These days, the company is in a much different position, with revenue and profits growing steadily, despite interest rates remaining high and the Upstart Macro Index, which is at a similar level to where it was then, indicating an elevated default risk.

Upstart may have to deliver a few more quarters of this kind of contribution profit growth to give the stock a boost, but shares have a lot of upside potential over the long term, especially if the headwinds in the macro environment ease,

Jeremy Bowman has positions in Upstart. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Upstart. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3013. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

#3004. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#2998. Cowboys rookie report: Caleb Downs, Malachi Lawrence hurt

Dallas had another win within reach, but a fourth-quarter embarrassment ended in a 33–30 overtime loss to Arizona. For the rookie class, LT Overton supplied a takeaway, Malachi Lawrence generated some pressure, and Caleb Downs' afternoon ended early with a concussion.

But here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that.

(55 defensive snaps | 4 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 QB hits | 0 pressures)

Downs offered some resistance against the run and was credited with two run stops, one extremely impressive one on fourth down on the goal line. His coverage was less encouraging with all three targets against him completed for 49 yards.

His day then ended after he suffered a concussion attempting to tackle Tyler Allgeier on the running back's fourth-quarter touchdown reception. There were useful contributions near the line, but too much production allowed through the air.

(40 defensive snaps | 0 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 1 QB hit | 2 pressures)

Lawrence's pass rush provided more than his empty tackle column suggests. He produced two pressures on 24 pass-rush snaps and registered a quarterback hit, although he could not turn those opportunities into a sack.

Across 40 defensive snaps, Dallas needed more finishing production from its first-round edge defender, especially when it mattered most in the closing portion of the game. He injured his ankle in the game and could miss some time.

(16 defensive snaps | 1 tackle | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 QB hits )

Barham had a limited role behind Shemar James and DeMarvion Overshown. His coverage results were modestly encouraging allowing one reception for six yards on two targets. However, one tackle and no plays behind the line made this another quiet outing. His small workload limits how much can be concluded about the performance.

(39 total snaps | 0 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 QB hits | 1 pressure | 1 fumble recovery)

Overton delivered the rookie group's clearest positive when he recovered Bam Knight's fumble after Overshown forced the ball loose late in the second quarter. Securing that possession mattered. His work elsewhere was quieter, with one pressure on 19 pass-rush snaps and no tackles or sacks. The recovery was valuable, but Dallas still needs more consistent disruption from his defensive opportunities.

(10 ST snaps | 0 targets | 0 receptions | 0 receiving yards | 0 TD)

Brown's involvement remained almost entirely on special teams. With just one offensive snap and no targets, there was no meaningful receiving performance to evaluate. Staying involved on game day is a step forward, but his offensive opportunity remains extremely limited.

#2992. Federal Reserve Board requests public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 2:30 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955.
